en: Knowledge is declared to be fivefold, namely: sensory knowledge (ābhinibodhika-jñāna), scriptural knowledge (śruta-jñāna), clairvoyant knowledge (avadhi-jñāna), mind-reading knowledge (manaḥparyaya-jñāna), and omniscience (kevala-jñāna).

Among these, four types of knowledge are set aside and established [as not to be taught]; they are not recited, not fully recited, and not authorized for instruction. However, regarding scriptural knowledge, recitation, full recitation, authorization, and formal exposition proceed.

The Bodhisattva’s Ten Grounds 1. The Ground of Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*) 2. The Ground of Purity (*Vimalā-bhūmi*) 3. The Ground of Radiance (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*) 4. The Ground of Flaming Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*) 5. The Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*) 6. The Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*) 7. The Ground of Far-Going (*Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*) 8. The Ground of Immovability (*Acalā-bhūmi*) 9. The Ground of Good Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*) 10. The Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*)

If the recitation (*uddesa*), detailed recitation (*samuddesa*), authorization (*aṇunnā*), and exposition (*anuoga*) of scriptural knowledge (*suyanāṇa*) proceed, does the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and exposition proceed for that which is included within the *aṅgas* (*aṅgapaviṭṭha*), or does the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and exposition proceed for that which is outside the *aṅgas* (*aṅgabāhira*)? [Answer: The recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and exposition proceed for that which is included within the *aṅgas*, and the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and exposition also proceed for that which is outside the *aṅgas*. However, with reference to this specific formal commencement (*paṭṭhavaṇa*), the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and exposition proceed for that which is outside the *aṅgas*.
— End of Document —

If the recitation (*uddesa*), detailed recitation (*samuddesa*), authorization (*aṇunnā*), and formal instruction (*anuoga*) proceed for the *aṅgabāhira* (texts outside the canonical limbs), then do the recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and formal instruction proceed for the *kāliya* (texts of the present era) as well? Or do they proceed for the *ukkāliya* (texts of the past era)? They proceed for the *kāliya*—recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and formal instruction—and they also proceed for the *ukkāliya*—recitation, detailed recitation, authorization, and formal instruction. However, with respect to this specific commencement (*paṭṭhavaṇa*), the recitation up to the formal instruction proceeds for the *ukkāliya*.

If the recitation (*uddesa*), up to the exposition (*anuyoga*), of the *utkālika* texts proceeds, does the recitation, up to the exposition, of the *āvaśyaka* proceed? Or does the recitation, up to the exposition, of that which is distinct from the *āvaśyaka* proceed? [The answer is: The recitation, up to the exposition, of the *āvaśyaka* proceeds, and the recitation, up to the exposition, of that which is distinct from the *āvaśyaka* also proceeds. However, with reference to this specific commencement (*paṭṭhavaṇa*), it is the exposition of the *āvaśyaka*.

If the *anuyoga* of the *Āvaśyaka* is the *Āvaśyaka* itself, is it a single *aṅga*, multiple *aṅgas*, a *śrutaskandha*, multiple *śrutaskandhas*, a chapter (*adhyayana*), multiple chapters, a section (*uddeśa*), or multiple sections? The *Āvaśyaka* is not a single *aṅga*, nor multiple *aṅgas*; it is not a *śrutaskandha*, nor multiple *śrutaskandhas*; it is not a chapter, nor multiple chapters; it is not a section, nor multiple sections.
Therefore, I shall set aside the *āvaśyaka*, I shall set aside the *śruta*, I shall set aside the *khaṇḍa*, and I shall set aside the *adhyayana*.
And wherever one should know [a section], one should set it aside completely.

And even where one does not know [the specific details], one should deposit [the requisites] there at a crossroads. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 8) What is that *āvaśyaka*? *Āvaśyaka* is declared to be fourfold; namely: *nāmāvaśyaka*, *sthāpanāvaśyaka*, *dravyāvaśyaka*, and *bhāvāvaśyaka*.

What is the essential rite by name (*nāmāvassaya*)? The essential rite by name is that for which the name "essential rite" (*āvassaya*) is applied to a single soul or a non-soul, to many souls or many non-souls, or to both [soul and non-soul] or to both [many souls and many non-souls]. That is the essential rite by name.

What is that? It is the formal rite of the necessary (*ṭhavaṇāvassaya*). The formal rite of the necessary is: when, whether in woodwork, bookwork, painting, plasterwork, or in objects made by knotting, weaving, stuffing, or joining; or in dice, or in cowrie shells; whether one or many; whether by way of a representation of reality (*sabbhāva-ṭhavaṇā*) or a representation of unreality (*asabbhāva-ṭhavaṇā*), the designation "the necessary" (*āvassaya*) is established—that is the formal rite of the necessary.
What is the distinction between name (nāma) and designation (ṭhavaṇā)? Name is lifelong; designation may be temporary or lifelong.

What is that which is the substance-essential-duty (davvāvassaya)? Substance-essential-duty is declared to be twofold: from the perspective of scripture (āgama) and from the perspective of non-scripture (nōāgama).
—End of Text—

What is the *āgama* (scriptural) substance-essential duty (*davvāvassaya*)? The scriptural substance-essential duty is that for which the word "Āvassaya" has been studied, mastered, learned, measured, thoroughly mastered; which is identical in name, identical in sound, with no missing syllables, no extra syllables, no omitted syllables, unerring, not muddled, not slurred, complete, with a complete sound, uttered from the throat and lips, and received through the oral instruction of a teacher. Yet, in that regard, it pertains to recitation, questioning, review, and religious discourse, but not to reflection. Why? Because it is said, "Non-engagement [in the true sense] is substance."
—End of Text—

According to the Naigama [naya], if one person is engaged in [the ritual], there is one substance-essential (dravyāvaśyaka) from the perspective of scripture; if two are engaged, there are two substance-essentials from the perspective of scripture; if three are engaged, there are three substance-essentials from the perspective of scripture. Thus, as many as are engaged, so many are those substance-essentials for the Naigama according to scripture. It is exactly the same for the Vyavahāra [naya]. According to the Saṅgraha [naya], whether one or many are engaged, or whether it is a single engagement or multiple engagements, from the perspective of scripture it is either a single substance-essential or substance-essentials; however, for that [naya], it is a single substance-essential. According to the Ṛjusūtra [naya], if one person is engaged, there is one substance-essential from the perspective of scripture; it does not accept plurality. For the three Śabda-nayas, the knower who is engaged is not a real entity (avastu). Why? Because if he is engaged, he is not a knower; if he is a knower, he is not engaged. Therefore, there is no substance-essential from the perspective of scripture. This is the substance-essential according to scripture.

What then is non-scriptural (nōāgama) substance-essential-duty (davvāvassaya)? Non-scriptural substance-essential-duty is declared to be threefold: substance-essential-duty as the body of the knower (jāṇagasarīra-davvāvassaya), substance-essential-duty as the body of the potential being (bhaviyasarīra-davvāvassaya), and substance-essential-duty distinct from both the body of the knower and the body of the potential being (jāṇagasarīra-bhaviyasarīravattiritta-davvāvassaya).

What is the substance-essential activity (*davvāvassaya*) of the knowing body (*jāṇagasarīra*)? The substance-essential activity of the knowing body is as follows: having seen the body of one who knows the meaning of the word "essential activity" (*āvassaya*), which is free from death, cast off, discarded, and abandoned by the soul—whether it be on a bed, on a mat, in a place of rest (*nisīhiyā*), or on the surface of the Siddha-stone—someone might say: "Aha! By means of this aggregate of a body, through a state perceived by the Jina, the word 'essential activity' was proclaimed, expounded, demonstrated, shown, pointed out, and illustrated. What is the illustration? "This was once a pot of honey; this was once a pot of ghee. That is the substance-essential activity of the knowing body.

What is the *bhaviyasarīra-davvāvassaya* (the substance-essential activity of the destined body)? The *bhaviyasarīra-davvāvassaya* refers to those living beings who have emerged from the birth-womb and, with this very same collection of bodily constituents, will at a future time learn the word "Āvassaya" through the disposition taught by the Jina, though they do not yet learn it. What is the illustration? "This one will become a jar of honey; this one will become a jar of ghee. That is the *bhaviyasarīra-davvāvassaya*.

What is that which is the substance-essential (dravyāvaśyaka) distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the one destined to become [a knower]? The substance-essential distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the one destined to become [a knower] is declared to be threefold; namely: worldly (laukika), pertaining to false doctrines (kuprāvacanika), and supramundane (lokottarika).

What, then, is the worldly substance-essential duty (*laukika-dravyāvaśyaka*)? Worldly substance-essential duty is as follows: those such as kings, lords, provincial governors, district officials, householders, wealthy merchants, guild-leaders, army commanders, and caravan leaders, at dawn when the night has passed and the pure morning has arrived; when the light has become pale-white like the opening petals of full-blown blue and red lotuses; when the sun, the thousand-rayed maker of day, has risen, blazing with splendor like the red *aśoka* flower, the *kiṃśuka*, the parrot’s beak, or the guñjā berry; and when it awakens the clusters of lotuses in the ponds—they perform the substance-essential duties consisting of washing the face, cleansing the teeth, oiling the head, applying mustard seeds, green herbs, eye-salve, incense, flowers, garlands, perfumes, betel, and clothing. Thereafter, they go to the royal palace, a temple, a grove, a park, an assembly hall, or a pavilion. This is the worldly substance-essential duty.
— End of Text —

What, then, is the material essential duty (*davvāvassaya*) of those with false doctrines (*kuppāvayaṇiya*)? The material essential duty of those with false doctrines refers to these: the Carakas, Cīrikas, Carmakhaṇḍikas, Bhikkhuṇḍas, Paṇḍuraṅgas, Goyamas, Govvaiyas, Gihidhammas, Dhammacintagas, Aviruddhas, Viruddhas, Vuddhasāvagas, and others of similar kind—these followers of heretical sects who, at the break of dawn when the night has passed and the sun is blazing with its radiance, perform the material essential duties consisting of the smearing, sweeping, sprinkling, incense, flowers, perfumes, garlands, and so forth, for Indra, Skanda, Rudra, Śiva, Vaiśramaṇa, a god, a Nāga, a Yakṣa, a Bhūta, a Muguṇḍa, an Āryā, a Durgā, or a Koṭṭakiriyā. This is the material essential duty of those with false doctrines.
— End of Text —

What is that supramundane substance-essential (lōguttariyaṁ davvāvassayaṁ)? It refers to those who have abandoned the application of ascetic virtues, who lack compassion for the six classes of living beings, who are like unbridled horses or unrestrained elephants—scraped, polished, with oiled lips, and clad in white robes—who, having wandered according to their own will outside the command of the Jinas, present themselves for the essential rite (āvassaya) at both times; this is that supramundane substance-essential. This is that substance-essential pertaining to the bodies of the knower and the future being. This is that substance-essential from the perspective of non-scriptural authority (nōāgama). This is that substance-essential.

What is that which is the essential duty of internal disposition (*bhāvāvassaya*)? The essential duty of internal disposition is declared to be twofold: that which is according to scripture (*āgama*) and that which is not according to scripture (*no-āgama*).

What is that which is the essential duty (*āvaśyaka*) from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*)? The essential duty from the perspective of scripture is: one who knows [the scriptures] and is engaged [in them]. That is the essential duty from the perspective of scripture.

What is that which is the essential duty from the perspective of non-scripture (*no-āgama*)? The essential duty from the perspective of non-scripture is declared to be threefold, namely: worldly (*laukika*), pertaining to false doctrines (*kupravacanīya*), and supramundane (*lokottara*).
What is that worldly essential duty (*lōiya-bhāvāvassaya*)? Worldly essential duty is: in the forenoon, the *Bhārata*; in the afternoon, the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
That is the worldly essential duty.

What is that which is the essential practice of the nature belonging to false doctrines (*kuppāvayaṇiyaṃ bhāvāvassayaṃ*)? The essential practice of the nature belonging to false doctrines is as follows: those wandering mendicants, bark-clad ascetics, and so forth, up to those belonging to heretical sects, who perform these essential practices of the nature such as the *ijjañjali*, *homa*, *japa*, *udurukka*, and *namokkāra*—that is the essential practice of the nature belonging to false doctrines.

What is that which is the transcendent essential practice of the spirit (*lōguttariyaṃ bhāvāvassayaṃ*)? The transcendent essential practice of the spirit is this: when a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman—with their mind fixed on that, their thought directed toward that, their inclination set on that, their resolve established in that, their purpose devoted to that, their affection centered on that, and their being permeated by the cultivation of that—performing the essential practice at both times of day without directing their mind elsewhere, that is the transcendent essential practice of the spirit. That is the essential practice of the spirit from the perspective of non-scriptural knowledge (*nōāgamaō*). That is the essential practice of the spirit.
For him,
there are these synonymous designations with various sounds and various syllables.
The *āvaśyaka*, the necessary duties, constant restraint, purification,
the group of six chapters (*adhyayana*), knowledge, right conduct, and the path. — Aṇuogaddārāim 30.
Since it must necessarily be performed by both the ascetic and the lay follower within each day and night,
it is therefore called "essential" (āvassaya). — Aṇuogaddārāim 31.
That is the *āvaśyaka*.
What then is the *śruta* (scriptural knowledge)? *Śruta* is declared to be fourfold: *nāma-śruta*, *sthāpanā-śruta*, *dravya-śruta*, and *bhāva-śruta*.

What is that which is called "scripture by name" (*nāmaśruta*)? Scripture by name is that for which the designation "scripture" is applied to a single soul (*jīva*), or a non-soul (*ajīva*), or many souls, or many non-souls, or both [soul and non-soul], or both [many souls and many non-souls]. That is scripture by name.

What is that which is scriptural representation (*ṭhavaṇāsuya*)? Scriptural representation is that which—in woodwork, painting, textile work, plasterwork, or in knotted objects, woven objects, stuffed objects, or composite objects, or in dice, or in cowrie shells—whether one or many, whether as a representation of reality (*sabbhāva-ṭhavaṇā*) or as a representation of unreality (*asabbhāva-ṭhavaṇā*), is established as "scripture" (*suya*). That is scriptural representation. What is the distinction between name (*nāma*) and representation (*ṭhavaṇā*)? A name (*nāma*) is lifelong; a representation (*ṭhavaṇā*) may be temporary or it may be lifelong.

What is that which is scriptural knowledge as substance (*dravya-śruta*)? Scriptural knowledge as substance is declared to be twofold: that which is through the *āgama* (the authoritative scripture) and that which is not through the *āgama*.

What is scriptural knowledge as substance (*āgamao davvasuyaṃ*)? Scriptural knowledge as substance is that for which the word "scripture" (*suya*) has been studied, mastered, learned, measured, and fully internalized, yet not [fully realized] through contemplation. Why? Because it is called "substance" due to the lack of actual application (*anuvōga*). According to the *Naigama* standpoint, when one person is engaged [in study], that is one instance of scriptural knowledge as substance. Why? Because if the knower were actually engaged [in realization], it would not be [mere] substance. That is scriptural knowledge as substance according to scripture.

What, then, is scriptural knowledge as non-scriptural substance (*nōāgamaō davvasuyaṃ*)? Scriptural knowledge as non-scriptural substance is declared to be threefold, namely: scriptural knowledge as the substance of the body of the knower (*jāṇagasarīradavvasuyaṃ*), scriptural knowledge as the substance of the body of the potential being (*bhaviyasarīradavvasuyaṃ*), and scriptural knowledge as the substance distinct from both the body of the knower and the body of the potential being (*jāṇagasarīra-bhaviyasarīra-vatirittaṃ davvasuyaṃ*).

What is that which is scriptural knowledge as substance pertaining to the body of the knower (*jñāyaka-śarīra-dravya-śruta*)? Scriptural knowledge as substance pertaining to the body of the knower—regarding the term "scriptural knowledge" (*sūtra*), it refers to the very body of the knower who has mastered the subject matter (*padārtha-adhikāra*), which is devoid of, departed from, fallen away from, and relinquished of [the current] physical existence; this should be described exactly as previously stated, up until: "that is scriptural knowledge as substance pertaining to the body of the knower."

What is that which is scriptural knowledge as a substance belonging to the body of one destined for liberation (bhaviyasarīradavvasuya)? Scriptural knowledge as a substance belonging to the body of one destined for liberation refers to those living beings who have emerged from the womb and birth; it should be described in the same manner as [the section on] substance-essential-activity (davvāvassaya), up until: "that is scriptural knowledge as a substance belonging to the body of one destined for liberation."

What is that which is scriptural knowledge as substance (*dravya-śruta*) distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the potential knower? Scriptural knowledge as substance distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the potential knower consists of what is written on palm leaves (*pattaya*) or in books (*poṭṭhaya*). Alternatively, scriptural knowledge as substance distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the potential knower is declared to be fivefold, namely: egg-born (*aṇḍaya*), cotton-born (*boṇḍaya*), insect-born (*kīḍaya*), hair-born (*vālaya*), and bark-born (*vāgaya*). What is that which is egg-born? Egg-born refers to the down of swans and the like; that is egg-born. What is that which is cotton-born? Cotton-born refers to cotton and the like; that is cotton-born. What is that which is insect-born? Insect-born is declared to be fivefold, namely: silk cloth (*paṭṭa*), Malaya cloth (*malaē*), fine cloth (*aṃsuē*), Chinese silk (*cīṇaṃsuē*), and red-dyed cloth (*kimirāga*); that is insect-born. What is that which is hair-born? Hair-born is declared to be fivefold, namely: woolen cloth (*uṇṇiē*), camel-hair cloth (*uṭṭiē*), deer-hair cloth (*miyalōmiē*), goat-hair cloth (*kutava*), and hair-cloth made of various fibers (*kiṭṭisa*); that is hair-born. What is that which is bark-born? Bark-born refers to hemp cloth (*saṇa*) and the like; that is bark-born. That is scriptural knowledge as substance distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the potential knower. That is non-scriptural knowledge as substance (*noāgamao davvasuyaṃ*); that is scriptural knowledge as substance (*davvasuyaṃ*).
What, then, is scriptural knowledge (*bhāvaśruta*)? It is declared to be twofold, namely: that which consists of the scripture (*āgama*) and that which does not consist of the scripture (*noāgama*).

What is scriptural knowledge as a state (*bhāvaśruta*) from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*)? Scriptural knowledge as a state from the perspective of scripture is that which is possessed by one who knows [the scriptures] and is currently engaged in them; that is scriptural knowledge as a state from the perspective of scripture. What is scriptural knowledge as a state not from the perspective of scripture (*noāgama*)? Scriptural knowledge as a state not from the perspective of scripture is taught to be of two kinds, namely: worldly (*laukika*) and transcendental (*lokottara*).

What is that which is worldly scriptural knowledge not derived from scripture (*lōiyaṃ nōāgamatō bhāvasuyaṃ*)? It is that which has been conceptualized by the ignorant and those with false views according to their own arbitrary intellect and thought, namely: the *Bhārata*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Bhīmāsurutta*, the *Kōḍillaya*, the *Ghōḍayamuha*, the *Sagaḍabhadriyā*, the *Kappāsiya*, the *Nāgasuhuma*, the *Kanagasattarī*, the *Vēsiya*, the *Vaïsēsiya*, the *Buddhavayaṇa*, the *Kāvila*, the *Lōgāyata*, the *Saṭṭhitanta*, the *Māḍhara*, the *Purāṇa*, the *Vāgaraṇa*, dramas and the like; or else, the seventy-two arts, the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (*saṅgōvaṅga*). This is that which is worldly scriptural knowledge not derived from scripture.
— End of Document —

What is the supramundane *bhāva-śruta* that is not derived from scripture (*nō-āgama*)? The supramundane *bhāva-śruta* that is not derived from scripture is that which was proclaimed by the Arhats, the Blessed Ones, who possess arisen knowledge and vision, who know the past, present, and future, who are omniscient and all-seeing, who are honored, revered, and worshipped throughout the three worlds, and who possess unimpeded, supreme knowledge and vision; it is the twelve-fold collection of the *Gaṇipiṭaka*, namely: the *Āyāra*, the *Sūyagaḍa*, the *Ṭhāṇa*, the *Samavāya*, the *Vivāhapannattī*, the *Nāyādhammakahā*, the *Uvāsagadasā*, the *Antagaḍadasā*, the *Anuttarōvavāiyadasā*, the *Paṇhāvāgaraṇāiṃ*, the *Vivāgasuya*, and the *Diṭṭhivāya*. This is the supramundane *bhāva-śruta* that is not derived from scripture. This is *bhāva-śruta* that is not derived from scripture. This is *bhāva-śruta*.
For him,
there are these synonymous designations, expressed through various etymologies and various phonetic variations.
*Suya*, *sutta*, *gantha*, *siddhanta*, *sāsana*, *āṇā*, *vayaṇa*, *uvaēsa*, *pannavaṇā*, and *āgama* are synonyms for *sūtra*. —
Aṇuogaddārāim 48.
That is what is heard.

What is that which is called "aggregates" (khandha)? Aggregates are declared to be fourfold: name-aggregate (nāma-khandha), designation-aggregate (ṭhavaṇā-khandha), substance-aggregate (davva-khandha), and state-aggregate (bhāva-khandha).
What, then, is the aggregate of names (nāmakhandha)? Regarding the aggregate of names, the designations (nāmaṭṭhavaṇā) should be stated according to the sequence previously mentioned.

What is that which constitutes a substance-aggregate (*davvakhaṇḍha*)? A substance-aggregate is declared to be of two kinds, namely: from the perspective of scripture (*āgamao*) and not from the perspective of scripture (*nōāgamao*). What is a substance-aggregate from the perspective of scripture? A substance-aggregate from the perspective of scripture refers to one for whom the word "aggregate" (*khaṇḍha*) has been studied; the rest is to be recited as in the case of the "substance-entrustment" (*davvāvassaya*), with the only difference being the substitution of the term "aggregate" (*khaṇḍha*), continuing up to: "What is a substance-aggregate distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future-being? A substance-aggregate distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future-being is declared to be of three kinds, namely: sentient (*sacitta*), insentient (*acitta*), and mixed (*mīsa*).

What, then, are animate material aggregates? Animate material aggregates are declared to be of many kinds, namely: the back of a horse, the back of an elephant, the back of a *kinnara*, the back of a *kimpurisa*, the back of a great serpent (*mahoraga*), the back of a *gandharva*, and the back of a bull. These are the animate material aggregates.

What is that which constitutes non-conscious matter-aggregates (*acitta-davvakhandha*)? Non-conscious matter-aggregates are declared to be of many kinds, namely: aggregates consisting of two parts (*dupaesiya*), aggregates consisting of three parts (*tipaesiya*), up to aggregates consisting of ten parts (*dasapaesiya*), aggregates consisting of numerable parts (*saṅkhejjapaesiya*), aggregates consisting of innumerable parts (*asaṅkhejjapaesiya*), and aggregates consisting of infinite parts (*aṇantapaesiya*). This is what constitutes non-conscious matter-aggregates.

What is that which is a mixed substance-aggregate (*mīsaē davvakhandhē*)? A mixed substance-aggregate is taught to be of many kinds, namely: the front part of an army, the middle part of an army, and the rear part of an army. This is that which is a mixed substance-aggregate.

Alternatively, the substance-aggregate distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future being (*jāṇagasarīra-bhaviyasarīra-vattirittē davvakhandhē*) is taught to be of three kinds, namely: the whole aggregate (*kasiṇakhandhē*), the partial aggregate (*akasiṇakhandhē*), and the aggregate of manifold substances (*anēgadaviyakhandhē*).

What, then, are the total-body forms (*kasiṇakhandhā*)? The total-body forms are: the body of a horse, the body of an elephant, [the body of a *kinnara*, the body of a *kimpurisa*, the body of a *mahoraga*], the body of a *gandharva*, and the body of a bull. These are the total-body forms.

What, then, are non-whole aggregates (*akasiṇakkhandha*)? Non-whole aggregates are: the two-part aggregate, the three-part aggregate, [up to] the ten-part aggregate, the numerable-part aggregate, the innumerable-part aggregate, and the infinite-part aggregate. These are the non-whole aggregates.

What is that? It is the aggregate of multiple substances (*anēgadavvakkhandha*). Within that very [aggregate], one part is diminished while another part is increased; that is the aggregate of multiple substances. That is the substance-aggregate existing apart from the body of the knower (*jñāyakaśarīra*) and the body of the being (*bhavyaśarīra*). That is the substance-aggregate by way of non-scriptural knowledge (*noāgama*). That is the substance-aggregate. What is that? It is the aggregate of states (*bhāvakkhandha*). The aggregate of states is declared to be of two kinds: by way of scriptural knowledge (*āgama*) and by way of non-scriptural knowledge (*noāgama*).

What, then, is the category of existence according to scripture (āgama)? The category of existence according to scripture consists of the knower who is engaged [in the process of knowing]; that is the category of existence according to scripture.

What, then, is the non-scriptural (noāgama) category of the substance-group (bhāvakhandha)? The non-scriptural category of the substance-group is that which is designated as the "substance-group" within the *Āvaśyaka* scriptural collection (*suyakhandha*), which is produced through the combination, assembly, and gathering of these very six chapters (*ajjhayaṇa*) beginning with *Sāmāyika*. That is the non-scriptural category of the substance-group; that is the substance-group.
Regarding this, there are synonyms (*nāmadhejja*) for it—having different sounds and different spellings—which are as follows:

A group (gaṇa), a category (kāya), a class (nikāya), a section (khaṇḍa), a division (varga), as well as a heap (rāśi), a cluster (puñja), a mass (piṇḍa), a collection (nigara), a combination (saṅghāta), a multitude (ākula), and an aggregate (samūha). — Aṇuogaddārāim 64.
That is the aggregate.
These are the subject-matters and topics of the *Āvaśyaka*:
namely—
Abstinence from blameworthy activity, praise [of the Tīrthaṅkaras], and the practice of the virtues [of the fivefold obeisance].

Reproving one who has committed a fault, treating the wound [of transgression], and indeed maintaining the virtues— this is the summary of the essential meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) of the *Āvaśyaka* taught in brief. (Aṇuogaddārā 67)
Furthermore, I shall explain each individual chapter (*ajjhayaṇa*). Aṇuogaddārā 68:

They are as follows—*sāmāiya*, *caüvīsatthaō*, *vandaṇayaṃ*, *paḍikkamaṇaṃ*, *kāussaggo*, and *paccakkhāṇaṃ*. Therein, the first chapter is *sāmāiya*; it has these four doors of analysis (*anuōgadārā*), namely: introduction (*uvakkamē*), exposition (*nikkhēvē*), following (*anugamē*), and investigation (*naē*).
— End of Text —

What is that? It is *upakrama* (approach/application). *Upakrama* is declared to be sixfold, namely: nominal *upakrama*, locational *upakrama*, substantial *upakrama*, spatial *upakrama*, temporal *upakrama*, and modal *upakrama*. Nominal and locational [upakramas] have already been explained. What is that substantial *upakrama*? It is declared to be twofold: through scripture (*āgama*) and non-scriptural (*no-āgama*). Regarding the non-scriptural, as far as [the categories of] the body of the knower and the body of the potential being, substantial *upakrama* is declared to be threefold: sentient, insentient, and mixed.

What is that which constitutes the *sacitta-dravyopakrama* (the physical approach involving living beings)? The *sacitta-dravyopakrama* is declared to be threefold, namely: [approach] toward bipeds, quadrupeds, and those without feet (*apada*). Each of these, moreover, is declared to be twofold: namely, preparatory treatment (*parikarma*) and the destruction of the object (*vastuvināśa*).

What is that which involves two-footed attendants? Two-footed attendants include: actors, dancers, wrestlers, boxers, fist-fighters, jesters, storytellers, bards, reciters, mimes, jugglers, puppeteers, minstrels, panegyrists, and Magadhan bards.
This is what is meant by two-footed attendants.
What is the four-footed service (*caüppayaüvakkamē*)? Four-footed service consists of horses, elephants, and so forth; that is four-footed service.
What is the footless service (*apayaüvakkamē*)? Footless service consists of mangoes, hog-plums, and so forth; that is footless service. That is animate material service (*saccittē davvōvakammē*).

What, then, is non-sentient material acquisition (acitta-davvōvakkama)? Non-sentient material acquisition consists of sugar-candy and the like, molasses and the like, and fish-roe and the like. This is non-sentient material acquisition.

What is that which is mixed material effort (*mīsaē davvōvakkamē*)? Mixed material effort is as follows: when one is mounted on a horse, adorned with a saddle, a mirror, and so forth. That is mixed material effort. That is material effort distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future being. That is material effort by way of non-scriptural knowledge (*nōāgamaō*). That is material effort.
What is the preparation of the field (*khettovakamma*)? The preparation of the field refers to when fields are prepared by means of plows, hoes, and so forth; that is the preparation of the field.

What is the preparation of time (*kālovakamma*)? The preparation of time refers to when the measurement of time is performed by means of water-clocks (*nāliya*) and so forth; that is the preparation of time.
— End of Section —

What is that? Disposition-based application (bhāvovakkama). Disposition-based application is declared to be of two kinds: namely, scriptural (āgamao) and non-scriptural (nōāgamao). What is that which is scriptural disposition-based application? Scriptural disposition-based application is one who possesses knowledge and is engaged [in it]. That is scriptural disposition-based application. What is that which is non-scriptural disposition-based application? Non-scriptural disposition-based application is declared to be of two kinds: namely, commendable (pasattha) and uncommendable (apasattha). What is that which is uncommendable disposition-based application? It is the procuress Gaṇikā [acting] for ministers and others; that is uncommendable disposition-based application. What is that which is commendable disposition-based application? Commendable disposition-based application is [the service] for teachers and others; that is commendable disposition-based application. That is non-scriptural disposition-based application; that is disposition-based application; that is application (uvakkama).

Alternatively, the sixfold method of exposition (*uvakkama*) is taught as follows: sequence (*ānupuvvī*), name (*nāma*), measure (*pamāṇa*), the subject matter (*vattavvayā*), the topical division (*atthāhigāra*), and inclusion (*samōyāra*).

What is that sequence (*ānupuvvī*)? Sequence is declared to be tenfold, namely: name-sequence (*nāmāṇupuvvī*), arrangement-sequence (*ṭhavaṇāṇupuvvī*), substance-sequence (*davvāṇupuvvī*), space-sequence (*khettāṇupuvvī*), time-sequence (*kālāṇupuvvī*), enumeration-sequence (*ukkittaṇāṇupuvvī*), calculation-sequence (*gaṇaṇāṇupuvvī*), shape-sequence (*saṇṭhāṇāṇupuvvī*), conduct-sequence (*sāmāyāriyāṇupuvvī*), and state-sequence (*bhāvāṇupuvvī*).
What is that name-sequence? Name and arrangement have already been explained.
What is that? Substantive sequential order (dravyānupūrvī). Substantive sequential order is taught to be of two kinds, namely: through scripture (āgamataḥ) and not through scripture (no-āgamataḥ).

What, then, is *dravyānupūrvī* from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*)? *Dravyānupūrvī* from the perspective of scripture is that for which the word "sequence" (*ānupūrvī*) has been studied, mastered, internalized, measured, and fully conquered, up to [the stage of] non-contemplation (*anuprekṣā*). Why? Because it is said that "non-activity (*anupayoga*) is substance (*dravya*). According to the *Naigama* [view], when one person is engaged in non-activity, there is one *dravyānupūrvī* from the perspective of scripture, and so on. Why? Because if the knower (*jñāyaka*) were not engaged in non-activity, it would not exist. That is *dravyānupūrvī* from the perspective of scripture. What, then, is *dravyānupūrvī* from the perspective of what is not scripture (*no-āgama*)? It is declared to be threefold: namely, *dravyānupūrvī* as the body of the knower (*jñāyakaśarīra*), *dravyānupūrvī* as the body of the future knower (*bhavyaśarīra*), and *dravyānupūrvī* apart from the bodies of the knower and the future knower. What, then, is *dravyānupūrvī* as the body of the knower? It is the body of one who knows the subject matter of the sequence, which is free from death, cast off, abandoned, and relinquished; the rest is to be explained just as in the case of *dravyāvaśyaka*, up to: that is *dravyānupūrvī* as the body of the knower.

What, then, is the substantial serial order of the destined body (*bhaviya-sarīra davvāṇupuvvī*)? It is as follows: those living beings who have emerged from the womb at birth; the rest is as described for the substantial necessary state (*davvāvassaya*), up until: that is the substantial serial order of the destined body.

What is that? What is substance-succession (dravyānupūrvī) as distinct from the bodies of the knower and the bodies of those destined to be knowers? Substance-succession as distinct from the bodies of the knower and the bodies of those destined to be knowers is declared to be twofold, namely: arranged (ovaṇihiyā) and unarranged (anōvaṇihiyā). Of these, that which is arranged is set aside; of these, that which is unarranged is declared to be twofold, namely: according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints] and according to the Saṅgraha [standpoint].

What is that? The non-sequential substance-anupūrvī according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints]. The non-sequential substance-anupūrvī according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra is declared to be fivefold, namely: the exposition of the eight positions (*aṣṭapadaprarūpaṇatā*), the enumeration of the permutations (*bhaṅgasamutkīrtanatā*), the demonstration of the permutations (*bhaṅgopadarśanatā*), the application (*samoyāra*), and the investigation (*anugama*).

What, then, is the exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama-Vyavahāra [standpoints]? The exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama-Vyavahāra is as follows: a triad (three-partite) is a sequential entity (ānupūrvī); a tetrad (four-partite) is a sequential entity; and so on up to a decad (ten-partite) is a sequential entity; a numerable-partite is a sequential entity; an innumerable-partite is a sequential entity; and an infinite-partite is a sequential entity. A single atom (paramāṇu-pudgala) is a non-sequential entity (anānupūrvī). A dyad (two-partite) is an indescribable entity (avaktavyaka). Multiple triads are sequential entities; multiple tetrads, and so on up to multiple infinite-partites, are sequential entities. Multiple atoms are non-sequential entities. Multiple dyads are indescribable entities. This is the exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama-Vyavahāra.

What is the purpose of this exposition of the eight points regarding the *negama* and *vyavahāra* [standpoints]? Through this exposition of the eight points regarding the *negama* and *vyavahāra* [standpoints], the enumeration of the logical permutations (*bhaṅga*) is accomplished.

What is the purpose of this exposition of the permutations according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra standpoints? By means of this exposition of the permutations according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra standpoints, the demonstration of the permutations is carried out.

The Bodhisattva’s Ten Grounds The first ground is named "The Joyous" (*Pramuditā*). It is so called because the Bodhisattva, having attained the path of seeing, experiences a vast and unprecedented joy through the realization of the nature of reality. The second ground is named "The Stainless" (*Vimalā*). It is so called because the Bodhisattva has purified the stains of the transgressions of body, speech, and mind, as well as the stains of the afflictions associated with the desire realm. The third ground is named "The Radiant" (*Prabhākārī*). It is so called because the Bodhisattva’s wisdom increases greatly, illuminating the meaning of the Dharma like the light of the sun. The fourth ground is named "The Flaming" (*Arciṣmatī*). It is so called because the Bodhisattva’s fire of wisdom blazes forth, burning away the fuel of the afflictions and the secondary afflictions. The fifth ground is named "The Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*). It is so called because it is extremely difficult to overcome the subtle afflictions and the conceptualizations of the two extremes. The sixth ground is named "The Manifest" (*Abhimukhī*). It is so called because the Bodhisattva is face-to-face with the profound dependent origination, which is the gateway to the emptiness of phenomena. The seventh ground is named "The Far-Reaching" (*Dūraṅgamā*). It is so called because the Bodhisattva travels far beyond the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, proceeding toward the ultimate goal. The eighth ground is named "The Immovable" (*Acalā*). It is so called because the Bodhisattva has attained mastery over the non-conceptual state and is no longer moved by the winds of effort or the dualistic perceptions of subject and object. The ninth ground is named "The Excellent Intelligence" (*Sādhumatī*). It is so called because the Bodhisattva possesses the supreme intelligence that skillfully distinguishes all aspects of the Dharma and teaches them to others. The tenth ground is named "The Cloud of Dharma" (*Dharmameghā*). It is so called because the Bodhisattva is like a great cloud, raining down the Dharma upon all sentient beings and covering the entire expanse of the Buddha-fields.

What, then, is the demonstration of the modes (*bhaṅgōvadaṁsaṇayā*) according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints]? The demonstration of the modes according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra is as follows: (1) A triad (*tipaēsiya*) is a sequential entity (*āṇupuvvī*); a monad (*paramāṇupōggala*) is a non-sequential entity (*aṇāṇupuvvī*); a dyad (*dupaēsiya*) is an indescribable entity (*avattavvaē*). Alternatively, (2) triads are sequential entities; monads are non-sequential entities; dyads are indescribable entities. Alternatively, (3) a triad and a monad are a sequential entity and a non-sequential entity respectively; this constitutes a fourfold permutation (*caübhaṅgō*). Alternatively, (4) a triad and a dyad are a sequential entity and an indescribable entity respectively; this constitutes a fourfold permutation. Alternatively, (5) a monad and a dyad are a non-sequential entity and an indescribable entity respectively; this constitutes a fourfold permutation. Alternatively, (6) a triad, a monad, and a dyad are a sequential entity, a non-sequential entity, and an indescribable entity respectively. Alternatively, (7) a triad, a monad, and two dyads are a sequential entity, a non-sequential entity, and two indescribable entities respectively. Alternatively, (8) a triad, monads, and a dyad are a sequential entity, non-sequential entities, and an indescribable entity respectively. Alternatively, (9) a triad, monads, and two dyads are a sequential entity, non-sequential entities, and two indescribable entities respectively. Alternatively, (10) three triads, a monad, and a dyad are sequential entities, a non-sequential entity, and an indescribable entity respectively. Alternatively, (11) three triads, monads, and two dyads are sequential entities, a non-sequential entity, and two indescribable entities respectively. Alternatively, (12) three triads, monads, and a dyad are sequential entities, non-sequential entities, and an indescribable entity respectively. Alternatively, (13) three triads, monads, and two dyads are sequential entities, non-sequential entities, and two indescribable entities respectively. This is the demonstration of the modes according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints].

What is that which is called "conjunction" (*samōyārē*)? Regarding the substances in sequential order (*āṇupuvvidavvāiṁ*) of the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints], with what do they conjoin? Do they conjoin with substances in sequential order, with substances not in sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvidavvēhiṁ*), or with substances that are indescribable (*avattavvayadavvēhiṁ*)? The substances in sequential order of the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints] conjoin with substances in sequential order; they do not conjoin with substances not in sequential order, nor do they conjoin with substances that are indescribable.

Regarding the non-successive substances (*anānupūrvī-dravya*) of the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints], with what do they coincide? Do they coincide with successive substances (*ānupūrvī-dravya*), with non-successive substances, or with indescribable substances (*avaktavyaka-dravya*)? For the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints], non-successive substances do not coincide with successive substances; they coincide with non-successive substances; they do not coincide with indescribable substances.

With what substances do the "indescribable" (avaktavyaka) substances of the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints] coincide? Do they coincide with substances that are sequential (ānupūrvī), with substances that are non-sequential (anānupūrvī), or with substances that are indescribable? The "indescribable" substances of the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints] do not coincide with sequential substances, nor do they coincide with non-sequential substances; they coincide with indescribable substances. This is "coincidence" (samoyāra).

What is that? It is the sequential exposition (*anugama*). The sequential exposition is declared to be of nine kinds, namely:— The exposition of the nature of the states (*santapayaparūvaṇayā*), the measure of substances (*davvapamāṇa*), the space occupied (*khētta*), and the contact (*phusaṇā*).
Time, interval, part, state, and relative magnitude.

(Aṇuogaddārā 91) According to the *negama* and *vyavahāra* [standpoints], do substances that possess sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) exist or not? They certainly exist. According to the *negama* and *vyavahāra* [standpoints], do substances that lack sequential order (*anānupūrvī*) exist or not? They certainly exist. According to the *negama* and *vyavahāra* [standpoints], do substances that are indescribable (*avaktavyaka*) exist or not? They certainly exist.

Regarding the substances of the sequential (āṇupuvvi) negamas and their transactions: are they numerable, innumerable, or infinite? They are not numerable, nor are they innumerable; they are infinite. In the same way, it should be stated that the non-sequential (aṇāṇupuvvi) substances and the indescribable (avattavvaga) substances are also infinite.

Regarding the substances of the negama-vyavahāra [standpoint] in their sequential order, in what portion of the universe would they exist—would they exist in a numerable part, an innumerable part, numerable parts, innumerable parts, or the entire universe? With respect to a single substance, it would exist in a numerable part of the universe, or it would exist in an innumerable part, or it would exist in numerable parts, or it would exist in innumerable parts, or it would exist in the entire universe. With respect to multiple substances, they would necessarily exist in the entire universe.

Regarding the substances that do not follow the serial order (*anānupūrvī*) of the transactions of the city-dwellers, how many parts of the world would they occupy? Would they occupy a numerable part of the world, or even the whole world? With respect to a single substance, it would not occupy a numerable part of the world; it would occupy an innumerable part of the world; it would not occupy numerable parts of the world; it would not occupy innumerable parts of the world; nor would it occupy the whole world. With respect to multiple substances, they would necessarily occupy the whole world. In this same manner, the substances that are "indescribable" (*avaktavyaka*) are to be explained.
