Regarding the substances of *negama-vavahāra* (the Naigama and Vyavahāra viewpoints) that follow the sequence of time (*āṇupuvvi-davvāiṃ*), how many parts of the world do they occupy? Do they occupy a numerable part, an innumerable part, numerable parts, innumerable parts, or the entire world? With respect to a single substance (*egadavvaṃ paḍucca*), they occupy either a numerable part of the world, or an innumerable part, or numerable parts, or innumerable parts, or the entire world. With respect to multiple substances (*nānādavvāiṃ paḍucca*), they necessarily occupy the entire world. Question regarding the non-sequential substances (*aṇāṇupuvvi-davvāṇaṃ*) of the *negama-vavahāra*: With respect to a single substance, they do not occupy a numerable part; they occupy an innumerable part; they do not occupy numerable parts; they do not occupy innumerable parts; nor do they occupy the entire world. With respect to multiple substances, they necessarily occupy the entire world. The same should be stated for the indeterminate substances (*avattavva-davvāṇi*).

Regarding the substances of the *anupūrvīs* (successive arrangements) of the *negama-vyavahāra* (the conventional mode of discourse): for how long do they exist in terms of time? With respect to a single substance (*ekadravya*), the minimum duration is one moment (*samaya*) and the maximum is an incalculable period of time (*asaṅkhyeya-kāla*). With respect to multiple substances (*nānādravya*), it is necessarily for all time (*sarvaddhā*). The same should be stated for the substances that are *anānupūrvīs* (non-successive) and the substances that are *avaktavyaka* (indescribable).

Regarding the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints], what is the duration of the interval (*antara*) between *ānupūrvī* substances in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, it is at least one moment (*samaya*) and at most an infinite (*ananta*) period of time; with respect to multiple substances, there is no interval. Regarding the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints], what is the duration of the interval between *anānupūrvī* substances in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, it is at least one moment and at most an innumerable (*asaṅkhyeya*) period of time; with respect to multiple substances, there is no interval. Regarding the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints], what is the duration of the interval between *avaktavyaka* substances in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, it is at least one moment and at most an infinite period of time; with respect to multiple substances, there is no interval.
— End of Section —

Regarding the substances that are *anānupūrvī* (non-successive) according to the *negama-vavahāra* [standpoints], what portion of the remaining substances do they constitute? Do they constitute a numerable part (*saṅkhejjaï-bhāga*), an innumerable part (*asaṅkhejjaï-bhāga*), numerable parts (*saṅkhejjēsu bhāgēsu*), or innumerable parts (*asaṅkhejjēsu bhāgēsu*)? They do not constitute a numerable part; they do not constitute an innumerable part; they do not constitute numerable parts; they necessarily constitute innumerable parts. Regarding the substances that are *avaktavyaka* (indescribable) according to the *negama-vavahāra* [standpoints], what portion of the remaining substances do they constitute? Do they constitute a numerable part, and so on, up to innumerable parts? They do not constitute a numerable part; they constitute an innumerable part; they do not constitute numerable parts; they do not constitute innumerable parts. The same should be stated for the *avaktavyaka* substances as well.

Regarding the substances of the sequential (āṇupuvvi) classes of worldly transactions: in which state (bhāva) do they exist—is it in the emergent state (udaïya), the subsidential state (uvasamiya), the destroyed state (khaïya), the subsided-destroyed state (khaōvasamiya), the transformational state (pāriṇāmiya), or the combined state (sannivāiya)? They necessarily exist in the beginningless transformational state (sāipāriṇāmiya). The non-sequential substances (aṇāṇupuvvi) and the indescribable substances (avattavvagadavva) should be explained in exactly the same way.
—End of Text—

"Venerable Sir, among these substances of the *negama-vavahāra* [standpoints]—namely, sequential substances (*āṇupuvvidavva*), non-sequential substances (*aṇāṇupuvvidavva*), and indescribable substances (*avattavvagadavva*)—which are fewer, which are more, which are equal, or which are specifically greater, when considered from the perspective of substance (*davvaṭṭhayā*), from the perspective of space-points (*paesaṭṭhayā*), or from the perspective of both substance and space-points (*davvaṭṭha-paesaṭṭhayā*)? "Gautama! From the perspective of substance: all the indescribable substances of the *negama-vavahāra* are the fewest; the non-sequential substances are specifically greater; and the sequential substances are infinitely greater. From the perspective of space-points: all the non-sequential substances of the *negama-vavahāra*, being devoid of space-points (*apaesaṭṭhayā*), are the fewest; the indescribable substances, possessing space-points, are specifically greater; and the sequential substances, possessing space-points, are infinitely greater. From the perspective of both substance and space-points: all the indescribable substances of the *negama-vavahāra*, considered as substance, are the fewest; the non-sequential substances, considered as substance and devoid of space-points, are specifically greater; the indescribable substances, considered as space-points, are specifically greater; the sequential substances, considered as substance, are infinitely greater; and those same [sequential substances], considered as space-points, are infinitely greater. This is the *anugama* (synopsis); this is the *negama-vavahāra* *anovaṇihiyā* (non-technical) *dravyānupūrvī*."

What then is the non-sequential enumeration of substances according to the method of grouping (*saṅgraha*)? The non-sequential enumeration of substances according to the method of grouping is declared to be fivefold, namely: the exposition of the eight categories (*aṭṭhapayaparūvaṇayā*), the enumeration of the possible permutations (*bhaṅgasamukkittaṇayā*), the demonstration of the permutations (*bhaṅgōvadaṁsaṇayā*), the application (*samōyārē*), and the investigation (*anugamē*).

What is that? It is the exposition of the eight categories according to the Saṅgraha (Compendium) standpoint. The exposition of the eight categories according to the Saṅgraha standpoint is as follows: the ascending series consisting of three parts; the ascending series consisting of four parts; the ascending series up to ten parts; the ascending series consisting of numerable parts; the ascending series consisting of innumerable parts; the ascending series consisting of infinite parts; the single atom as the non-ascending series; and the two-part aggregate as the indescribable. This is the exposition of the eight categories according to the Saṅgraha standpoint.

What is the purpose of this exposition of the eightfold statement regarding the category of *saṅgraha* (comprehension)? By means of this exposition of the eightfold statement regarding *saṅgraha*, the enumeration of its logical alternatives (*bhaṅga*) is performed. What, then, is this enumeration of the alternatives of *saṅgraha*? The enumeration of the alternatives of *saṅgraha* is as follows: there is succession (*āṇupuvvī*), there is non-succession (*aṇāṇupuvvī*), and there is the indescribable (*avattavvaē*). Or, there is both succession and non-succession; or, there is both succession and the indescribable; or, there is both non-succession and the indescribable; or, there is succession, non-succession, and the indescribable. Thus, these are the seven alternatives (*bhaṅga*). This is the enumeration of the alternatives of *saṅgraha*. What is the purpose of this enumeration of the alternatives of *saṅgraha*? By means of this enumeration of the alternatives of *saṅgraha*, the demonstration of the combinations of those alternatives (*bhaṅgōvandasaṇayā*) is performed.

The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a shallow pool with a clear bottom, where one can see the shells, pebbles, and gravel, and where fish dart about; such a person is seen by others as one who has entered the stream, crossed over, and reached the further shore. The person who is like a deep pool with a hidden bottom, where one cannot see the shells, pebbles, and gravel, nor where fish dart about; such a person is seen by others as one who has entered the stream, crossed over, and reached the further shore. The person who is like a deep pool with a hidden bottom, where one cannot see the shells, pebbles, and gravel, nor where fish dart about; such a person is seen by others as one who is a non-returner, having completely transcended the realm of sensual desire. The person who is like a deep pool with a hidden bottom, where one cannot see the shells, pebbles, and gravel, nor where fish dart about; such a person is seen by others as one who is an Arhat, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and departed for the forest. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and departed for the forest after saying: 'Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world... [as above] ...these, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, what is the meaning of this statement: 'The Blessed One has risen from his seat and departed for the forest after saying: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world... [as above] ...these, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world"? Friend, it is because the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma without making distinctions, having opened up the door to the Deathless, and having poured forth the rain of the Deathless, that when he rises from his seat and departs for the forest, he says: 'Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world... [as above] ...these, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed that monk: "Friend, do you understand the meaning of what the Blessed One said in brief, and how you have explained it? "I do not, friend. "In that case, friend, listen and pay close attention; I will speak. "Yes, friend," that monk replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: "Friend, the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma without making distinctions, having opened up the door to the Deathless, and having poured forth the rain of the Deathless, so that when he rises from his seat and departs for the forest, he says: 'Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world... [as above] ...these, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. And what, friend, is the meaning of this statement: 'The person who is like a shallow pool with a clear bottom... such a person is seen by others as one who has entered the stream, crossed over, and reached the further shore'? Here, friend, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: 'The Blessed One is an Arhat, a Fully Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, and blessed. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the Noble Ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. It is because of these four factors of stream-entry that the person who is like a shallow pool with a clear bottom is seen by others as one who has entered the stream, crossed over, and reached the further shore. And what, friend, is the meaning of this statement: 'The person who is like a deep pool with a hidden bottom... such a person is seen by others as one who has entered the stream, crossed over, and reached the further shore'? Here, friend, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...and he possesses the virtues dear to the Noble Ones... But he does not possess the higher wisdom of one beyond training regarding things previously unheard, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering. It is because of these four factors of stream-entry and the lack of this higher wisdom that the person who is like a deep pool with a hidden bottom is seen by others as one who has entered the stream, crossed over, and reached the further shore. And what, friend, is the meaning of this statement: 'The person who is like a deep pool with a hidden bottom... such a person is seen by others as one who is a non-returner, having completely transcended the realm of sensual desire'? Here, friend, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...and he possesses the virtues dear to the Noble Ones... Furthermore, he has abandoned the five lower fetters. It is because of these four factors of stream-entry, the lack of higher wisdom, and the abandonment of the five lower fetters that the person who is like a deep pool with a hidden bottom is seen by others as one who is a non-returner, having completely transcended the realm of sensual desire. And what, friend, is the meaning of this statement: 'The person who is like a deep pool with a hidden bottom... such a person is seen by others as one who is an Arhat, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge'? Here, friend, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...and he possesses the virtues dear to the Noble Ones... Furthermore, he has abandoned the five lower fetters and cultivated the five higher fetters. It is because of these four factors of stream-entry, the lack of higher wisdom, the abandonment of the five lower fetters, and the cultivation of the five higher fetters that the person who is like a deep pool with a hidden bottom is seen by others as one who is an Arhat, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. When this was said, that monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Magnificent, friend! Magnificent, friend! It is as if someone were to set upright what was overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Just so, friend Ānanda, the Dhamma has been made clear by the Venerable Ānanda in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, and I go for refuge to the Saṅgha. May the Venerable Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last."

What is that? It is the demonstration of the divisions of the category of inclusion (*saṅgaha*). As for the demonstration of the divisions of the category of inclusion: three-partite [substances] are "successive" (*āṇupuvvī*); a single atom (*paramāṇu-poggala*) is "non-successive" (*aṇāṇupuvvī*); and a two-partite [substance] is "inexpressible" (*avattavva*). Alternatively, three-partite substances and atoms are both "successive" and "non-successive. Alternatively, three-partite substances and two-partite substances are both "successive" and "inexpressible. Alternatively, atoms and two-partite substances are both "non-successive" and "inexpressible. Alternatively, three-partite substances, atoms, and two-partite substances are "successive," "non-successive," and "inexpressible. Thus, these are the seven divisions. This is the demonstration of the divisions of the category of inclusion.
—End of Text—

What is the inclusion (samōyārē) of the summary (saṅgaha)? Regarding the summary, where do the substances of sequential order (āṇupuvvidavvāiṁ) find their inclusion? Do they include with substances of sequential order, with substances of non-sequential order (aṇāṇupuvvidavvēhiṁ), or with substances that are indescribable (avattavvagadavvēhiṁ)? The substances of sequential order of the summary include with substances of sequential order; they do not include with substances of non-sequential order, nor do they include with substances that are indescribable. Thus, both [categories] include within their own respective places (saṭṭhāṇē). This is the inclusion.
What is that which follows? Following is declared to be of eight kinds, namely:—

There is no [comparison in terms of] the description of the types of heat, the quantity of substance, the space occupied, the contact, the duration, the interval, the parts, the states, or the relative magnitude. — Āvaśyakaniryukti 107.

Do the sequential substances (*ānupūrvī-dravya*) of the *saṅgraha* category exist or not? They certainly exist; thus it is for both [categories]. Are the sequential substances of the *saṅgraha* category numerable (*saṅkhyeya*), innumerable (*asaṅkhyeya*), or infinite (*ananta*)? They are neither numerable, nor innumerable, nor infinite; they are necessarily one heap (*rāśi*). Thus it is for both. In what portion of the universe (*loka*) do the sequential substances of the *saṅgraha* category reside? Do they reside in a numerable part, an innumerable part, numerable parts, innumerable parts, or the entire universe? They do not reside in a numerable part, nor in an innumerable part, nor in numerable parts, nor in innumerable parts; they necessarily reside in the entire universe. Thus it is for both. How many portions of the universe do the sequential substances of the *saṅgraha* category occupy? Do they occupy a numerable part, up to the entire universe? They do not occupy a numerable part, nor an innumerable part, nor numerable parts, nor an innumerable part; they necessarily occupy the entire universe. Thus it is for both.

Regarding the sequence of substances of the *saṅgraha* (the collective): in terms of time, how long do they last? They last for all time (*savvaddhā*). The same applies to both [the *anuyoga* and *vyatireka*]. Regarding the interval between the sequential substances of the *saṅgraha*: in terms of time, what is the interval? There is no interval. The same applies to both. Regarding the sequential substances of the *saṅgraha*, in what portion of the remaining substances would they exist—would they exist in a numerable part, or up to an innumerable part? They would not exist in a numerable part; they would not exist in an innumerable part; they would not exist in numerable parts; they would not exist in innumerable parts; they necessarily exist in a third part (*tibhāga*). The same applies to both. Regarding the sequential substances of the *saṅgraha*, in which state (*bhāva*) would they exist? They necessarily exist in the state that is beginningless and transformational (*sāipāriṇāmika*). The same applies to both. There is no comparison of "few or many" (*appābahu*). This is the *anugama* (examination). This is the non-enumerated substantial sequential order (*aṇovaṇihiyā davvāṇupuvvī*) of the *saṅgraha*. This is the non-enumerated substantial sequential order.

What then is the arranged sequence of substances (*ovaṇihiyā davvāṇupuvvī*)? The arranged sequence of substances is declared to be threefold, namely: the forward sequence (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), the reverse sequence (*pacchāṇupuvvī*), and the non-sequential (*aṇāṇupuvvī*).

What is the sequence in ascending order (*pūrvānupūrvī*)? The sequence in ascending order consists of: the substance of motion (*dharmāstikāya*), the substance of rest (*adharmāstikāya*), the substance of space (*ākāśāstikāya*), the substance of soul (*jīvāstikāya*), the substance of matter (*pudgalāstikāya*), and time (*addhāsamaya*). This is the sequence in ascending order. What is the sequence in descending order (*paścānupūrvī*)? The sequence in descending order consists of: time (*addhāsamaya*) up to the substance of motion (*dharmāstikāya*). This is the sequence in descending order. What is the non-sequence (*anānupūrvī*)? Non-sequence consists of the mutual multiplication of these same [categories] arranged in a series starting from one and increasing by one, minus two. This is the non-sequence.
—End of Text—

Alternatively, the arranged (ovaṇihiyā) substance-succession (*dravyānupūrvī*) is taught to be threefold, namely: forward succession (*pūrvānupūrvī*), reverse succession (*paścānupūrvī*), and non-succession (*anānupūrvī*). What is forward succession? Forward succession is: a single atom (*paramāṇu-pudgala*), a two-partite, a three-partite, up to a ten-partite, a numerable-partite, an innumerable-partite, and an infinite-partite [skandha]. This is forward succession. What is reverse succession? Reverse succession is: from an infinite-partite down to a two-partite and a single atom. This is reverse succession. What is non-succession? It is the mutual combination of these very same [categories] starting from one and increasing by one, extending through an infinite series; this is non-succession. This is the arranged substance-succession. This is the substance-succession distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the potential being. This is the substance-succession from the non-scriptural perspective (*noāgama*). This is substance-succession.
What is the sequence of space? The sequence of space is taught to be twofold, namely:
the conventional and the non-conventional.

In that regard, that which is "deposited" (ovaṇihiyā) is set aside; in that regard, that which is "not deposited" (aṇovaṇihiyā) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: according to the *negama-vavahāra* and according to the *saṅgraha*.

What is the non-enumerated spatial sequence (*kṣetrānupūrvī*) according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints]? The non-enumerated spatial sequence according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra is taught to be fivefold, namely: the exposition of the eight categories (*aṣṭapadaprarūpaṇatā*), the enumeration of the permutations (*bhaṅgasamuddeśanā*), the demonstration of the permutations (*bhaṅgopadarśanā*), the application (*samavatāra*), and the analysis (*anugama*). What is the exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra? The exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra is as follows: that which occupies three space-points (*pradeśa*) is a sequential entity (*ānupūrvī*); likewise up to that which occupies ten space-points is a sequential entity; that which occupies a numerable number of space-points is a sequential entity; and that which occupies an innumerable number of space-points is a sequential entity. That which occupies one space-point is a non-sequential entity (*anānupūrvī*); that which occupies two space-points is an indescribable entity (*avaktavyaka*). Multiple entities occupying three space-points are sequential entities; likewise up to multiple entities occupying ten space-points are sequential entities, and so on up to multiple entities occupying an innumerable number of space-points being sequential entities; multiple entities occupying one space-point are non-sequential entities; and those occupying two space-points are indescribable entities. This is the exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra.
What is the purpose of this exposition of the eight points regarding the conventions of worldly business?

By means of this exposition of the eightfold propositions (*aṣṭapadaprarūpaṇā*) of the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints], the enumeration of the permutations (*bhaṅgasamuddeśana*) of the Naigama and Vyavahāra is performed. What is that enumeration of the permutations of the Naigama and Vyavahāra? The enumeration of the permutations of the Naigama and Vyavahāra is as follows: there is succession (*ānupūrvī*), there is non-succession (*anānupūrvī*), and there is the indescribable (*avaktavyaka*). Thus, by way of the substance-succession (*dravyānupūrvī*), the same twenty-six permutations are to be stated for the space-succession (*kṣetrānupūrvī*) as well, up until that which is the enumeration of the permutations of the Naigama and Vyavahāra.

What is the purpose of this enumeration of the modes (*bhaṅga*) of the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints]? By means of this enumeration of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra, the demonstration of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra is effected. What is that demonstration of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra? The demonstration of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra is as follows: that which occupies three space-points is a sequential entity (*ānupūrvī*); that which occupies one space-point is a non-sequential entity (*anānupūrvī*); that which occupies two space-points is an indescribable entity (*avaktavyaka*). Three sequential entities occupying three space-points each; non-sequential entities occupying one space-point each; non-sequential entities occupying two space-points each; and indescribable entities occupying two space-points each. Or else: three occupying three space-points and one occupying one space-point are a sequential entity and a non-sequential entity respectively. In this same manner, according to the sequence of substance-analogy (*dravyānupūrvī*), twenty-six modes are to be stated, up until: "This is the demonstration of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra."

What is this "inclusion" (*samōyārē*)? By inclusion, one asks: in what do the substances of the sequential order (*āṇupuvvidavvāiṃ*) of the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints] include themselves? Do they include themselves through substances of the sequential order, through substances not of the sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvidavvēhiṃ*), or through substances that are indescribable (*avattavvayadavvēhiṃ*)? For the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints], the substances of the sequential order include themselves through substances of the sequential order; they do not include themselves through those not of the sequential order, nor do they include themselves through substances that are indescribable. Thus, it should be stated that both include themselves within their own respective domains. This is inclusion.
What is that? It is the sequential exposition (*anugama*). The sequential exposition is declared to be of nine kinds, namely:
the exposition of the nature of the states (*santapayaparūvaṇayā*), the measure of substances (*davvapamāṇa*), the space occupied (*khettaphusaṇā*), and so forth.
Time, interval, part, state, and indeed the relative magnitude (of karmic matter). — Aṇuogaddārāim 115.

Do the substances that are *ānupūrvī* (sequential) according to the *negama* and *vyavahāra* viewpoints exist or not? They certainly exist. Likewise for both [the other types of sequential substances]. Are the *ānupūrvī* substances according to the *negama* and *vyavahāra* viewpoints numerable, innumerable, or infinite? They are not numerable, not innumerable, but infinite. Likewise for both. Regarding the *ānupūrvī* substances according to the *negama* and *vyavahāra* viewpoints, in what portion of the universe do they reside? Do they reside in a numerable part, an innumerable part, numerable parts, innumerable parts, or the entire universe? With respect to a single substance, it may reside in a numerable part of the universe, or it may reside in an innumerable part, or it may reside in numerable parts, or it may reside in innumerable parts, or it may reside in the universe minus a portion (*deśona*). With respect to multiple substances, they necessarily reside in the entire universe.

Regarding the question of non-sequential substances among the transactions of the city-dwellers: with respect to a single substance, it would not exist in a numerable fraction [of the world], it would exist in an innumerable fraction, it would not exist in numerable fractions, it would not exist in innumerable fractions, nor would it exist in the entire world; however, with respect to multiple substances, it would necessarily exist in the entire world. The same should be stated for indeterminate substances as well.

Regarding the substances of sequential order (*āṇupuvvidavvāiṃ*) of the non-corporal world, how many parts of the world do they occupy? Do they occupy a numerable part, up to the entire world? With respect to a single substance, they occupy either a numerable part, or an innumerable part, or a numerable number of parts, or an innumerable number of parts, or they occupy the world minus a fraction (*dēsūṇaṃ lōgaṃ*). With respect to multiple substances, they necessarily occupy the entire world. As for substances of non-sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvidavvāiṃ*) and indescribable substances (*avattavvagadavvāiṃ*), it is as with space; however, their occupation (*phusaṇā*) must be stated [as follows].

Regarding the sequence of substances of the transactions of the guilds, for how long do they exist in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, the minimum is one moment and the maximum is an incalculable period of time; with respect to multiple substances, it is necessarily for all time. The same applies to both [the other two types of transactions].

Regarding the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints], what is the duration of the interval (*antara*) between successive substances (*ānupūrvī-dravyas*) in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, it is at least one moment and at most an incalculable period of time (*asaṅkhyeya-kāla*). With respect to multiple substances, there is no interval. This is the same for both [the negama and vyavahāra standpoints]. Regarding the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints], in what proportion do the successive substances exist relative to the remaining substances? All three [categories] are as described in the *dravyānupūrvī*. Regarding the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints], in which state (*bhāva*) do the successive substances exist? They necessarily exist in the state that is beginningless and transformational (*sādi-pāriṇāmika-bhāva*). This is the same for both. "O Venerable One, among these successive substances, non-successive substances, and indescribable substances of the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints], which are fewer, which are more, which are equal, or which are specifically greater, when considered from the perspective of substance (*dravyārthatas*), from the perspective of space-points (*pradeśārthatas*), or from the perspective of both substance and space-points? Gautama: "In terms of substance, O Gautama, the indescribable substances of the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints] are the fewest of all. The non-successive substances in terms of substance are specifically greater; the successive substances in terms of substance are incalculably greater. In terms of space-points, the non-successive substances of the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints] are the fewest of all because they lack space-points (*apradeśārthatas*). The indescribable substances in terms of space-points are specifically greater; the successive substances in terms of space-points are incalculably greater. In terms of both substance and space-points: the indescribable substances of the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints] in terms of substance are the fewest of all. The non-successive substances in terms of substance and the indescribable substances in terms of space-points are specifically greater. The successive substances in terms of substance are incalculably greater, and those very same [successive substances] in terms of space-points are incalculably greater. This concludes the *anugama* (synthetic treatment). This concludes the unclassified spatial succession (*anopanidhiya-kṣetrānupūrvī*) of the negama and vyavahāra [standpoints]."
— End of Text —

What is the sequential order of the field (*khetta-aṇupuvvī*) according to the method of synthesis (*saṅgaha*)? The sequential order of the field is taught as fivefold, namely: the exposition of the eight categories (*aṭṭhapayaparūvaṇayā*), the enumeration of the permutations (*bhaṅgasamukkittaṇayā*), the demonstration of the permutations (*bhaṅgōvadaṁsaṇayā*), the application (*samōyārē*), and the analysis (*anugamē*). What is the exposition of the eight categories according to the method of synthesis? That which is immersed in three spatial points (*tipaēsa-ogāḍha*) is a sequential entity (*āṇupuvvī*); that which is immersed in four spatial points is a sequential entity; likewise up to that which is immersed in ten spatial points is a sequential entity; that which is immersed in a numerable number of spatial points is a sequential entity; that which is immersed in an innumerable number of spatial points is a sequential entity; that which is immersed in a single spatial point is a non-sequential entity (*aṇāṇupuvvī*); and that which is immersed in two spatial points is an indescribable entity (*avattavvaē*). This is the exposition of the eight categories according to the method of synthesis. What is the purpose of this exposition of the eight categories according to the method of synthesis? By means of this exposition of the eight categories according to the method of synthesis, the enumeration of the permutations (*bhaṅgasamukkittaṇayā*) of the method of synthesis is accomplished.

What, then, is the enumeration of the modes of the synthetic (saṅgraha) standpoint? There is the sequential (āṇupuvvī), there is the non-sequential (aṇāṇupuvvī), and there is the indescribable (avattavvaē); or else, there is both the sequential and the non-sequential. Thus, as it was stated for the substance-sequence (davvāṇupuvvī) in the synthetic standpoint, so should it be recited here up until: "this is the enumeration of the modes of the synthetic standpoint."

What is the purpose of this enumeration of the modes (*bhaṅga*) of the synthetic method (*saṅgraha*)? By means of this enumeration of the modes of the synthetic method, the demonstration of the modes of the synthetic method is accomplished. What is that demonstration of the modes of the synthetic method? A triad of space-points (*tipaesōgāḍha*) is the sequential (*āṇupuvvī*); a single space-point (*ēgapaesōgāḍha*) is the non-sequential (*aṇāṇupuvvī*); a dyad of space-points (*dupaesōgāḍha*) is the indescribable (*avattavvaē*). Or else, a triad of space-points and a single space-point are both the sequential and the non-sequential. In this manner, just as it was stated for the synthetic method regarding the sequential order of substance (*davvāṇupuvvī*), so too should it be stated for the sequential order of space (*khettāṇupuvvī*), up until: "This is the demonstration of the modes of the synthetic method."

What is that [which constitutes] inclusion (*samoyāra*)? The substances of the sequential order (*āṇupuvvidavva*)—in what do they include? Do they include among the substances of the sequential order, among the substances of the non-sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvidavva*), or among the substances of the indescribable (*avattavvagadavva*)? They include in all three of their own respective places. That is inclusion. What is that [which constitutes] the method of following (*aṇugama*)? It is declared to be eightfold:
[the exposition of the existence of the subject (*santapayaparūvaṇayā*)], up to [the comparison of] smallness and greatness (*appābahuṃ*), which does not exist [here].

Regarding the substances of the *saṅgraha* (comprehensive) sequence: do they exist or not? They certainly exist; thus it is for all three [types of sequences]. The remaining sections are to be explained for the *kṣetrānupūrvī* (spatial sequence) just as they were for the *dravyānupūrvī* (substantial sequence) concerning the *saṅgraha*, up until the section on *anugama* (correlation). This concludes the non-enumerated *kṣetrānupūrvī* of the *saṅgraha*. This concludes the non-enumerated *kṣetrānupūrvī*.

What is that which is the sequential order of space by way of enumeration (*ovaṇihiyā khettāṇupuvvī*)? The sequential order of space by way of enumeration is declared to be threefold; namely: forward sequence (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), reverse sequence (*pacchāṇupuvvī*), and non-sequence (*aṇāṇupuvvī*). What is that which is the forward sequence? The forward sequence is: the nether world (*ahōlōē*), the horizontal world (*tiriyalōē*), and the upper world (*uḍḍhalōē*). This is the forward sequence.

What is that [classification] in reverse order (*pacchāṇupuvvī*)? It is the upper world, the middle world, and the lower world; this is the reverse order. What is that [classification] in non-sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvī*)? It is the mutual comparison of forms through this very series (*seḍhī*) beginning with one, increasing by one, and consisting of groups of three; this is the non-sequential order.

The sequence of the spatial realms of the lower world (*aholoka-khetta-aṇupuvvī*) is threefold: in direct order (*pūrvānupūrvī*), in reverse order (*paścānupūrvī*), and in non-sequential order (*anānupūrvī*). What is the direct order? It is: Ratnaprabhā, Śarkarāprabhā, Vālukāprabhā, Paṅkaprabhā, Dhūmaprabhā, Tamaḥprabhā, and Tamastamaḥprabhā. This is the direct order. What is the reverse order? From Tamastamaḥprabhā down to Ratnaprabhā. This is the reverse order. What is the non-sequential order? It is the mutual permutation of these same [realms] arranged in a series starting from one and increasing by one up to seven, minus two. This is the non-sequential order. The sequence of the spatial realms of the transverse world (*tiryaṅ-loka-khetta-aṇupuvvī*) is threefold: in direct order, in reverse order, and in non-sequential order. What is the direct order?
In Jambūdvīpa, Lavaṇa, Dhāyaka, Kāloda, Puṣkara, Varuṇa,
Kṣīra, Ghṛta, Khoya, Nandi, Aruṇavara, Kuṇḍala, and Rucaka. (Aṇuogaddārāim 121)
Indeed,

from Jambūdvīpa, the remaining infinite continents— such as Bhuyagavara, Kusavara, and Koñcavara, along with their ornaments and so forth— are situated without any intervening space. (Aṇuogaddārāim 122)

Ornaments, clothing, and perfumes; blue lotuses, sesame seeds, and earth-treasures; jewels; mountain ranges, lakes, rivers, victory lands (*vijaya*), intermediate ranges (*vakkhāra*), and celestial realms (*kappinda*). — Āvaśyaka Niryukti 123.
The peaks that are the abodes of Kuru and Mandara, as well as the constellations, the moon, and the sun; the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and bhūtas; and the ocean Sayambhuramaṇa. (Aṇuogaddārā 124)

This is the sequence in direct order (*pūrvānupūrvī*). What is the sequence in reverse order (*paścānupūrvī*)? The sequence in reverse order begins from the Self-Existent Ocean (*Svayambhūramaṇa*) down to Jambūdvīpa. This is the sequence in reverse order.

What is non-sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvī*)? Non-sequential order is the mutual juxtaposition of various forms along this very same scale (*seḍhī*) which begins with one, increases by one, and extends to an infinite number of divisions; that is non-sequential order. The sequential order of the spatial region of the upper world (*uḍḍhalōyakhēttāṇupuvvī*) is explained as threefold: namely, forward sequential order (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), reverse sequential order (*pacchāṇupuvvī*), and non-sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvī*). What is forward sequential order? Forward sequential order is: Saudharma, Īśāna, Sanatkumāra, Māhendra, Brahmaloka, Lāntaka, Mahāśukra, Sahasrāra, Ānata, Prāṇata, Āraṇa, Acyuta, the Graiveyaka vimānas, the Anuttara vimānas, and the Īṣatprāgbhāra [vimāna]; that is forward sequential order.
What is that which is in reverse order? Reverse order begins from Īsippabbhāra and goes up to Sōhamma; that is reverse order.

What is non-succession (*aṇāṇupuvvī*)? Non-succession consists of the mutual multiplication of this very same series—beginning with one, increasing by one, extending to fifteen members—minus two. That is non-succession. Alternatively, the arranged spatial succession (*ovaṇihiyā khettāṇupuvvī*) is declared to be threefold: namely, prior succession (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), posterior succession (*pacchāṇupuvvī*), and non-succession (*aṇāṇupuvvī*). What is prior succession? Prior succession consists of [atoms] occupying one space-point (*paēsa*), occupying two space-points, up to occupying an infinite number of space-points. That is prior succession. What is posterior succession? Posterior succession consists of [atoms] occupying an infinite number of space-points, down to occupying one space-point. That is posterior succession. What is non-succession? Non-succession consists of the mutual multiplication of this very same series—beginning with one, increasing by one, extending to an infinite number of members—minus two. That is non-succession. That is the arranged spatial succession; that is spatial succession.
What is the sequential order by time (*kālāṇupuvvī*)? The sequential order by time is taught to be twofold, namely: the arranged (*ovaṇihiyā*) and the unarranged (*aṇovaṇihiyā*).

In this regard, that which is "deposited" (ovaṇihiyā) is set aside. Therein, that which is "not deposited" (aṇovaṇihiyā) is declared to be twofold, namely: according to the *negama-vavahāra* [standpoint] and according to the *saṅgraha* [standpoint].

What is the "non-deposited" temporal sequence (*kālāṇupuvvī*) according to the *negama-vavahāra*? That temporal sequence is declared to be fivefold, namely: the exposition of the eightfold arrangement (*aṭṭhapayaparūvaṇayā*), the enumeration of the logical permutations (*bhaṅgasamukkittaṇayā*), the demonstration of the permutations (*bhaṅgōvadaṁsaṇayā*), the application (*samōyārē*), and the investigation (*anugamē*).

What is that exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints]? It is as follows: the *ānupūrvī* (successive order) existing for three time-units (*samaya*), up to the *ānupūrvī* existing for ten time-units, the *ānupūrvī* existing for a numerable number of time-units, the *ānupūrvī* existing for an innumerable number of time-units, the *anānupūrvī* (non-successive order) existing for one time-unit, and the *avaktavya* (indescribable) existing for two time-units; likewise, the *ānupūrvi*s existing for three time-units, the *anānupūrvi*s existing for one time-unit, and the *avaktavya*s existing for two time-units. This is the exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra standpoints. What is the purpose of this exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra standpoints? By means of this exposition of the eight categories according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra standpoints, the enumeration of the logical alternatives (*bhaṅga*) of the Naigama and Vyavahāra standpoints is accomplished.

The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to take all the grass, twigs, branches, and foliage found in this Jambudvīpa and pile them together into a single heap, and if someone were to reduce that heap by a single hair-tip every hundred years until it was entirely exhausted, Ānanda, that heap of grass, twigs, branches, and foliage would be exhausted more quickly than the aeons during which the Tathāgata has maintained mindfulness and clear comprehension. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s maintenance of mindfulness and clear comprehension is immeasurable. The venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One; it is marvelous, Blessed One! How great is the Blessed One’s maintenance of mindfulness and clear comprehension! How vast is the Blessed One’s maintenance of mindfulness and clear comprehension! For how long, Blessed One, has the Blessed One maintained mindfulness and clear comprehension? What is that? It is the exposition of the modes (bhaṅga) of the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints]. The exposition of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra is as follows: there is the sequential (āṇupuvvī), there is the non-sequential (aṇāṇupuvvī), and there is the indescribable (avattavvaē). Thus, by means of the substance-sequence (davvāṇupuvvī), those same twenty-six modes are to be stated for the time-sequence (kālāṇupuvvī) as well, up until: "this is the exposition of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra. What is the purpose of this exposition of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra? By means of this exposition of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra, the demonstration of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra is accomplished.

The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a lotus flower growing in the mud; the person who is like a lotus flower growing in the water; the person who is like a lotus flower growing on the bank; and the person who is like a lotus flower growing out of the water. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower growing in the mud? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, overwhelmed by sensual lust, and he cannot free his mind from that obsession. He dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will, overwhelmed by ill will, and he cannot free his mind from that obsession. He dwells with his mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, and he cannot free his mind from that obsession. He dwells with his mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse, and he cannot free his mind from that obsession. He dwells with his mind obsessed by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt, and he cannot free his mind from that obsession. Just as a lotus flower grows in the mud, so too is such a person called 'one like a lotus flower growing in the mud. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower growing in the water? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, yet he is able to free his mind from that obsession. Just as a lotus flower grows in the water, so too is such a person called 'one like a lotus flower growing in the water. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower growing on the bank? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, yet he is able to free his mind from that obsession. Having freed his mind from those obsessions, he dwells having transcended them. Just as a lotus flower grows on the bank, so too is such a person called 'one like a lotus flower growing on the bank. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower growing out of the water? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned sensual desire for the realm of sense-pleasures, has abandoned ill will, has abandoned sloth and torpor, has abandoned restlessness and remorse, and has abandoned doubt. He dwells with a mind that is purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability. Just as a lotus flower grows out of the water, so too is such a person called 'one like a lotus flower growing out of the water. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. ---------------------------------------------------------------------

What is that? It is the demonstration of the modes (bhaṅga) according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra [standpoints]. Regarding the demonstration of the modes of the Naigama and Vyavahāra: that which exists for three time-units (*samaya*) is *ānupūrvī*; that which exists for one time-unit is *anānupūrvī*; and that which exists for two time-units is *avaktavyaka*. Those existing for three time-units are *ānupūrvi*s; those existing for one time-unit are *anānupūrvi*s; and those existing for two time-units are *avaktavyaka*s. Alternatively, that which exists for three time-units and that which exists for one time-unit are both *ānupūrvī* and *anānupūrvī*. In this same manner, according to the sequence of substance (*dravya-ānupūrvī*), twenty-six modes are to be stated, up until: "This is the demonstration of the modes according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra."

What then is *samōyārē* (correspondence)? *Samōyārē* refers to the correspondence of the substances (*davvāiṃ*) of the sequential series (*āṇupuvvi*) with one another. Do they correspond with substances that are sequential, with substances that are non-sequential (*aṇāṇupuvvi*), or with substances that are indescribable (*avattavvaga*)? Thus it should be stated that all three correspond within their own respective categories; that is *samōyārē*.

What is that? It is the sequential exposition (*anugama*). The sequential exposition is declared to be ninefold, as follows:— The exposition of the nature of the states (*santapayaparūvaṇayā*), the measure of substances (*davvapamāṇa*), and the [measure of] space (*khētta*), as well as contact (*phusaṇā*).
Time, interval, part, state, and relative magnitude (appābahua).
— Aṇuogaddārā 134.

Do the substances of sequential order (*āṇupuvvi-davva*) exist according to the *negama* and *vyavahāra* viewpoints? They certainly exist; thus it is for both [viewpoints]. Are the substances of sequential order according to the *negama* and *vyavahāra* viewpoints numerable, innumerable, or infinite? They are not numerable, not innumerable, and not infinite; thus it is for both [viewpoints]. Regarding the substances of sequential order according to the *negama* and *vyavahāra* viewpoints, in how many parts of the world do they exist? Do they exist in a numerable part, an innumerable part, in numerable parts, in innumerable parts, or in the entire world? With respect to a single substance, it may exist in a numerable part of the world, or it may exist in an innumerable part, or it may exist in numerable parts, or it may exist in innumerable parts, or it may exist in the world minus a portion. With respect to multiple substances, they necessarily exist in the entire world. Thus, the substance of non-sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvi*) should be stated according to another method in all questions. Likewise, the substances of the "inexpressible" (*avattavvaga*) should also be stated exactly as the contact was explained for spatial sequential order (*khetta-āṇupuvvī*) in the section on temporal sequential order (*kāla-āṇupuvvī*).

Regarding the substances that follow the sequence (*āṇupuvvidavvāiṃ*) according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra viewpoints, for how long do they exist in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, the minimum is three moments (*samaya*) and the maximum is an incalculable period of time (*asaṅkhējjaṃ kālaṃ*). With respect to multiple substances, it is for all time (*savvaddhā*). Regarding the substances that do not follow the sequence (*aṇāṇupuvvidavvāiṃ*) according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra viewpoints, for how long do they exist in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, neither at a minimum nor at a maximum, it is one moment. With respect to multiple substances, it is for all time. Regarding the substances that are "indescribable" (*avattavvagadavvāiṃ*) according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra viewpoints, for how long do they exist in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, neither at a minimum nor at a maximum, it is two moments. With respect to multiple substances, it is for all time. Regarding the interval (*antara*) between substances that follow the sequence according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra viewpoints, for how long does it last in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, the minimum is one moment and the maximum is two moments. With respect to multiple substances, there is no interval. Regarding the interval between substances that do not follow the sequence according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra viewpoints, for how long does it last in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, the minimum is two moments and the maximum is an incalculable period of time. With respect to multiple substances, there is no interval. Regarding the interval between "indescribable" substances according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra viewpoints, for how long does it last in terms of time? With respect to a single substance, the minimum is one moment and the maximum is an incalculable period of time. With respect to multiple substances, there is no interval. Regarding the question of what portion of the remaining substances the substances that follow the sequence constitute according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra viewpoints—the state (*bhāva*) is exactly as in the case of spatial sequence (*khetta-āṇupuvvī*), and the comparison of smallness and greatness (*appābahu*) should also be understood in the same way. This concludes the analysis (*anugama*); this concludes the non-sequential temporal sequence (*aṇovaṇihiyā kālāṇupuvvī*) according to the Naigama and Vyavahāra viewpoints.

What, then, is the non-sequential order of time (*aṇōvaṇihiyā kālāṇupuvvī*) according to the compendium (*saṅgaha*)? The non-sequential order of time is declared to be fivefold: the exposition of the eight points (*aṭṭhapayaparūvaṇayā*), the enumeration of the permutations (*bhaṅgasamukkittaṇayā*), the demonstration of the permutations (*bhaṅgōvandasaṇayā*), the application (*samōyārē*), and the method of following (*anugamē*).

What is that? It is the exposition of the eight points of the *saṅgraha* (compendium). These same five sections regarding the *saṅgraha* as they were explained for the *kṣetrānupūrvī* (spatial succession) should likewise be recited for the *kālānupūrvī* (temporal succession); however—the terminology concerning "duration" (*sthiti*) applies up until the section on "examination" (*anugama*). This is the non-sequential temporal succession of the *saṅgraha*; this is the non-sequential temporal succession.

What is that which is the sequential order of time by way of enumeration (*ovaṇihiyā kālāṇupuvvī*)? The sequential order of time by way of enumeration is declared to be threefold; namely: forward sequence (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), reverse sequence (*pacchāṇupuvvī*), and non-sequence (*aṇāṇupuvvī*). What is that which is the forward sequence? The forward sequence is: a moment (*samaē*), a series (*āvaliyā*), a breath (*āṇāpāṇū*), a short duration (*thōvē*), a lava, a muhūrta, a day and night (*ahōrattē*), a fortnight (*pakkhē*), a month (*māsē*), a season (*uū*), a solstice (*ayaṇē*), a year (*saṁvaccharē*), a yuga (*jugē*), a hundred years, a thousand years, a hundred thousand years, a *puvvaṅga*, a *puvva*, a *tuḍiyaṅga*, a *tuḍiya*, an *aḍaḍaṅga*, an *aḍaḍa*, an *avavaṅga*, an *avava*, a *huhuyaṅga*, a *huhuya*, an *uppalaṅga*, an *uppala*, a *paümaṅga*, a *paüma*, a *nalinaṅga*, a *nalina*, an *atthaniuraṅga*, an *atthaniura*, an *aüyaṅga*, an *aüya*, a *naüyaṅga*, a *naüya*, a *paüyaṅga*, a *paüya*, a *cūliyaṅga*, a *cūliyā*, a *sīsapahēliyaṅga*, a *sīsapahēliyā*, a *paliōvama*, a *sāgarōvama*, an *ōsappiṇī*, an *ussappiṇī*, a cycle of increase and decrease (*pōggalapariyaṭṭē*), past time (*atītadaddhā*), future time (*anāgataddhā*), and all time (*savvaddhā*). This is the forward sequence.

What is that which is reverse order (*pacchāṇupuvvī*)? It is from all time (*savvaddhā*) down to a single moment (*samaē*); that is reverse order. What is that which is non-order (*aṇāṇupuvvī*)? Non-order is the mutual comparison of this very same sequence (*sēḍhī*)—which begins with one, increases by one, and extends to an infinite number of members—minus two; that is non-order.

Alternatively, the arranged sequential order of time (*ovaṇihiyā kālāṇupuvvī*) is declared to be threefold, namely: forward sequence (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), reverse sequence (*pacchāṇupuvvī*), and non-sequence (*aṇāṇupuvvī*). What is the forward sequence? The forward sequence consists of: duration of one moment, duration of two moments, duration of three moments, up to duration of ten moments, duration of a numerable number of moments, and duration of an innumerable number of moments. This is the forward sequence. What is the reverse sequence? The reverse sequence consists of: duration of an innumerable number of moments, down to duration of one moment. This is the reverse sequence. What is the non-sequence? The non-sequence consists of these same [categories] starting from one, up to less than two (i.e., all possible combinations). This is the non-sequence. This is the arranged sequential order of time. This is the sequential order of time.
—End of Text—

What is the serial order of enumeration (*ukkittaṇāṇupuvvī*)? The serial order of enumeration is declared to be threefold: namely, the forward order (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), the reverse order (*pacchāṇupuvvī*), and the non-sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvī*). What is the forward order? The forward order is as follows: Ṛṣabha, Ajita, Sambhava, Abhinandana, Sumati, Padmaprabha, Supārśva, Candraprabha, Suvidhi, Śītala, Śreyāṃsa, Vāsupūjya, Vimala, Ananta, Dharma, Śānti, Kunthu, Ara, Malli, Munisuvrata, Nami, Ariṣṭanemi, Pārśva, and Vardhamāna. This is the forward order.

What is that which is in reverse order (*pacchāṇupuvvī*)? Reverse order refers to [the sequence] from Vardhamāna back to Ṛṣabha; that is reverse order. What is that which is non-sequential (*aṇāṇupuvvī*)? Non-sequential refers to the mutual combination of this very same series—starting from one and increasing by one up to twenty-four—which is reduced by two; that is non-sequential. That is sequential enumeration (*ukkittaṇāṇupuvvī*).

What is that? Enumeration in sequential order (*gaṇaṇāṇupuvvī*). Enumeration in sequential order is taught as threefold; namely: forward sequence (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), reverse sequence (*pacchāṇupuvvī*), and non-sequential (*aṇāṇupuvvī*). What is that? Forward sequence. Forward sequence is: one, ten, hundred, thousand, ten thousand, hundred thousand, ten hundred thousand, ten million (*koḍī*), ten times ten million, hundred times ten million, ten times hundred times ten million. That is forward sequence.

What is sequential order (pacchāṇupuvvī)? Sequential order consists of one hundred ten million [units] down to one; that is sequential order. What is non-sequential order (aṇāṇupuvvī)? Non-sequential order is the mutual multiplication of the figures on this very same scale—which begins with one and increases by one up to one hundred ten million—arranged in a diagonal line; that is non-sequential order. That is the sequential order of enumeration (gaṇaṇāṇupuvvī).

What is the serial order of figures (*saṇṭhāṇāṇupuvvī*)? The serial order of figures is declared to be threefold: namely, the forward order (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), the reverse order (*pacchāṇupuvvī*), and the non-sequential order (*aṇāṇupuvvī*). What is the forward order? The forward order consists of: the symmetrical square (*samacaüraṁsa*), the oblong (*naggōha*), the circular (*parimaṇḍala*), the triangular (*sāī*), the hunchbacked (*khujjē*), the dwarf (*vāmaṇē*), and the misshapen (*huṇḍē*). This is the forward order. What is the reverse order? The reverse order consists of: the misshapen up to the symmetrical square. This is the reverse order. What is the non-sequential order? The non-sequential order is the mutual permutation of these same [figures] arranged in a sequence starting from one and increasing by one, up to six. This is the non-sequential order; this is the serial order of figures.

What is the sequential order of conduct (*sāmāyāriyāṇupuvvī*)? The sequential order of conduct is declared to be threefold; namely: forward sequence (*puvvāṇupuvvī*), reverse sequence (*aṇāṇupuvvī*), and random sequence (*aṇāṇupuvvī*). What is the forward sequence?
[The forward sequence...]
*Ichchā*, *micchā*, *tahakkāra*, *āvassiyā*, *nisīhiyā*,
*āpucchaṇā*, *paḍipucchā*, *chandaṇā*, and *nimantaṇā*. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 143)

Furthermore, the tenfold conduct (*sāmācārī*) regarding formal admission (*upasampadā*) occurs in time. That is the sequence in direct order (*pūrvānupūrvī*). What is the sequence in reverse order (*paścānupūrvī*)? Reverse order begins with formal admission and ends with desire (*icchā*); that is the sequence in reverse order. What is the non-sequential order (*anānupūrvī*)? Non-sequential order consists of the mutual combination of these same [terms] arranged in a series starting from one and increasing by one up to ten, minus two; that is the non-sequential order. This concludes the sequential order of the conduct.

What is the sequence of states (*bhāvānupūrvī*)? The sequence of states is declared to be threefold: namely, the forward sequence (*pūrvānupūrvī*), the reverse sequence (*paścānupūrvī*), and the non-sequence (*anānupūrvī*). What is the forward sequence? [It consists of] the emergent (*udayika*), the subsidential (*upaśamika*), the destructive (*kṣāyika*), the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśamika*), the natural (*pāriṇāmika*), and the combined (*sānnipātika*); that is the forward sequence. What is the reverse sequence? [It consists of] the combined state down to the emergent; that is the reverse sequence. What is the non-sequence? The non-sequence is the mutual permutation of these same [six states] arranged in a series starting from one and increasing by one, less two; that is the non-sequence. That is the sequence of states; that is the sequence (*ānupūrvī*).
What is that which is called "name"? Name is declared to be of ten kinds, namely: one-name, two-name, three-name, four-name, five-name, six-name, seven-name, eight-name, nine-name, and ten-name.
What is that which is called "the single name"? Regarding the single name:
whatever names there may be for substances, qualities, and modifications—
The designations are explained by means of the refinement of their traditional scriptures (*āgama*).
This is "that which has a single name."
What is that which has two names? Two-name [words] are declared to be of two kinds, namely:

those consisting of a single syllable (*egakkhariya*) and those consisting of multiple syllables (*anēgakkhariya*). What is that which consists of a single syllable? Those consisting of a single syllable are declared to be of many kinds, namely: *hrīḥ*, *śrīḥ*, *dhīḥ*, *strī*. That is what consists of a single syllable. What is that which consists of multiple syllables? Those consisting of multiple syllables are declared to be of many kinds, namely: *kaṇṇā*, *vīṇā*, *latā*, *mālā*. That is what consists of multiple syllables.

Alternatively, names are declared to be of two kinds, namely: names of living beings (*jīvanāma*) and names of non-living things (*ajīvanāma*). What is a name of a living being? A name of a living being is declared to be of many kinds, such as: Devadatta, Yaṣṇadatta, Viṣṇudatta, Somadatta. This is a name of a living being. What is a name of a non-living thing? A name of a non-living thing is declared to be of many kinds, such as: a jar, a cloth, a mat, a chariot. This is a name of a non-living thing.

Alternatively, there are two types of names, which are taught as follows: the specific (*visēsiya*) and the non-specific (*avisēsiya*). The non-specific refers to substance (*davva*); the specific refers to living substance (*jīvadavva*) and non-living substance (*ajīvadavva*). The non-specific refers to living substance; the specific refers to hell-beings (*nēraïya*), animals (*tirikkhajōṇiya*), humans (*maṇussa*), and gods (*dēva*). The non-specific refers to hell-beings; the specific refers to those in the *Rayaṇappabhā*, *Sakkarappabhā*, *Vāluyappabhā*, *Paṅkappabhā*, *Dhūmappabhā*, *Tamā*, and *Tamatamā* [earth hells]. The non-specific refers to hell-beings of the *Rayaṇappabhā* earth; the specific refers to those who are fully developed (*pajjatta*) and those who are not fully developed (*apajjatta*). In this manner, it continues up to: the non-specific refers to hell-beings of the *Tamatamā* earth; the specific refers to those who are fully developed and those who are not fully developed. The non-specific refers to animals; the specific refers to one-sensed (*ēgindiya*), two-sensed (*bēindiya*), three-sensed (*tēindiya*), four-sensed (*caürindiya*), and five-sensed (*pañcindiya*) beings. The non-specific refers to one-sensed beings; the specific refers to earth-bodied (*puḍhavikāiya*), water-bodied (*āukāiya*), fire-bodied (*tēukāiya*), air-bodied (*vāukāiya*), and plant-bodied (*vaṇassaïkāiya*) beings. The non-specific refers to earth-bodied beings; the specific refers to subtle earth-bodied (*suhumapuḍhavikāiya*) and gross earth-bodied (*bādarapuḍhavikāiya*) beings. The non-specific refers to subtle earth-bodied beings; the specific refers to fully developed subtle earth-bodied and not fully developed subtle earth-bodied beings. The non-specific refers to gross earth-bodied beings; the specific refers to fully developed gross earth-bodied and not fully developed gross earth-bodied beings. This same method applies to water-bodied, fire-bodied, air-bodied, and plant-bodied beings, with their divisions into non-specific, specific, fully developed, and not fully developed, to be stated accordingly. The non-specific refers to two-sensed beings; the specific refers to fully developed two-sensed and not fully developed two-sensed beings. In the same way, the three-sensed and four-sensed beings are also to be stated.

[The beings are classified as follows: Unspecified five-sensed animals of the animal realm (*pañcendriya-tiryagyoni*); specified as aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm, terrestrial five-sensed animals of the animal realm, and aerial five-sensed animals of the animal realm. Unspecified aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as spontaneously generated (*saṃmūrchima*) aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm and womb-born (*garbhavyutkrāntika*) aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm. Unspecified spontaneously generated aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as fully developed (*paryāpta*) spontaneously generated aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm and undeveloped (*aparyāpta*) spontaneously generated aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm. Unspecified womb-born aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as fully developed womb-born aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm and undeveloped womb-born aquatic five-sensed animals of the animal realm. Unspecified terrestrial five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals and reptilian (*parisarpa*) terrestrial five-sensed animals. Unspecified four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals; specified as spontaneously generated four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals and womb-born four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals. Unspecified spontaneously generated four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as fully developed spontaneously generated four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals and undeveloped spontaneously generated four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals of the animal realm. Unspecified womb-born four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as fully developed womb-born four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals of the animal realm and undeveloped womb-born four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals of the animal realm. Unspecified reptilian terrestrial five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as chest-reptiles (*uraparisarpa*) and limb-reptiles (*bhujaparisarpa*). These too should be described as spontaneously generated—both fully developed and undeveloped—and womb-born—both fully developed and undeveloped. Unspecified aerial five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as spontaneously generated aerial five-sensed animals and womb-born aerial five-sensed animals. Unspecified spontaneously generated aerial five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as fully developed spontaneously generated aerial five-sensed animals and undeveloped spontaneously generated aerial five-sensed animals. Unspecified womb-born aerial five-sensed animals of the animal realm; specified as fully developed womb-born aerial five-sensed animals and undeveloped womb-born aerial five-sensed animals. Unspecified human beings (*manuṣya*); specified as spontaneously generated humans and womb-born humans. Unspecified spontaneously generated humans; specified as fully developed spontaneously generated humans and undeveloped spontaneously generated humans. Unspecified womb-born humans; specified as fully developed womb-born humans and undeveloped womb-born humans. Alternatively, unspecified womb-born humans; specified as those from lands of action (*karmabhūmi*), those from non-lands of action (*akarmabhūmi*), and those from intermediate islands (*antaradvīpa*); and further specified as having a lifespan of numerable years or an incalculable number of years, and as being fully developed or undeveloped.

The gods are [divided into] the undifferentiated and the differentiated; the undifferentiated are the *bhavanavāsīs*, *vāṇamantarās*, *jōisiyas*, and *vēmāṇiyas*. The undifferentiated *bhavanavāsīs* are [further divided into] the differentiated: *asurakumārās*, *nāgakumārās*, *suvaṇṇakumārās*, *vijjukumārās*, *aggikumārās*, *dīvakumārās*, *udahikumārās*, *disākumārās*, *vāukumārās*, and *thaṇiyakumārās*. For all of these, the distinctions of the undifferentiated and differentiated, as well as the mature (*pajjattaya*) and immature (*apajjattaya*), should be stated. The undifferentiated *vāṇamantarās* are [further divided into] the differentiated: *pisāyās*, *bhūyās*, *jakkhās*, *rakkhasās*, *kinnarās*, *kumpurisās*, *mahōragās*, and *gandhavvās*. For these also, the distinctions of the undifferentiated and differentiated, as well as the mature and immature, should be stated. The undifferentiated *jōisiyas* are [further divided into] the differentiated: the moon, the sun, the planets, the lunar mansions (*nakkhatta*), and the stars (*tārārūva*). For these also, the distinctions of the undifferentiated and differentiated, as well as the mature and immature, should be stated.

The celestial beings (*vaimānika*) are divided into those who have not been specified (*aviśeṣita*) and those who have been specified (*viśeṣita*). Those who have been specified are further divided into those belonging to the *kalpa* heavens (*kalpōvaga*) and those who have transcended the *kalpas* (*kalpātītaga*). Regarding those belonging to the *kalpa* heavens who have not been specified, and those who have been specified, their subdivisions—such as those of the *Saudharma*, *Īśāna*, *Sanatkumāra*, *Māhendra*, *Brahmaloka*, *Lāntaka*, *Mahāśukra*, *Sahasrāra*, *Ānata*, *Prāṇata*, *Āraṇa*, and *Acyuta* heavens—should be stated according to the distinctions of the unspecified, the specified, the fully developed (*paryāpta*), and the not fully developed (*aparyāpta*). Regarding those who have transcended the *kalpas* who have not been specified, and those who have been specified, they are divided into those of the *Graiveyaka* and those born in the *Anuttara* (Supreme) realms. Regarding those of the *Graiveyaka* who have not been specified, and those who have been specified, they are divided into the lower, middle, and upper *Graiveyakas*. Regarding those of the lower *Graiveyakas* who have not been specified, and those who have been specified, they are divided into the lower-lower, lower-middle, and lower-upper *Graiveyakas*. Regarding those of the middle *Graiveyakas* who have not been specified, and those who have been specified, they are divided into the middle-lower, middle-middle, and middle-upper *Graiveyakas*. Regarding those of the upper *Graiveyakas* who have not been specified, and those who have been specified, they are divided into the upper-lower, upper-middle, and upper-upper *Graiveyakas*. For all of these, the subdivisions of the unspecified, the specified, the fully developed, and the not fully developed should be stated. Regarding those born in the *Anuttara* realms who have not been specified, and those who have been specified, they are divided into the *Vijaya*, *Vaijayanta*, *Jayanta*, *Aparājita*, and *Sarvārthasiddha* [palaces]. For all of these as well, the subdivisions of the unspecified, the specified, the fully developed, and the not fully developed should be stated.

The unqualified non-living substance (*ajīvadavva*) is qualified as the category of motion (*dhammatthikāya*), the category of rest (*adhammatthikāya*), the category of space (*āgāsatthikāya*), the category of matter (*poggalatthikāya*), and time (*addhāsamae*). The unqualified category of matter (*poggalatthikāya*) is qualified as a single atom (*paramāṇupoggala*), a two-partite particle (*dupaesie*), a three-partite particle (*tipaesie*), and so on up to an infinite-partite particle (*anantapaesie*). This is the "two-fold name" (*dunāma*).

What is that which is named "name" (nāma)? Name is declared to be threefold, namely: substantial name (davvanāma), quality name (guṇanāma), and mode name (pajjavanāma). What is that which is substantial name? Substantial name is declared to be sixfold: the substance of motion (dhammatthikāya) up to the unit of time (addhāsamae). This is substantial name.

What is that which is called "quality-name" (*guṇanāma*)? Quality-names are declared to be fivefold, namely: color-name (*vaṇṇanāma*), and so on, up to shape-name (*saṇṭhāṇanāma*). What is that which is called "color-name"? Color-names are declared to be fivefold, namely: black color-name, blue color-name, red color-name, yellow color-name, and white color-name. That is the color-name. What is that which is called "odor-name" (*gandhanāma*)? Odor-names are twofold, namely: pleasant odor-name and unpleasant odor-name. That is the odor-name. What is that which is called "taste-name" (*rasanāma*)? Taste-names are declared to be fivefold, namely: bitter taste-name, pungent taste-name, astringent taste-name, sour taste-name, and sweet taste-name. That is the taste-name. What is that which is called "touch-name" (*phāsanāma*)? Touch-names are declared to be eightfold, namely: hard touch-name, soft touch-name, heavy touch-name, light touch-name, cold touch-name, hot touch-name, smooth touch-name, and rough touch-name. That is the touch-name. What is that which is called "shape-name" (*saṇṭhāṇanāma*)? Shape-names are declared to be fivefold, namely: circular shape-name, spherical shape-name, triangular shape-name, quadrangular shape-name, and elongated shape-name. That is the shape-name. That is the quality-name.

What, then, is the name based on modification (*pajjavanāma*)? The name based on modification is declared to be of many kinds, as follows: one-fold black, two-fold black, three-fold black, up to ten-fold black, numerable-fold black, innumerable-fold black, and infinite-fold black. In the same way, blue, red, yellow, and white are also to be stated. One-fold pleasant odor, two-fold pleasant odor, three-fold pleasant odor, up to infinite-fold pleasant odor; in the same way, unpleasant odor is also to be stated. One-fold bitter, up to infinite-fold bitter; in the same way, pungent, astringent, sour, and sweet are also to be stated. One-fold hard, up to infinite-fold hard; in the same way, soft, heavy, light, cold, hot, smooth, and rough are also to be stated. This is the name based on modification.
Furthermore, that name is of three kinds: feminine, masculine, and neuter. I shall explain the exposition of these three as well. (Aṇuogaddārā 152)
In that regard, for a man there are four [vowels]: a, ā, ī, and ū; these same four, excluding the vowel o, belong to a woman. (Aṇuogaddārā 153)
The vowels *aṃ*, *iṃ*, *uṃ*, and *anta* (the nasalized *m*) are to be understood as neuter; from here I shall provide examples for all three of these. (Aṇuogaddārā 154)
The king has the vowel *ā*; the mountain and the peak have the vowel *ī*; Viṣṇu has the vowel *ū*; and among men, the tree has the vowel *ō*. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 155)
Among the names of women, those ending in *ā* are Mālā; those ending in *ī* are Sirī and Lacchī; and those ending in *ū* are Jambū and Vahū. (Āyāraṅga-sutta, Anuyogadvāra 156)
Words ending in *aṅka*, *iṅka*, *acchi*, *uṅka*, *pīlu*, and *mahu* are neuter nouns. (Aṇuogaddārā 157)
This is that which has three names.

What is that fourfold [naming]? Fourfold naming is declared to be of four kinds, namely: by scripture (āgama), by worldly convention (loka), by nature (prakṛti), and by modification (vikāra). What is that by scripture? By scripture: "lotuses," "waters," "pools. That is by scripture. What is that by worldly convention? By worldly convention: "they here, they here"; "cloth here, cloth here"; "pot here, pot here"; "chariot here, chariot here. That is by worldly convention. What is that by nature? By nature: "fire," "these two," "cloths," "these two," "garlands," "these. That is by nature. What is that by modification? By modification: "the tip of a staff" (daṇḍasya agram) becomes "staff-tip" (daṇḍāgram); "she has come" (sā āgatā) becomes "she-come" (sāgatā); "curd this" (dadhi idam) becomes "curd-this" (dadhīdam); "river here" (nadī īhate) becomes "river-here" (nadīhatā); "honey water" (madhu udakam) becomes "honey-water" (madhūdakam); "bride carries" (vadhū ūhate) becomes "bride-carries" (vadhūhatā). That is by modification. That is fourfold naming.

What then is the fivefold naming (pañcanāma)? The fivefold naming is declared to be of five kinds, namely: the nominal (nāmika), the particle (naipātika), the verbal (ākhyātika), the prepositional (aupasargika), and the mixed (miśra). "Horse" is a nominal; "indeed" is a particle; "runs" is a verbal; "around" is a prepositional; "self-restrained" is a mixed [term]. This is the fivefold naming.

What is that which is called *chāyā* (modification)? *Chāyā* is declared to be sixfold, namely: arising (*audayika*), subsidential (*upaśamika*), destructive (*kṣāyika*), destructive-subsidential (*kṣayopaśamika*), transformational (*pāriṇāmika*), and combined (*sānnipātika*). What is that which is arising? Arising is declared to be twofold, namely: arising itself (*udaya*) and that produced by arising (*udayanippanna*). What is that which is arising? Arising is through the rising of the eight types of karma; that is arising. What is that which is produced by arising?
