That produced by arising is declared to be twofold, namely: produced by the arising of the soul (*jīva*) and produced by the arising of non-soul (*ajīva*). What is that which is produced by the arising of the soul? That produced by the arising of the soul is declared to be manifold, namely: hell-being, animal, human, god; earth-body being up to mobile-body being; anger-passion up to greed-passion; female gender, male gender, neuter gender; black-leśyā up to white-leśyā; wrong view, lack of restraint, non-consciousness, ignorance, with food-intake, with limited vision, with yoga, in saṃsāra, non-perfected, not possessing omniscience; that is that which is produced by the arising of the soul.

What, then, is that which is produced from the arising of non-living matter (*ajīvodayanippanna*)? That which is produced from the arising of non-living matter is declared to be of many kinds, namely: the physical body (*orāliya*), or matter transformed by the activity of the physical body; the transformational body (*veuvviya*), or matter transformed by the activity of the transformational body; and likewise, the assimilative body (*āhāraya*), the fiery body (*teyaga*), and the karmic body (*kammaya*) should be mentioned. [There are also] color, smell, taste, and touch transformed by activity (*paogapariṇāmiya*). This is that which is produced from the arising of non-living matter; this is that which is produced from arising; this is that which is arisen (*udaïya*).

What is that which is quiescent (*uvasamiya*)? Quiescence is declared to be of two kinds, namely: quiescence itself (*uvasama*) and that which is produced by quiescence (*uvasamanipphanna*). What is quiescence itself? Quiescence is the subsiding of the deluding karma (*mōhaṇijja-kamma*); that is quiescence itself. What is that which is produced by quiescence? That which is produced by quiescence is declared to be of many kinds, namely: one whose anger is quiescent, one whose pride is quiescent, one whose deceit is quiescent, one whose greed is quiescent, one whose attachment is quiescent, one whose aversion is quiescent, one whose deluding karma of right view is quiescent, one whose deluding karma of conduct is quiescent, the attainment of right conviction through quiescence, the attainment of conduct through quiescence, and the state of a quasi-arhat (*chaümattha-vīyarāga*) whose passions (*kasāya*) are quiescent; that is what is produced by quiescence, and that is quiescence itself.

What is that which is destroyed (*khaia*)? It is declared to be twofold: namely, destruction itself (*khaa*) and that which is produced by destruction (*khayanipphanna*). What is destruction itself? It is the destruction of the eight types of karmic matter (*kamma-payaḍi*); that is destruction itself. What is that which is produced by destruction? That which is produced by destruction is declared to be manifold, as follows: The Arhat, the Jina, the Kevalin, the possessor of arisen knowledge and vision; one whose obscuration of sensory cognition (*ābhiṇibōhiya-ñāṇāvaraṇa*) is destroyed, whose obscuration of scriptural cognition (*suya-ñāṇāvaraṇa*) is destroyed, whose obscuration of clairvoyant cognition (*ōhi-ñāṇāvaraṇa*) is destroyed, whose obscuration of mind-cognition (*maṇapajjava-ñāṇāvaraṇa*) is destroyed, whose obscuration of omniscient cognition (*kevala-ñāṇāvaraṇa*) is destroyed; one who is without obscuration, free from obscuration, whose obscuration is destroyed, liberated from the karma of the obscuration of cognition; the possessor of absolute vision, the all-seeing; one whose sleep (*nidda*) is destroyed, whose drowsiness (*niddānidda*) is destroyed, whose somnambulism (*payala*) is destroyed, whose deep sleep (*payalāpayala*) is destroyed, whose heavy stupor (*thīṇagiddhī*) is destroyed; one whose obscuration of eye-vision (*cakkhu-dasaṇāvaraṇa*) is destroyed, whose obscuration of non-eye-vision (*acakkhu-dasaṇāvaraṇa*) is destroyed, whose obscuration of clairvoyant vision (*ōhi-dasaṇāvaraṇa*) is destroyed, whose obscuration of absolute vision (*kevala-dasaṇāvaraṇa*) is destroyed; one who is without obscuration, free from obscuration, whose obscuration is destroyed, liberated from the karma of the obscuration of vision; one whose pleasant feeling (*sāyavēyaṇijja*) is destroyed, whose unpleasant feeling (*asāyavēyaṇijja*) is destroyed; one who is without feeling, free from feeling, whose feeling is destroyed, liberated from the karma of pleasant and unpleasant feeling; one whose anger (*kōha*) is destroyed, whose pride (*māṇa*) is destroyed, whose deceit (*māyā*) is destroyed, whose greed (*lōha*) is destroyed, whose attachment (*pēja*) is destroyed, whose aversion (*dōsa*) is destroyed; one whose deluding karma of vision (*dasaṇa-mōhaṇijja*) is destroyed, whose deluding karma of conduct (*caritta-mōha*) is destroyed; one who is without delusion, free from delusion, whose delusion is destroyed, liberated from the karma of delusion; one whose hellish lifespan (*nēraïyāua*) is destroyed, whose animal lifespan (*tirikkhajōṇiyāua*) is destroyed, whose human lifespan (*maṇussāua*) is destroyed, whose celestial lifespan (*dēvāua*) is destroyed; one who is without lifespan, free from lifespan, whose lifespan is destroyed, liberated from the karma of lifespan; one who is liberated from the various bondages of gait (*gaï*), birth (*jāi*), body (*sarīra*), limbs (*aṅga*), minor limbs (*uvaṅga*), binding (*bandhaṇa*), molecular integration (*saṅghāyaṇa*), skeletal structure (*saṅghayaṇa*), physical form (*saṇṭhāṇa*), and the various types of atoms and molecules (*aṇēgabōndivinda-saṅghāya*); one whose auspicious name-karma (*subhanāmē*) is destroyed, whose inauspicious name-karma (*asubhanāmē*) is destroyed; one who is without name, free from name, whose name-karma is destroyed, liberated from the karma of auspicious and inauspicious names; one whose high lineage (*uccāgōē*) is destroyed, whose low lineage (*nīyāgōē*) is destroyed; one who is without lineage, free from lineage, whose lineage-karma is destroyed, liberated from the karma of auspicious and inauspicious lineages; one whose obstruction to giving (*dāṇantarāē*) is destroyed, whose obstruction to gain (*lābhantarāē*) is destroyed, whose obstruction to enjoyment (*bhōgantarāē*) is destroyed, whose obstruction to utilization (*uvabhōgantarāē*) is destroyed, whose obstruction to power (*vīriyantarāē*) is destroyed; one who is without obstruction, free from obstruction, whose obstructions are destroyed, liberated from the karma of obstructions; the Perfected One (*siddha*), the Awakened One (*buddha*), the Liberated One (*mutta*), the One who has attained final bliss (*parinivvuḍa*), the One who has reached the end (*antagaḍa*), the One for whom all suffering has been exhausted (*savvadukkhappahīṇa*). That is what is produced by destruction. That is what is destroyed.

What is that which is subsided (*khayovasamiya*)? That which is subsided is declared to be of two kinds, namely: subsidence itself (*khayovasama*) and that which is produced by subsidence (*khayovasama-nipphanna*). What is that which is subsidence itself? Subsidence itself is the subsidence of the four destructive karmas (*ghāti-karma*): through the subsidence of knowledge-obscuring (*ñānāvaraṇijja*), perception-obscuring (*daṃsaṇāvaraṇijja*), deluding (*mōhaṇijja*), and obstructive (*antarāya*) karma. This is that which is subsidence itself. What is that which is produced by subsidence? That which is produced by subsidence is declared to be of many kinds, namely: the attainment of sensory-cognition (*ābhinibōhiya-ñāṇa*) produced by subsidence; up to the attainment of mind-reading cognition (*maṇapajjava-ñāṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of sensory ignorance (*mai-aññāṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of scriptural ignorance (*suya-aññāṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of clairvoyance (*vibhaṅga-ñāṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of visual perception (*cakkhu-daṃsaṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of non-visual perception (*acakkhu-daṃsaṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of limited perception (*ōhi-daṃsaṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of right perception (*sammatta-daṃsaṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of wrong perception (*micchā-daṃsaṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of mixed perception (*sammāmicchā-daṃsaṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of the conduct of equanimity (*sāmāiya-caritta*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of the conduct of re-institution (*chēdōvaṭṭhāvaṇa-caritta*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of the conduct of purity through avoidance (*parihāra-visuddhiya-caritta*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of the conduct of subtle passion (*suhuma-saṃparāya-caritta*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of the conduct of partial purity (*carittācaritta*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of generosity (*dāṇa*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of gain (*lābha*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of enjoyment (*bhōga*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of utilization (*uvabhōga*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of energy (*vīriya*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of the energy of the fool (*bāla-vīriya*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of the energy of the wise (*paṇḍiya-vīriya*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of the energy of the fool-and-wise (*bāla-paṇḍiya-vīriya*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of the sense of hearing (*sōindiya*) produced by subsidence, up to the attainment of the sense of touch (*phāsindiya*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of one who maintains the *Āyāra* produced by subsidence; the attainment of one who maintains the *Sūyagaḍa* produced by subsidence, up to the attainment of one who maintains the *Diṭṭhivāya* produced by subsidence; the attainment of one who possesses the nine *pūrvas* (*navapuvvī*) produced by subsidence, up to the attainment of one who possesses the fourteen *pūrvas* (*caüddasapuvvī*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of a leader of a group (*gaṇī*) produced by subsidence; the attainment of an expounder (*vāyae*) produced by subsidence. This is that which is produced by subsidence. This is that which is subsided.

What is that which is transformational (*pāriṇāmika*)? Transformational [matter] is declared to be of two kinds, namely: beginningless transformational (*anādi-pāriṇāmika*) and with-beginning transformational (*sādi-pāriṇāmika*). What is that which is with-beginning transformational? With-beginning transformational is declared to be of many kinds, namely:
old wine, old molasses, old ghee, and old rice grains.
Clouds, cloud-trees, twilight, and cities of the Gandharvas. (Aṇuogaddārā 162)

Meteors, atmospheric fires, thunder, lightning, thunderclaps, firebrands, yakṣa-flames, smoke, dust-storms, eclipses of the moon, eclipses of the sun, halos around the moon, halos around the sun, secondary moons, secondary suns, Indra’s bow (rainbows), water-fish, portents, non-confusing phenomena, rain, clouds, villages, cities, earth, mountains, subterranean realms, celestial abodes, hells, the [seven] earths from Ratnaprabhā up to Tamatamā, [the heavens] from Saudharma up to Ācyuta, the Graiveyakas, the Anuttaras, the Īṣatprāgbhāra, and atoms ranging from two-particled up to infinite-particled matter—this is that which is beginningless and transformational (*anādi-pāriṇāmika*). What is that which is beginningless and transformational? The medium of motion (*dhammatthikāya*), the medium of rest (*adhammatthikāya*), the medium of space (*āgāsatthikāya*), the medium of souls (*jīvatthikāya*), the medium of matter (*poggalatthikāya*), time (*addhāsamae*), the world (*loka*), and the non-world (*aloka*), as well as souls (*jīva*) and non-souls (*ajīva*), those destined for liberation (*bhavasiddhiya*) and those not destined for liberation (*abhavasiddhiya*)—this is that which is beginningless and transformational; this is that which is transformational.

What is that which is called *sannivāiya* (combined)? *Sannivāiya* refers to all those states (*bhāva*) that are produced by the combination of two, three, four, or five of these very states—namely, the arisen (*udaïya*), the subsided (*uvasamiya*), the destroyed (*khaïya*), the subsided-and-destroyed (*khaōvasamiya*), and the innate (*pāriṇāmiya*). In this regard, there are ten combinations of two, ten combinations of three, five combinations of four, and one combination of five. Among them, those ten combinations of two are as follows: there is that which is called the arisen state produced from the subsided; there is that which is called the arisen state produced from the destroyed; there is that which is called the arisen state produced from the subsided-and-destroyed; there is that which is called the arisen state produced from the innate; there is that which is called the subsided state produced from the destroyed; there is that which is called the subsided state produced from the subsided-and-destroyed; there is that which is called the subsided state produced from the innate; there is that which is called the destroyed state produced from the subsided-and-destroyed; there is that which is called the destroyed state produced from the innate; and there is that which is called the subsided-and-destroyed state produced from the innate.

What is that which is named "produced from the active" (*udaiya*) and "accomplished through subsidence" (*uvasama*)? "Active" refers to a human being; "subsided" refers to the passions (*kasāya*). This is what is named "produced from the active" and "accomplished through subsidence. What is that which is named "produced from the active" and "accomplished through destruction" (*khaya*)? "Active" refers to a human being; "destroyed" refers to right conviction (*sammatta*). This is what is named "produced from the active" and "accomplished through destruction. What is that which is named "produced from the active" and "accomplished through destruction-subsidence" (*khaovasama*)? "Active" refers to a human being; "destruction-subsided" refers to the sense-faculties (*indiya*). This is what is named "produced from the active" and "accomplished through destruction-subsidence. What is that which is named "produced from the active" and "accomplished through modification" (*pāriṇāmiya*)? "Active" refers to a human being; "modified" refers to the soul (*jīva*). This is what is named "produced from the active" and "accomplished through modification. What is that which is named "subsided" and "accomplished through destruction"? Subsided passions and destroyed right conviction—this is what is named "subsided" and "accomplished through destruction. What is that which is named "subsided" and "accomplished through destruction-subsidence"? Subsided passions and destruction-subsided sense-faculties—this is what is named "subsided" and "accomplished through destruction-subsidence. What is that which is named "subsided" and "accomplished through modification"? Subsided passions and the modified soul—this is what is named "subsided" and "accomplished through modification."

What is that which is named "produced by destruction and subsidence"? Right conviction (*samyaktva*) is produced by destruction; the sense organs (*indriya*) are produced by subsidence. This is what is named "produced by destruction and subsidence. What is that which is named "produced by destruction and transformation" (*pāriṇāmika*)? Right conviction is produced by destruction; the soul (*jīva*) is transformative. This is what is named "produced by destruction and transformation. What is that which is named "produced by subsidence and transformation"? The sense organs are produced by subsidence; the soul is transformative. This is what is named "produced by subsidence and transformation. In this regard, those ten triple combinations (*tigasañjoga*) are as follows: (1) There is that which is named "produced by emergence, subsidence, and destruction" (*udaiya-uvasamiya-khaya-nipphanna*). (2) There is that which is named "produced by emergence, subsidence, and subsidence-destruction" (*udaiya-uvasamiya-khaovasama-nipphanna*). (3) There is that which is named "produced by emergence, subsidence, and transformation" (*udaiya-uvasamiya-pāriṇāmiya-nipphanna*). (4) There is that which is named "produced by emergence, destruction, and subsidence-destruction" (*udaiya-khaiya-khaovasama-nipphanna*). (5) There is that which is named "produced by emergence, destruction, and transformation" (*udaiya-khaiya-pāriṇāmiya-nipphanna*). (6) There is that which is named "produced by emergence, subsidence, and transformation" (*udaiya-khaovasamiya-pāriṇāmiya-nipphanna*). (7) There is that which is named "produced by subsidence, destruction, and subsidence-destruction" (*uvasamiya-khaiya-khaovasama-nipphanna*). (8) There is that which is named "produced by subsidence, destruction, and transformation" (*uvasamiya-khaiya-pāriṇāmiya-nipphanna*). (9) There is that which is named "produced by subsidence, subsidence-destruction, and transformation" (*uvasamiya-khaovasamiya-pāriṇāmiya-nipphanna*). (10) There is that which is named "produced by destruction, subsidence, and transformation" (*khaiya-khaovasamiya-pāriṇāmiya-nipphanna*).

(1) What is that which is called "produced from the arisen," "the subsided," and "the accomplished through destruction"? "The arisen" refers to the human being; "the subsided" refers to the passions (*kaṣāya*); "the accomplished through destruction" refers to right conviction (*samyaktva*). This, indeed, is what is called "produced from the arisen," "the subsided," and "the accomplished through destruction. (2) What is that which is called "produced from the arisen," "the subsided," and "the accomplished through subsidence and destruction"? "The arisen" refers to the human being; "the subsided" refers to the passions; "the accomplished through subsidence and destruction" refers to the sense-faculties (*indriya*). This, indeed, is what is called "produced from the arisen," "the subsided," and "the accomplished through subsidence and destruction. (3) What is that which is called "produced from the arisen," "the subsided," and "the accomplished through transformation"? "The arisen" refers to the human being; "the subsided" refers to the passions; "the accomplished through transformation" refers to the soul (*jīva*). This, indeed, is what is called "produced from the arisen," "the subsided," and "the accomplished through transformation."

(4) What is that which is produced from the arisen (*udaiya*), the destroyed (*khāiya*), and the subsided-destroyed (*khaovasamiya*)? "The arisen" refers to the human being; "the destroyed" refers to right conviction (*sammatta*); "the subsided-destroyed" refers to the sense-faculties (*indriya*). This is that which is produced from the arisen, the destroyed, and the subsided-destroyed. (5) What is that which is produced from the arisen, the destroyed, and the transformational (*pāriṇāmiya*)? "The arisen" refers to the human being; "the destroyed" refers to right conviction; "the transformational" refers to the soul (*jīva*). This is that which is produced from the arisen, the destroyed, and the transformational. (6) What is that which is produced from the arisen, the subsided-destroyed, and the transformational? "The arisen" refers to the human being; "the subsided-destroyed" refers to the sense-faculties; "the transformational" refers to the soul. This is that which is produced from the arisen, the subsided-destroyed, and the transformational.

(7) What is that which is called "subsided" (*uvasamiya*), "destroyed" (*khaïya*), and "produced by destruction and subsidence" (*khayovasamanippanna*)? The passions (*kasāya*) are subsided; right conviction (*sammatta*) is destroyed; the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are produced by destruction and subsidence. This is what is called "subsided," "destroyed," and "produced by destruction and subsidence. (8) What is that which is called "subsided," "destroyed," and "produced by transformation" (*pāriṇāmiyanippanna*)? The passions are subsided; right conviction is destroyed; the soul (*jīva*) is characterized by transformation (*pāriṇāmiya*). This is what is called "subsided," "destroyed," and "produced by transformation. (9) What is that which is called "subsided," "subsided and destroyed," and "produced by transformation"? The passions are subsided; the sense-faculties are subsided and destroyed; the soul is characterized by transformation. This is what is called "subsided," "subsided and destroyed," and "produced by transformation. (10) What is that which is called "destroyed," "subsided and destroyed," and "produced by transformation"? Right conviction is destroyed; the sense-faculties are subsided and destroyed; the soul is characterized by transformation. This is what is called "destroyed," "subsided and destroyed," and "produced by transformation."

In this regard, there are five combinations of four factors; they are as follows: (1) there is that which is produced by the arisen (*udayika*), the subsided (*upaśamika*), the destroyed (*kṣāyika*), and that produced by destruction and subsidence (*kṣayopaśamaniṣpanna*); (2) there is that which is produced by the arisen, the subsided, the destroyed, and that produced by transformation (*pāriṇāmikanippanna*); (3) there is that which is produced by the arisen, the subsided, the destroyed and subsided, and that produced by transformation; (4) there is that which is produced by the arisen, the destroyed, the destroyed and subsided, and that produced by transformation; (5) there is that which is produced by the subsided, the destroyed, the destroyed and subsided, and that produced by transformation.

What is that which is produced from the arisen (*udaiya*), the subsided (*uvasamiya*), the destroyed (*khaiya*), and the subsided-and-destroyed (*khao-vasamiya*)? "Arisen" refers to a human being; "subsided" refers to the passions (*kasāya*); "destroyed" refers to right conviction (*sammatta*); and "subsided-and-destroyed" refers to the sense organs (*indiya*). This, indeed, is that which is produced from the arisen, the subsided, the destroyed, and the subsided-and-destroyed, as well as from the inherent (*pāriṇāmiya*). (2) What is that which is produced from the arisen, the subsided, the destroyed, and the inherent? "Arisen" refers to a human being; "subsided" refers to the passions; "destroyed" refers to right conviction; and "inherent" refers to the soul (*jīva*). This, indeed, is that which is produced from the arisen, the subsided, the destroyed, and the inherent. (3) What is that which is produced from the arisen, the subsided, the subsided-and-destroyed, and the inherent? "Arisen" refers to a human being; "subsided" refers to the passions; "subsided-and-destroyed" refers to the sense organs; and "inherent" refers to the soul. This, indeed, is that which is produced from the arisen, the subsided, the subsided-and-destroyed, and the inherent. (4) What is that which is produced from the arisen, the destroyed, the subsided-and-destroyed, and the inherent? "Arisen" refers to a human being; "destroyed" refers to right conviction; "subsided-and-destroyed" refers to the sense organs; and "inherent" refers to the soul. This, indeed, is that which is produced from the arisen, the destroyed, the subsided-and-destroyed, and the inherent. (5) What is that which is produced from the subsided, the destroyed, the subsided-and-destroyed, and the inherent? "Subsided" refers to the passions; "destroyed" refers to right conviction; "subsided-and-destroyed" refers to the sense organs; and "inherent" refers to the soul. This, indeed, is that which is produced from the subsided, the destroyed, the subsided-and-destroyed, and the inherent.

In that regard, as for that one fivefold conjunction, it consists of these: the nominal (*nāma*), the emergent (*udaya*), the subsidential (*upaśama*), the destructive (*kṣaya*), the subsidential-destructive (*kṣayopaśama*), and that which is produced by transformation (*pāriṇāmika*). What is this that is called the nominal, up to that which is produced by transformation? "The nominal" refers to a human being; "the subsidential" refers to the subsided passions (*kaṣāyas*); "the destructive" refers to right perception (*samyaktva*); "the subsidential-destructive" refers to the sense organs (*indriyas*); and "that which is produced by transformation" refers to the soul (*jīva*). This is the nominal, up to that which is produced by transformation.
This is the conjunctive; this is the sixfold [classification].
What is that which pertains to the names of the notes (*sattanāma*)? Regarding the names of the notes:
seven notes are proclaimed, namely—*ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, and the *pañcama* note.
Indeed, according to the *Nesā* (the science of sounds), seven notes (*sara*) have been explained.
(Ānuyogadvāra Sūtra 165) Regarding these seven notes, seven musical scales (*saraṭṭhāṇa*) are taught, as follows: [text continues]

One should produce the *sajja* note with the tip of the tongue, the *ṛṣabha* note with the chest, the *gāndhāra* note with the tip of the throat, and the *madhyama* note with the middle of the tongue. (Aṇuogaddārā 167)

One should declare the fifth [sign] by means of the nose; the sixth by means of the teeth and lips; and the seventh by means of the knitting of the eyebrows. These are explained as the locations of the signs. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 168)
Seven sounds dependent on living beings are taught,
namely:
The peacock cries out the *ṣaḍja* note; the cock, the *ṛṣabha*;
the swan, the *gāndhāra*; and the *gavēlaya* [crane] cries out the *madhyama*. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 170)
Now, in the season of the blossoming of flowers, the cuckoos sing in the fifth note,
the cranes and curlews in the sixth, and the peacocks in the seventh. (Aṇuogaddārā 171)
Seven musical tones are declared to be non-victorious, namely:
the *sajja* played by the drum, and the *gomuhī* [drum] playing the *ṛṣabha* tone.
The *saṅkha* (conch) sounds in *gāndhāra*, while the *jhallarī* (cymbal) [sounds] in *madhyama*.
The *goṣṭhikā* (cowherd’s drum), established upon four legs, [sounds] the fifth note.
The *āḍambara*, the *dhēvaïya*, and the great drum (*mahābhērī*) as the seventh.
(Aṇuogaddārā 174) Regarding these seven notes, seven characteristics of the notes are taught, namely:
One who is industrious obtains his livelihood, and what he has done does not perish;
he becomes beloved by cows, sons, friends, and women. (Aṇuogaddārā 176)
Riṣabha indeed gave away his sovereignty, his military command, and his wealth— clothing,
perfumes, ornaments, women, and couches. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 177)

In Gandhāra, those who have mastered the application of song, those whose livelihood is scholarship, poets skilled in the arts, and others who have reached the further shore of the sciences through their wisdom— Aṇuogaddārāim 178.
Those who possess the middle tone are indeed happy-living;
one who possesses the middle tone eats, drinks, and gives. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 179)
Those ending with the fifth vowel (u) become lords of the earth, heroes,
compilers [of scriptures], and leaders of many groups. (Aṇuogaddārāim 180)
Furthermore,
those who live by cruel means are hunters,
fowlers, fishermen, and fishers. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 181)
Those whose minds are full of craving become makers of strife;
they are foot-servants, messengers, wanderers, and burden-carriers. (Aṇuogaddārā 182)

Of these seven notes, three groups are declared, namely: the *ṣaḍja* group, the *madhyama* group, and the *gāndhāra* group. Of the *ṣaḍja* group, seven modulations (*mūrcchanās*) are declared, namely:
[list follows].
Maṅgī, Kōravvīyā, Harīyā, Rayaṇī, and Sārakantā as the sixth, and the seventh is named Sārasī; these are the pure and well-prepared [verses]. (Aṇuogaddārāim 184)
Seven *mucchaṇā* (musical scales) of Majjhimagāma are taught, namely:
Uttaramandā, Rayaṇī, Uttarā, and Uttarāyatā.
And the *samōkkantā* and *sōvīrā* [tunes] are beautiful; the seventh is [the *suddha-sāraṅgā*].
(Aṇuogaddārāim 186) Seven *mucchanās* (melodic modulations) are declared for the village of Gandhāra, namely: [list follows].
Nandī, Khuḍḍiyā, Pūrimā, Caütthī, Suddhagandhārā, and Uttaragandhārā is the fifth; these are the *mūrcchanās*. (Aṇuogaddārā 188)
That which is well-spread out to the north is to be known as the sixth [direction] from all sides;
however, that which extends toward the north and has its tip facing north is the seventh, called *mucchā*. (Aṇuogaddārā 189)
How many musical notes (*svara*) are there? What is the source (*yoni*) of song? How many measures (*samaya*) are there in a breath? And how many forms (*ākāra*) does song have? (Aṇuogaddārā 190)

There are seven notes (*svara*) originating from the navel, and song is the source of sound; the breaths are equal to the measure of the song, and there are three forms (*ākāra*) of song. (Aṇuogaddārā 191)
Beginning, carrying through the middle,
and abandoning at the end— these are the three modes of singing a song. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 192)
He who knows the six faults, the eight qualities, the three types of wealth, and the two statements, is well-trained and will enter the midst of the assembly. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 193)

Frightened, hurried, desirous, and agitated—these should be understood one by one; along with a voice like a crow’s and an unpleasant nose [sound], these are the six defects of singing. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 194)
Complete, rhythmic, adorned, measured, likewise not faltering, sweet, even, and well-modulated— these are the eight qualities of song. (Aṇuogaddārā 195)

Song is that which is purified by the chest, throat, and vocal cords; sung with soft and melodious words arranged in metrical feet, accompanied by rhythmic beats and proper tempo, and endowed with the fullness of seven musical scales. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 196)
The seven vowels are equal in syllable, equal in word, equal in tempo, equal in rhythm, equal in musical mode, equal in inhalation and exhalation, and equal in movement. (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.197)
It should be free from fault, substantial, supported by reason, adorned, concise, refined,
moderate, and indeed sweet. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 198)
That which is even, half-even, and uneven everywhere—these are the three types of poetic meters; a fourth is not found. (Aṇuogaddārā 199)
Both the *sakkayā* and *pāyayā* modes of expression are indeed praised when sung within the circle of melodies (*saramaṇḍala*) as words spoken by the seers (*isibhāsiya*). (Aṇuogaddārā 200)

Who sings sweetly? Who sings harshly and roughly? Who sings in the *catūra* (fourfold) style? Who sings in the *vilambita* (slow) and *druta* (quick) styles? And furthermore, who sings in the *vissara* (dissonant/indistinct) style? (Aṇuogaddārāim 201)
The *sāman* singer sings sweetly; Kālī sings harshly and shrilly;
Gaurī sings in a quadruple measure; the one-eyed woman sings with a lingering tone; the slow woman sings hurriedly; and Piṅgalā, however, sings in a discordant voice. (Aṇuogaddārā 202)
Seven notes, three scales, twenty-one melodic modulations, and forty-nine cadences; thus is completed the Circle of Notes (Saramaṇḍala). — Aṇuogaddārāim 203.
That is the name of the being.
What are those eight names? Eightfold is the division of speech as it is taught, namely:
In the case of a direct description (*niddesa*), the first [case] occurs; the second, however, is used for instruction (*uvaēsaṇa*).
Then, in the act of making [the gift], the fourth [stage] occurs at the time of the formal offering;
the fifth is at the time of receiving; and the sixth is at the time of the recipient’s own acceptance. (Aṇuogaddārā 206)
The seventh [case-ending] is for the purpose of location (*sannihāṇa*), while the eighth becomes that of address (*amantaṇī*).
(Aṇuogaddārāim 207) Among those, the first case-ending is used in a designation (*niddesa*) such as "this is he" or "I am this."
Furthermore, in the second [instruction], one says: "Do this or that.
In the third, regarding the performance, it is said: "It was done by him or by me."
"Handi namo sāhāe" is the fourth [formula] at the time of setting out.
"Avaṇaya gēṇha ya ēttō itō vā" is the fifth [formula] regarding taking from here or there. (Āvaśyakaniryukti 209)

The sixth [case] is used for this [possessor] or that [belonging], in relation to ownership (*sāmisambandha*). Furthermore, the seventh [case] occurs in relation to this [locus], as well as in the sense of a locus of time (*ādhārakālabhāva*).
The eighth [day] may be called "Address," just as one says, "O young man!
This is its name based on meaning (aṭṭhanāma).
What, then, is the ninefold name? In the ninefold name, nine poetic sentiments (*kavvarasa*) are proclaimed, namely:
[list follows].
The heroic, the erotic, the marvelous, and the furious are to be understood;
as well as the terrifying, the loathsome, the comic, the pathetic, and the tranquil.
(Āvaśyaka Niryukti 214)
In that regard, the heroic rasa (*vīra-rasa*) is characterized by non-resentment, fortitude, and prowess in the face of renunciation, the practice of austerity, and the destruction of hostile beings.
(Āvaśyakaniryukti 215)

He is indeed called a great hero who, having renounced his kingdom and gone forth into homelessness, effects the destruction of the faction of the great enemies that are desire and anger. (Aṇuogaddārā 216)

The aesthetic sentiment (rasa) called the erotic (siṅgāra) is that which produces desire for sexual union; its characteristics are adornment, graceful movement, coquetry, laughter, and playful dalliance. (Aṇuogaddārā 217)
The girdle-string, sweet, charming with its grace, and causing madness in the hearts of youths, gives forth a sound that is unrestrained. (Aṇuogaddārā 218)
That which is astonishing, unprecedented, and yet experienced before— a taste characterized by the arising of joy and sorrow— is called the marvelous (*adbhuta*). — Aṇuogaddārāim 219.
What else in this world of living beings is more wonderful than this:
that even matters pertaining to the three periods of time are known through the words of the Jina?
(Aṇuogaddārāim 220)

The *raudra-rasa* (furious sentiment) has as its causes a form that generates fear, sound, darkness, anxiety, and stories [of violence]; it possesses the symptoms of delusion, agitation, despair, and death. — Aṇuogaddārā 221.

With a face distorted by a frown, your lips bitten until they are covered in blood, you slaughter the animal like an asura; O one of terrifying roar, you are exceedingly fierce and cruel. (Aṇuogaddārā 222)

The rasa named *velaṇaya* arises from the transgression of discipline, modesty, secrets, and the preceptor’s wife; its characteristic signs are the production of shame and apprehension. (Āvaśyakaniryukti 223)
"What worldly activity could be more shameful than this, that even a modest woman should be restrained by her elders when she is being praised for having many children? — Āvaśyaka Niryukti 224.

The disgusting (*bībhatsa*) rasa is produced from contact with the sight of impure, putrid, and loathsome things; it is characterized by world-weariness (*nirveda*) and non-violence (*avihiṃsā*). (Aṇuogaddārāim 225)
Fortunate indeed are those who, at all times, release this wretched body— which is filled with foul-smelling secretions, naturally malodorous, and defiled by many impurities. (Aṇuogaddārāim 226)
Laughter arising from distortions or delays in appearance, age, dress, or speech is mental laughter (*manappahāsa*); its characteristic mark is manifest joy. (Aṇuogaddārā 227)
Sāmā laughs as she gazes at her brother-in-law, who has awakened from sleep while still smeared with mascara;
indeed, her waist bows down under the weight of her breasts as she laughs. (Aṇuogaddārā 228)

The rasa of compassion (*karuṇa*) has as its characteristics sorrow, lamentation, desolation, and weeping, arising from separation from loved ones, bondage, slaughter, disease, calamity, and distress. (Aṇuogaddārā 229)
O Puttī! Through his repeated separation, your face has become exhausted from brooding, with eyes filled with tears reaching to your cheeks, and it has grown weak. (Aṇuogaddārāim 230)

That which arises from the concentration of a monk who has attained sleeplessness, characterized by tranquility and the absence of perturbation— that essence is to be known as "tranquil. (Aṇuogaddārāim 231)

Just as the lotus-like face of a sage shines with abundant splendor— free from guile, sincere, and possessing a serene, tranquil, and gentle gaze— so too does [the face of the one who has attained the state of a Kevalin]. (Aṇuogaddārāim 232)
These nine poetic sentiments, arising from the thirty-two types of defects,
are to be understood through the verses as being either pure or mixed.
(Aṇuogaddārā 233)

This concludes the nine names. What then are the ten names? The ten names are explained as being of ten kinds, namely: by the primary sense (*goṇṇa*), by the non-primary sense (*nogoṇṇa*), by the occasion of acquisition (*āyāṇapaēṇaṃ*), by the opposite term (*paḍivakkhapaēṇaṃ*), by excellence (*pāhaṇṇayāē*), by established doctrine (*anāisiddhantēṇaṃ*), by name (*nāmēṇaṃ*), by a part (*avayavēṇaṃ*), by combination (*sañjōgēṇaṃ*), and by measure (*pamāṇēṇaṃ*).

What is that which is metaphorical (*goṇṇa*)? Metaphorical: he endures, thus "the endurer" (*khamana*); he performs penance, thus "the penancer" (*tavaṇa*); he burns, thus "the burner" (*jalaṇa*); he blows, thus "the blower" (*pavaṇa*). This is the metaphorical. What is that which is non-metaphorical (*no-goṇṇa*)? Akunta, sakunta; amugga, samugga; amudda, samudda; alāla, palāla; akuliya, sakuliya; no pala, asati, thus *palāsa*; amāivāhae, māivāhae; abīyavāvae, bīyavāvae; no indaṃ govayati, thus *indagova*. This is the non-metaphorical. What is that by way of a technical term (*āyāṇapaeṇa*)? The Āvaṃtī, Cāuraṅgijja, Asaṅkhaya, Ahātatthijja, Addaijja, Jaṇṇaijja, Purisaïjja, Ēlaijja, Vīriya, Dhamma, Magga, Samosaraṇa, Āhattahīya, Gantha, Jamaïya. This is that by way of a technical term.

What is that by way of opposition (*paḍivakkhapaēṇa*)? When new villages, towns, cities, market towns, hamlets, fortified towns, ports, settlements, camps, and encampments are being established, the inauspicious becomes auspicious; fire becomes cool; poison becomes sweet; in salt-pans, sourness becomes salty; what is red becomes black; what is a bitter gourd (*lāu*) becomes a cucumber (*alāu*); what is beautiful becomes safflower (*kusumbha*); and when speaking, one speaks with a distorted voice. That is by way of opposition. What is that by way of excellence (*pāhaṇṇayāē*)? In an Aśoka grove, a Saptaparṇa grove, a Campaka grove, a Mango grove, a Nāga grove, a Punnāga grove, a sugarcane grove, a grape grove, or a Śāla grove. That is by way of excellence. What is that by way of non-eternal doctrine (*anāisiddhantēṇa*)? The category of motion (*dhammatthikāē*) up to the unit of time (*addhāsamaē*). That is by way of non-eternal doctrine. What is that by way of name (*nāmēṇa*)? By name, it is raised up after the name of one’s father or grandfather. That is by way of name. What is that by way of a part (*avayavēṇa*)?
Horned, tusked, fanged, winged, hooved,
scaled, hairy, two-legged, four-legged, many-legged, tailed, maned, and crested. (Aṇuogaddārā 236)
One should recognize a warrior by his girdle, a woman by her garment,
a granary by its grain, and a poet by a single verse. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 237)
— End of Text —

That is [classification] by way of components. What is that [classification] by way of conjunction (*sañjōga*)? Conjunction is declared to be fourfold, namely: conjunction of substance (*davva-sañjōga*), conjunction of space (*khētta-sañjōga*), conjunction of time (*kāla-sañjōga*), and conjunction of state (*bhāva-sañjōga*). What is that conjunction of substance? Conjunction of substance is declared to be threefold, namely: with consciousness (*sacitta*), without consciousness (*acitta*), and mixed (*mīsa*). What is that with consciousness? "With consciousness" refers to: a cowherd by means of cows; a buffalo-herder by means of buffaloes; a sheep-herder by means of ewes; a camel-keeper by means of camels. That is "with consciousness. What is that without consciousness? "Without consciousness" refers to: one with an umbrella by means of an umbrella; one with a staff by means of a staff; one with a cloth by means of a cloth; one with a jar by means of a jar; one with a basket by means of a basket. That is "without consciousness. What is that mixed? "Mixed" refers to: a plowman by means of a plow; a cart-driver by means of a cart; a charioteer by means of a chariot; a boatman by means of a boat. That is "mixed. That is conjunction of substance.

What, then, is the combination of location (*khetta-sañjōga*)? The combination of location includes Bhārata, Airāvata, Haimavata, Hairaṇyavata, Harivarṣa, Ramyakavarṣa, Devakuru, Uttarakuru, Pūrvavideha, and Aparavideha; or alternatively, it includes Māgadha, Mālava, Saurāṣṭra, Marahaṭṭha, Koṅkaṇa, and Kosala. This is the combination of location.

What, then, is the conjunction of time? The conjunction of time consists of the periods of: the most auspicious of the auspicious (*susama-susamā*), the auspicious (*susamā*), the auspicious-unfortunate (*susama-dūsama*), the unfortunate-auspicious (*dūsama-susamā*), the unfortunate (*dūsama*), and the most unfortunate of the unfortunate (*dūsamadūsama*); or else, it consists of the rainy season (*pāusa*), the monsoon (*vāsāratta*), autumn (*sarada*), winter (*hēmanta*), spring (*vasanta*), and summer (*gimha*). This is the conjunction of time.

What is that which is association by disposition (*bhāvasañjōga*)? Association by disposition is declared to be twofold: namely, the commendable (*pasattha*) and the non-commendable (*apasattha*). What is the commendable? The commendable is: one who possesses knowledge through knowledge, one who possesses vision through vision, and one who possesses conduct through conduct. That is the commendable. What is the non-commendable? The non-commendable is: one who possesses anger through anger, one who possesses pride through pride, one who possesses deceit through deceit, and one who possesses greed through greed. That is the non-commendable. That is association by disposition; that is association.

What is that which is measured by means of measurement (*pamāṇa*)? Measurement is declared to be fourfold, namely: nominal measurement (*nāmappamāṇa*), conventional measurement (*ṭhavaṇappamāṇa*), substantial measurement (*davvappamāṇa*), and modal measurement (*bhāvappamāṇa*). What is that which is nominal measurement? Nominal measurement is when the name "measurement" is applied to a single soul (*jīva*) or non-soul (*ajīva*), to many souls or non-souls, or to both, or to many of both. That is nominal measurement. What is that which is conventional measurement? Conventional measurement is declared to be sevenfold, namely: [list follows].

In the case of constellations, deities, families, heretical sects, and groups, names given for the sake of livelihood or out of personal preference are called "intentional names" (*ābhippāiya-nāma*); however, "conventional names" (*ṭhavaṇā-nāma*) are of seven kinds. (Aṇuogaddārā 239)

What then are the names based on the lunar mansions (*nakkhattanāma*)? Regarding the names based on the lunar mansions: one born under Kattikā is called Kattiya, Kattiyadatta, Kattiyadhamma, Kattiyasamma, Kattiyadeva, Kattiyadāsa, Kattiyasena, or Kattiyarakkhita. One born under Rohiṇī is called Rohiṇiya, Rohiṇidatta, Rohiṇidhamma, Rohiṇisamma, Rohiṇideva, Rohiṇidāsa, Rohiṇisena, or Rohiṇirakkhita. In this manner, the names should be stated for all the lunar mansions. Here are the summary verses (*saṅgahaṇigāhā*).
Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, then Āśleṣā, Maghā, and the two Phalgunīs. (Aṇuogaddārā 241)
Hasta, Citrā, Svāti, Viśākhā, and likewise Anurādhā;
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and likewise Uttarāṣāḍhā. (Aṇuogaddārā 242)
Abhijit,
Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and the two Bhādrapadās,
Revatī, Aśvinī, and Bharaṇī— this is the sequence of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). (Aṇuogaddārāim 243)
This is the section on the names of the constellations (*nakkhatta*).

What is the section on the names of the deities (*dēvaya*)? Regarding the names of the deities: those born under the constellation Agni are named Aggiya, Aggidinna, Aggidhamma, Aggisamma, Aggidēva, Aggidāsa, Aggisēna, and Aggirakkhiya. In this manner, the names of all the deities of the constellations should be recited. Herein, too, there are summary verses (*saṅgahaṇigāhā*): --------------------------------------------------------------------- (This is the section on the names of the constellations. What is the section on the names of the deities? Regarding the names of the deities: those born under the constellation Agni are named Aggiya, Aggidinna, Aggidhamma, Aggisamma, Aggidēva, Aggidāsa, Aggisēna, and Aggirakkhiya. In this manner, the names of all the deities of the constellations should be recited. Herein, too, there are summary verses:
Agni [is the deity] of Payāvaī; Rudra of Sōmā; Aditi of Bahassai;
the Serpents of Piti; Bhaga of Ajjamā; Savitā of Taṭṭhā; and Vāyu and Indagga [are the deities] of [the respective constellations].
(Āvaśyaka Niryukti 245)
Mitra, Indra, Nirṛti, Āp, Viśva, as well as Brahmā,
Viṣṇu, Vasu, Varuṇa, Aryaman, and Vivardhin— these are [the lords] of the constellations Puṣya,
Āśleṣā, and Jyeṣṭhā. (Aṇuogaddārāim 246)

What is that which is a name by divine designation (*dēvaya-nāma*)? What is that which is a name by family (*kula-nāma*)? A name by family includes: Ugra, Bhoga, Rājanya, Kṣatriya, Ikṣvāku, Nāta, and Kauravya. This is a name by family. What is that which is a name by religious sect (*pāsaṇḍa-nāma*)? Śramaṇa, Paṇḍaraga, Bhikkhu, Kāvāliya, Tāvasaya, and Parivrājaka. This is a name by religious sect. What is that which is a name by guild (*gaṇa-nāma*)? Malla, Malladinna, Malladhamma, Mallasamma, Malladeva, Malladāsa, Mallasena, and Mallarakkhita. This is a name by guild. What is that which is a name by livelihood (*jīviya-nāma*)? A name by livelihood includes: Avakara, Ukkuruḍa, Ujjhiya, Kajjava, and Suppa. This is a name by livelihood. What is that which is a name by inclination (*ābhippāiya-nāma*)? Amba, Niba, Babula, Palāsa, Siṇa, Pīlu, and Karīra. This is a name by inclination. This concludes the measurement of designations (*ṭhavaṇappamāṇa*).

What is that which is the measure of substance (*davvappamāṇa*)? The measure of substance is declared to be sixfold, namely: the substance-category of motion (*dhammatthikāya*), and so on, up to the unit of time (*addhāsamae*). This is the measure of substance. What is that which is the measure of state (*bhāvappamāṇa*)? The measure of state is declared to be fourfold, namely: compound (*sāmāsiya*), derivative (*taddhita*), verbal root (*dhātu*), and etymology (*nirutti*). What is that which is the compound? There are seven types of compounds, namely:
*Daṇḍa*, *bahuvrīhi*, *karmadhāraya*, and likewise *dvigu*.
The *tappurisa* compound occurs in the sense of non-ownership (*avvaībhāva*) and in the *egasēsa* (single-remainder) formation; [the locative case] is used in the seventh [case].
— Aṇuogaddārāim 248.

What is the *dvanda* compound? *Dvanda*: teeth and lips are *dantoṣṭha*; breasts and belly are *stanodara*; garment and bowl are *vastrapātra*; horses and buffaloes are *aśvamahiṣa*; snake and mongoose are *ahinakula*. This is *dvanda*. What is the *bahuvrīhi* compound? *Bahuvrīhi*: "In this mountain there are flowering *kuṭaja* and *kadamba* trees"; thus, this mountain is a "flowering-*kuṭaja-kadamba*" mountain. This is *bahuvrīhi*. What is the *karmadhāraya* compound? *Karmadhāraya*: a white bull is a *dhavalavṛṣabha*; a black deer is a *kṛṣṇamṛga*; a white cloth is a *śvetapaṭa*; a red cloth is a *raktapaṭa*. This is *karmadhāraya*. What is the *digū* (dvigu) compound? Three bitter things are *trikaṭuka*; three sweet things are *trimadhura*; three qualities are *triguṇa*; three cities are *tripura*; three arrows are *triśara*; three lotuses are *tripuṣkara*; three dots are *tribindu*; three paths are *tripatha*; five rivers are *pañcanada*; seven elephants are *saptagaja*; nine horses are *navaturaga*; ten villages are *daśagrāma*; ten cities are *daśapura*. This is *dvigu*.

What is that [compound] which is *tappurisa*? *Tappurisa*—a crow at a watering place is a "watering-place-crow" (*titthakāga*), an elephant in the forest is a "forest-elephant" (*vanahatthī*), a boar in the forest is a "forest-boar" (*vanavarāha*), a buffalo in the forest is a "forest-buffalo" (*vanamahisa*), a peacock in the forest is a "forest-peacock" (*vanamayūra*). This is *tappurisa*. What is that [compound] which is *avvaībhāva* (possessive)? *Avvaībhāva*—along the village, along the river, along the moat, along the path. This is *avvaībhāva*. What is that [compound] which is *ēgasēsa* (remainder of one)? *Egasēsa*—as one man is so are many men; as many men are so is one man. As one field is so are many fields; as many fields are so is one field. As one rice plant is so are many rice plants; as many rice plants are so is one rice plant. This is *ēgasēsa*. This is *sāmāsia* (compound). What is that [derivative] which is *taddhita*? *Taddhita* is declared to be of eight kinds.

The derivative name (taddhita-nāma) is eightfold: [derived from] action (kamma), craft (sippa), praise (silōē), association (sañjōga), proximity (samīvaō), collection (sañjūhē), sovereignty (issariya), and offspring (avacca). — Aṇuogaddārāim 250.
—The End—

What is that which is called by the name of action (*kammanāma*)? By the name of action are meant: grass-carriers, wood-carriers, leaf-carriers, cooks, distillers of *sōttiya* liquor, makers of hemp-cloth, basket-makers, makers of leather bags, and makers of *kolāla* (lac-resin). This is that which is called by the name of action. What is that which is called by the name of craft (*sippanāma*)? By the name of craft are meant: leather-workers, fletchers, tailors, weavers, makers of fine cloth, makers of *uēṭaṭa* (woolen cloth), makers of *varūḍa* (grass mats), makers of *muñja* grass products, carpenters, makers of umbrellas, makers of sacrificial posts, paper-makers, painters, ivory-workers, plasterers, stonemasons, and makers of *kōṭṭima* (carved stone reliefs). This is that which is called by the name of craft. What is that which is called by the name of title (*silōganāma*)? By the name of title are meant: ascetics (*samaṇa*), brahmins (*māhaṇa*), and all holy men (*savvātihī*). This is that which is called by the name of title. What is that which is called by the name of relationship (*sañjōganāma*)? By the name of relationship are meant: the king’s father-in-law, the king’s son-in-law, the king’s brother-in-law, the king’s brother, and the king’s sister’s husband. This is that which is called by the name of relationship. What is that which is called by the name of proximity (*samīvanāma*)? By the name of proximity are meant: a city near a mountain is *Girinagara*; a city near Vidisa is the city of *Vedisa*; a city near the Venna river is *Vennāyaḍa*; a city near Tagara is *Tagarāyaḍa*. This is that which is called by the name of proximity.

What is that which is called a compound name (*sañjūhanāma*)? It consists of *taraṅgavatīkārē*, *malayavatīkārē*, *attāṇusaṭṭhikārē*, and *bindukārē*. This is that which is called a compound name. What is that which is called a name of sovereignty (*issariyanāma*)? A name of sovereignty includes a king, a lord, a chief minister, a provincial governor, a householder, a wealthy merchant, a guild-leader, a caravan leader, or a general. This is that which is called a name of sovereignty. What is that which is called a name of offspring (*avaccanāma*)? A name of offspring includes the mother of an Arhat, the mother of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavaṭṭi*), the mother of a Baladeva, the mother of a Vāsudeva, the mother of a king, the mother of a republican leader (*gaṇarāja*), or the mother of a messenger (*vāyaga*). This is that which is called a name of offspring. This concludes the section on secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).

What is that which is the verbal root (*dhātu*)? The verbal roots are: *bhū* in the sense of existence, belonging to the *parasmaipada*; *ēdh* in the sense of growth; *spardh* in the sense of rivalry; *gādh* in the sense of stability and desire; *granth* in the sense of tying; and *bādh* in the sense of crushing. This is the verbal root. What is that which is etymology (*nirukti*)? Etymology is: he lies on the earth, thus "buffalo" (*mahiṣa*); he wanders and makes a buzzing sound, thus "bee" (*bhramara*); it glitters again and again, thus "pestle" (*musala*); it hangs like a monkey, thus "wood-apple" (*kapittha*); it acts with consciousness and becomes a pit, thus "mud" (*cikkhalla*); its ears are erect, thus "owl" (*ulūka*); a garland of a girdle, thus "girdle" (*mekhalā*). This is etymology. This is the criterion of state (*bhāvapramāṇa*). This is the criterion (*pramāṇa*). This is the tenfold name (*daśanāma*). This is the name (*nāma*).

What is that which constitutes measurement? Measurement is declared to be fourfold, namely: measurement of substance (*dravya-pramāṇa*), measurement of space (*kṣetra-pramāṇa*), measurement of time (*kāla-pramāṇa*), and measurement of state (*bhāva-pramāṇa*).

What is that which concerns the measurement of substance (*davvappamāṇa*)? The measurement of substance is declared to be of two kinds: namely, that produced by space-points (*paēsanipphanna*) and that produced by divisions (*vibhāganipphanna*). What is that produced by space-points? It consists of a single-atom (*paramāṇu-poggala*), a two-space-point entity, up to a ten-space-point entity, a numerable-space-point entity, an innumerable-space-point entity, and an infinite-space-point entity. This is that produced by space-points. What is that produced by divisions? It is declared to be fivefold: namely, measure (*māṇa*), weight (*ummāṇa*), depth (*ōmāṇa*), counting (*gaṇima*), and container-measure (*paḍimāṇa*). What is measure? It is declared to be of two kinds: namely, the measure of grain (*dhannamāṇappamāṇa*) and the measure of liquids (*rasamāṇappamāṇa*). What is the measure of grain? Two *asatīs* make one *pasatī*; two *pasatīs* make one *sētiyā*; four *sētiyās* make one *kulaya*; four *kulayas* make one *pattha*; four *patthas* make one *āḍhaga*; four *āḍhagas* make one *dōṇa*; sixty *āḍhagas* make the smallest *kumbha*; eighty *āḍhagas* make the middle *kumbha*; one hundred *āḍhagas* make the largest *kumbha*; and eight hundred *āḍhagas* make one *vāha*. What is the purpose of this measure of grain? By means of this measure of grain, there comes about the defining characteristic for determining the quantity of grain contained in bags, sacks, baskets, storehouses, and granaries. This is the measure of grain.

What is the measure of liquid (rasamānappamāṇa)? The measure of liquid is established as being four times greater than the measure of grain (dhannamāṇappamāṇa) and joined with internal divisions; namely: the sixty-fourth part, the thirty-second part, the sixteenth part, the eighth part, the fourth part, the half-measure (addhamāṇī), and the full measure (māṇī). Two sixty-fourths make one thirty-second; two thirty-seconds make one sixteenth; two sixteenths make one eighth; two eighths make one fourth; two fourths make one half-measure; and two half-measures make one full measure. What is the purpose of this measure of liquid? By means of this measure of liquid, there comes about the characteristic for determining the measure of liquids contained in jars, pots, bowls, pitchers, water-cans, milk-pails, buckets, and basins. This is the measure of liquid. This is the measure (māṇa).

What is measurement (*ummāṇa*)? Measurement is that by which things are measured, as follows: half a *karisa*, a *karisa*; half a *pala*, a *pala*; half a *tulā*, a *tulā*; half a *bhāra*, a *bhāra*. Two half-*karisas* make one *karisa*; two *karisas* make half a *pala*; two half-*palas* make one *pala*. A *tulā* consists of five hundred *palas*; ten *tulās* make half a *bhāra*; twenty *tulās* make one *bhāra*. What is the purpose of this system of measurement? By means of this system of measurement, there occurs the determination of the measure and the definition of substances such as leaf-incense (*patta-agaru*), tagara, *cōyaya*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), molasses (*gula*), and *macchaṇḍiya*. This is measurement.

What is that which constitutes an insult (*ōmāṇē*)? An insult is that by which one is insulted, namely: with the hand, or with a staff, or with a bow, or with a yoke, or with a measuring rod, or with a die, or with a pestle.
A staff, a bow, a yoke, a measuring rod, a die, and a pestle—each is four cubits in length.
And know that a rope of ten *nālikās* is the measure for the designation of a field (*ōmāṇa*).
(Aṇuogaddārā 254) For a building site, the measure is a *hasta*; for a field, a *daṇḍa* and a *dhanus*; and for a road, a *pantha*.
And know that eating with a tube is by way of the notion of measuring.
(Aṇuogaddārā 255)

What is the purpose of this measurement by weight (*ōmāṇappamāṇa*)? By means of this measurement by weight, there occurs the characteristic determination of the measurement by weight for substances contained in pits, heaps, baskets, boxes, cloths, walls, or enclosures. That is measurement by weight. What is measurement by counting (*gaṇima*)? Measurement by counting is that which is counted, as follows: one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, ten hundred thousand, and a crore. What is the purpose of this measurement by counting? By means of this measurement by counting, there occurs the characteristic determination of the measurement by counting for substances related to income, expenditure, food, clothing, and wages. That is measurement by counting.

What is that which is measurement (*paḍimāṇa*)? Measurement is that by which something is measured, as follows: *guñjā*, *kāgaṇī*, *nipphāva*, *kammamāsa*, *maṇḍalaka*, and *suvaṇṇa*. Five *guñjās* make one *kammamāsa*; four *kāgaṇīs* (relative to a *kāgaṇī*) make one *kammamāsa*; three *nipphāvas* make one *kammamāsa*—thus, a *kammamāsa* consists of four [units] relative to a *kāgaṇī*. Twelve *kammamāsas* make one *maṇḍalaka*; thus, forty-eight *kāgaṇīs* make one *maṇḍalaka*. Sixteen *kammamāsas* make one *suvaṇṇa*; thus, sixty-four *kāgaṇīs* make one *suvaṇṇa*. What is the purpose of this measurement-standard (*paḍimāṇappamāṇa*)? By means of this measurement-standard, there occurs the characteristic definition of the measurement-standard for substances such as gold, silver, gems, pearls, conch-shells, stones, and coral. This is measurement; this is that which is produced through division; this is the measurement of substances.

What is the measurement of space (*khetta-pamāṇa*)? The measurement of space is of two kinds: that produced by location (*padesa-nipphanna*) and that produced by division (*vibhāga-nipphanna*). What is that produced by location? It is [space] occupying one location-point (*ekapadesogāḍha*), occupying two location-points, occupying three location-points, up to ten location-points, occupying a numerable number of location-points, and occupying an innumerable number of location-points. That is what is produced by location. What is that produced by division?

The finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), the span (*vihatthi*), the cubit (*rayaṇī*), the forearm (*kucchī*), the bow (*dhanu*), the league (*gāuya*), the *yojana*, the line (*seḍhī*), the plane (*payara*), and likewise the world (*loga*) and the non-world (*aloge*) are to be understood. (Aṇuogaddārā 258)

What is that which is called the finger (aṅgula)? The finger is declared to be threefold: namely, the personal finger (āyaṅgula), the standard finger (ussēhaṅgula), and the measurement finger (pamāṇaṅgula). What is that which is called the personal finger? The personal finger is as follows: when humans exist at any given time, their own finger-measure is such that twelve fingers make the face, nine faces make a man endowed with the proper measure; two such men make a *dōṇī* [a specific weight] for a man endowed with the proper measure; and half a *bhāra* when weighed makes a man endowed with the proper measure.
Those who are endowed with the proportions of length, breadth, and height, possessed of the qualities of marks and minor characteristics,
and born of the highest lineage— these should be known as supreme men. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 260)
Furthermore, superior men are eight hundred finger-breadths in height; inferior men are ninety-six [finger-breadths]; and those in the middle are four more [than the latter]. (Aṇuogaddārā 261)
Whether inferior or superior, those who are indeed devoid of the essence of self-mastery inevitably fall into the state of servitude to the highest of men. (Aṇuogaddārā 262)
— End of Text —

By this measure of the *āyaṅgula* (the personal finger-breadth), six finger-breadths make a *pāda* (foot); two *pādas* make a *vihatthī* (span); two *vihatthis* make a *rayaṇī* (cubit); two *rayaṇīs* make a *kucchī*; two *kucchīs* make a *daṇḍa*, a *dhanu* (bow), a *juga*, a *nāliyā*, an *akkha*, or a *musala*. Two thousand *dhanus* make a *gāuya* (league); four *gāuyas* make a *jōyaṇa* (yojana). What is the purpose of this *āyaṅgula* measure? By this *āyaṅgula* measure—whatever humans exist at any given time, their own finger-breadths are used to measure wells, tanks, lakes, rivers, ponds, lotus-pools, oblong pools, canals, lakes, rows of lakes, series of lakes, rows of lakes, groves, gardens, forests, thickets, forest ranges, temples, assembly halls, pavilions, stupas, moats, ramparts, walls, watchtowers, battlements, gates, gate-towers, palaces, houses, shelters, caves, shops, crossroads, junctions of three roads, junctions of four roads, marketplaces, intersections, main highways, paths, carts, vehicles, yokes, *gillis*, *thillis*, litters, and carriages; as well as iron tools, iron cauldrons, ladles, seats, beds, pillars, utensils, vessels, and equipment; and even the *jōyanas* of the present day are measured by it. Briefly stated, it is taught to be of three kinds: namely, the linear finger-breadth (*sūiaṅgula*), the planar finger-breadth (*payaraṅgula*), and the cubic finger-breadth (*ghanaṅgula*). A line (*seḍhī*) one unit long and consisting of a single space-point is a linear finger-breadth. A linear finger-breadth multiplied by a linear finger-breadth is a planar finger-breadth. A planar finger-breadth multiplied by a linear finger-breadth is a cubic finger-breadth. "Venerable Sir, among these—the linear finger-breadth, the planar finger-breadth, and the cubic finger-breadth—which is less than which, which is more than which, which is equal to which, or which is distinguished from which? "The linear finger-breadth is the smallest; the planar finger-breadth is infinitely greater; the cubic finger-breadth is infinitely greater. That is the *āyaṅgula*. Now, what is the *ussehaṅgula* (the standard finger-breadth)? The *ussehaṅgula* is taught to be of many kinds, namely: [text continues].

An atom (*paramāṇu*), a water-dust particle (*tasareṇu*), a rabbit-dust particle (*rahareṇu*), the tip of a hair, a louse-egg, a louse, and a barley-corn (*yava*) increase eightfold in succession. (Aṇuogaddārā 264)

The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Ten Powers. You should retain it thus. When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the Venerable Ānanda was delighted and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessing which a Tathāgata claims the place of the Bull, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Brahmā that has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone else in the world. What are the ten? (1) Here, monks, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. This is the first power of a Tathāgata. (2) He understands as it really is the result of the undertaking of karmic actions past, future, and present, in terms of possibilities and causes. This is the second power of a Tathāgata. (3) He understands as it really is the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, together with their defilements, purifications, and emergence. This is the third power of a Tathāgata. (4) He understands as it really is the various dispositions and inclinations of beings. This is the fourth power of a Tathāgata. (5) He understands as it really is the world with its many and varied elements and spheres. This is the fifth power of a Tathāgata. (6) He understands as it really is the degrees of the faculties of other beings, other persons. This is the sixth power of a Tathāgata. (7) He recollects his manifold past abodes, including one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction, and many eons of both expansion and contraction: ‘There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; there too I had such a name... Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details. This is the seventh power of a Tathāgata. (8) With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: ‘These beings who engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and performed actions based on wrong views, having passed away, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower realms, or hell; whereas these beings who engaged in good conduct by body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right views, and performed actions based on right views, having passed away, have reappeared in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing and understands how they fare according to their kamma. This is the eighth power of a Tathāgata. (9) He understands as it really is the destruction of the taints. This is the ninth power of a Tathāgata. (10) Through the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself in this very life, attains, and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it through direct knowledge. This is the tenth power of a Tathāgata. Monks, these are the ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessing which a Tathāgata claims the place of the Bull, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Brahmā that has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone else in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four grounds for self-confidence of a Tathāgata, possessing which a Tathāgata claims the place of the Bull, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Brahmā that has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone else in the world. What are the four? (1) ‘I claim to be fully awakened regarding all things. If anyone should challenge me regarding this—whether in the present life, in the next life, or in the future life—saying: “You do not possess full awakening regarding this thing,” and if I do not see any ground for that, then I abide with confidence, fearless and secure. This is the first ground for self-confidence of a Tathāgata. (2) ‘I claim to have destroyed the taints. If anyone should challenge me regarding this—whether in the present life, in the next life, or in the future life—saying: “These taints are not destroyed in you,” and if I do not see any ground for that, then I abide with confidence, fearless and secure. This is the second ground for self-confidence of a Tathāgata. (3) ‘I teach the Dhamma to my disciples so that they may practice it rightly. If anyone should challenge me regarding this—whether in the present life, in the next life, or in the future life—saying: “Those who practice according to the Dhamma do not attain the supreme goal of the holy life, nor do they realize it for themselves through direct knowledge and dwell therein,” and if I do not see any ground for that, then I abide with confidence, fearless and secure. This is the third ground for self-confidence of a Tathāgata. (4) ‘I teach the Dhamma to my disciples so that they may practice it rightly. If anyone should challenge me regarding this—whether in the present life, in the next life, or in the future life—saying: “Those who practice according to the Dhamma fall away from the supreme goal of the holy life, and do not realize it for themselves through direct knowledge and dwell therein,” and if I do not see any ground for that, then I abide with confidence, fearless and secure. This is the fourth ground for self-confidence of a Tathāgata. Monks, these are the four grounds for self-confidence of a Tathāgata, possessing which a Tathāgata claims the place of the Bull, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Brahmā that has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone else in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of analytical knowledge of a Tathāgata, possessing which a Tathāgata claims the place of the Bull, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Brahmā that has not been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone else in the world. What are the four? (1) Here, monks, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the meaning of what has been said in various ways. This is the first kind of analytical knowledge of a Tathāgata. (2) He understands as it really is the Dhamma in what has been said in various ways. This is the second kind of analytical knowledge of a Tathāgata. (3) He understands as it really is the phrasing in what has been said in various ways. This is the third kind of analytical knowledge of a Tathāgata. (4) He

What is that which is called an atom (*paramāṇu*)? An atom is declared to be of two kinds: namely, the subtle (*suhuma*) and the conventional (*vavahāria*). Among these, that which is subtle is set aside [as beyond practical discourse]. Therein, that which is conventional arises as a conventional atom through the collection, conjunction, and coming together of infinite-times-infinite subtle matter-particles (*poggala*). [The interlocutor asks: "Venerable sir, would it penetrate the edge of a sword or the edge of a razor? [The Teacher replies: "Yes, it would penetrate. [The interlocutor asks: "Would it be cut or broken there? [The Teacher replies: "No, this is not possible; for indeed, no weapon has effect there. [The interlocutor asks: "Venerable sir, would it pass right through the midst of a mass of fire? [The Teacher replies: "Yes, it would pass through. [The interlocutor asks: "Venerable sir, would it be burned there? [The Teacher replies: "No, this is not possible; for indeed, no weapon has effect there."

“Venerable sir, if one were to pass right through the center of that great cloud, Pukkhara-saṃvaṭṭaga, would one pass through it? “Yes, one would pass through it. “Would one become wet there? “No, this is not possible; for indeed, no weapon has effect there. “Venerable sir, if one were to come swiftly against the current of the great river Gaṅgā, would one meet with destruction there? “Yes, one would meet with destruction. “Would one suffer injury or perish there? “No, this is not possible; for indeed, no weapon has effect there. “Venerable sir, if one were to plunge into a whirlpool of water or a drop of water, would one suffer injury or perish there? “No, this is not possible; for indeed, no weapon has effect there.”
That which cannot indeed be cut or broken even by an extremely sharp weapon,
they— the perfected ones— declare to be the atom (*paramāṇu*), the first of all measurements. (Aṇuogaddārā 266)
— End of Text —

Through the aggregation, collection, and coming together of infinite practical (*vāvahāriya*) atoms (*paramāṇu-poggala*), there arises that which is called a "minute particle" (*usaṇha-saṇhiyā*), or a "subtle particle" (*saṇhasaṇhiyā*), or a "dust mote in sunlight" (*uḍḍharēṇū*), or a "tassarēṇū" (a mote blown by the wind), or a "raharēṇū" (a mote in a sunbeam). Eight minute particles make one subtle particle; eight subtle particles make one dust mote in sunlight; eight dust motes in sunlight make one *tassarēṇū*; eight *tassarēṇūs* make one *raharēṇū*; eight *raharēṇūs* make one hair-tip (*vālagga*) of the humans of Devakuru and Uttarakuru; eight hair-tips of the humans of Devakuru and Uttarakuru make one hair-tip of the humans of Harivarṣa and Ramyakavarṣa; eight hair-tips of the humans of Harivarṣa and Ramyakavarṣa make one hair-tip of the humans of Haimavata and Hairaṇyavatavarṣa; eight hair-tips of the humans of Haimavata and Hairaṇyavatavarṣa make one hair-tip of the humans of Pūrvavideha and Aparavideha; and eight hair-tips of the humans of Pūrvavideha and Aparavideha make one "likkhā" (a nit).

Eight *likkhās* make one *jūyā*; eight *jūyās* make one *javamajjha*; eight *javamajjhas* make one *ussēhaṅgula*. By this measure of the *aṅgula*, six *aṅgulas* make a foot (*pāda*), twelve *aṅgulas* make a span (*vihatthī*), twenty-four *aṅgulas* make a cubit (*rayaṇī*), and forty-eight *aṅgulas* make a *kucchī*. Ninety-six *aṅgulas* make one staff (*daṇḍa*), or bow (*dhaṇu*), or yoke (*juga*), or *nāliya*, or axle (*akkha*), or pestle (*musala*). By this measure of the bow, two thousand bows make a *gāuya*, and four *gāuyas* make a *jōyaṇa*. What is the purpose of this *ussēhaṅgula*? By this *ussēhaṅgula*, the body dimensions of hell-beings, animals, humans, and gods are measured.

"Venerable sir, what is the extent of the body-sizes of hell-beings as they are taught? Gautama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those maintained by the state of existence (*bhavadhāraṇijjā*) and those produced by subsequent transformation (*uttaraveuvviyā*). Therein, that which is maintained by the state of existence is at its minimum an infinitesimal fraction of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and at its maximum five hundred *dhanus*. Therein, that which is produced by subsequent transformation is at its minimum a numerable fraction of a finger-breadth, and at its maximum one thousand *dhanus*."

"Lord, what is the extent of the body-size (śarīrāvagāhanā) of the hell-beings in the Jewel-Lustre Earth (Ratnaprabhā-pṛthivī)? Gautama, it is of two kinds, namely: that which is innate (bhavadhāraṇijjā) and that which is acquired through supernormal power (uttaravaikriyā). Therein, that which is innate is at its minimum an infinitesimal fraction (asaṅkhyeya-bhāga) of a finger-breadth (aṅgula), and at its maximum seven cubits (dhanu), three spans (ratni), and six finger-breadths. Therein, that which is acquired through supernormal power is at its minimum a numerable fraction (saṅkhyeya-bhāga) of a finger-breadth, and at its maximum fifteen cubits, two spans, and twelve finger-breadths."

"Venerable sir, what is the extent of the body-dimensions of the hell-beings in the Sakkarappabhā earth? Goyama, they are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those maintained by the natural state (*bhavadhāraṇijjā*) and those produced by subsequent transformation (*uttaraveuvviyā*). Among these, that which is maintained by the natural state is at its minimum an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and at its maximum fifteen *dhanus* and two and a half *ratnis*. Among these, that which is produced by subsequent transformation is at its minimum a calculable fraction of a finger-breadth, and at its maximum thirty-one *dhanus* and one *ratni*."

"Venerable sir, what is the extent of the body-measure of the hell-beings and others in the Vālukāprabhā earth? "Gautama, it is declared to be of two kinds: namely, the natural (bhavadhāraṇijjā) and the further-transformed (uttaravēuvviyā). Therein, that which is the natural is at its minimum an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth (aṅgula), and at its maximum thirty-one cubits (dhanu) and one span (rayaṇī). Therein, that which is the further-transformed is at its minimum a calculable fraction of a finger-breadth, and at its maximum sixty-two cubits and two spans."

In this manner, the question regarding all the earth-hells (*puḍhavī*) should be recited. In the Paṅkaprabhā hell, the body-sustaining (*bhavadhāraṇijjā*) [body] is at its minimum one *asaṅkhyeya* part of an *aṅgula*, and at its maximum sixty-two *dhanus* and two *ratnīs*. The secondary-transformed (*uttaravēuvviyā*) [body] is at its minimum a *saṅkhyeya* part of an *aṅgula*, and at its maximum one hundred and twenty-five *dhanus*. In the Dhūmaprabhā hell, the body-sustaining [body] is at its minimum one *asaṅkhyeya* part of an *aṅgula*, and at its maximum one hundred and twenty-five *dhanus*. The secondary-transformed [body] is at its minimum one *asaṅkhyeya* part of an *aṅgula*, and at its maximum two hundred and fifty *dhanus*. In the Tamaḥprabhā hell, the body-sustaining [body] is one *asaṅkhyeya* part of an *aṅgula* at its minimum, and two hundred and fifty *dhanus* at its maximum. The secondary-transformed [body] is at its minimum a *saṅkhyeya* part of an *aṅgula*, and at its maximum five hundred *dhanus*. "O Lord, what is the magnitude of the body-extension (*sarīrōgāhaṇā*) of the hell-beings (*nēraïya*) in the Tamatamaḥprabhā hell? "Gautama, it is declared to be of two kinds: namely, the body-sustaining and the secondary-transformed. Therein, that which is the body-sustaining is at its minimum one *asaṅkhyeya* part of an *aṅgula*, and at its maximum five hundred *dhanus*. Therein, that which is the secondary-transformed is at its minimum a *saṅkhyeya* part of an *aṅgula*, and at its maximum one thousand *dhanus*."

"Venerable Sir, what is the extent of the body-size of the Asura-kumāras declared to be? Gautama, it is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the natural (bhavadhāraṇijjā) and the supernaturally transformed (uttaravēuvviyā).
