Therein, that which is the natural body-size is at its minimum an infinitesimal fraction of a finger-breadth (aṅgula), and at its maximum seven *rayaṇīs*. Therein, that which is the supernaturally transformed body-size is at its minimum a numerable fraction of a finger-breadth, and at its maximum one hundred thousand *yojanas*. In this manner, according to the sequence of the Asura-kumāras, it should be stated up to the Stanita-kumāras."

"Venerable Sir, what is the extent of the body-measure (śarīrāvagāhanā) of the earth-bodied beings (puḍhavikāiya)? Goyama! At the minimum it is an incalculable fraction (asaṅkhejjabhāga) of an aṅgula, and at the maximum also an incalculable fraction of an aṅgula. This should be stated for the subtle (suhuma), the general (ōhiya), the incomplete (apajjattaga), and the complete (pajjattaga). It should be stated for the gross (bāyara), the general, the incomplete, and the complete. Thus it should be stated up to the complete gross air-bodied beings (vāukāiya)."

"O Venerable One, what is the extent of the body-occupation (*śarīrāvagāhanā*) of the vegetable-bodied beings (*vanaspatikāyika*) declared to be? O Gautama, it is at the minimum an incalculable fraction (*asaṃkhyeyabhāga*) of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and at the maximum slightly more than a thousand *yojanas*. For the subtle vegetable-bodied beings—whether general, or immature (*aparyāptaka*), or mature (*paryāptaka*)—the extent for all three is at the minimum an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth and at the maximum also an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth. For the gross vegetable-bodied beings, it is at the minimum an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth and at the maximum slightly more than a thousand *yojanas*; for the immature ones, it is at the minimum an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth and at the maximum also an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth; for the mature ones, it is at the minimum an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth and at the maximum slightly more than a thousand *yojanas*."

Regarding the question concerning two-sensed beings: O Gautama! At the minimum, an incalculable fraction (*asaṅkhyeya-bhāga*) of an *aṅgula*; at the maximum, twelve *yojanas*. For those who are immature (*aparyāptaka*), at the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum also an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*. For those who are mature (*paryāptaka*), at the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum twelve *yojanas*. Regarding the question concerning three-sensed beings: O Gautama! At the minimum, an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*; at the maximum, three *gavyūtas*. For those who are immature, at the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum also an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*. For those who are mature, at the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum three *gavyūtas*. Regarding the question concerning four-sensed beings: O Gautama! At the minimum, an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*; at the maximum, four *gavyūtas*. For those who are immature, at the minimum and at the maximum, an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*. For those who are mature, at the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum four *gavyūtas*. Regarding the question concerning five-sensed animals (*pañcendriya-tiryag-yoni*): O Venerable One, how large is the body-extent (*śarīra-avagāhanā*) declared to be? O Gautama! At the minimum, an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*; at the maximum, one thousand *yojanas*. Regarding the question concerning five-sensed aquatic animals: O Gautama! It is exactly the same. Regarding the question concerning spontaneously born (*saṃmūrchima*) five-sensed aquatic animals: O Gautama! At the minimum, an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*; at the maximum, one thousand *yojanas*. Regarding the question concerning immature spontaneously born five-sensed aquatic animals: O Gautama! At the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum also an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*. Regarding the question concerning mature spontaneously born five-sensed aquatic animals: O Gautama! At the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum one thousand *yojanas*. Regarding the question concerning womb-born (*garbha-vakrāntika*) five-sensed aquatic animals: O Gautama! At the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*; at the maximum, one thousand *yojanas*. Regarding the question concerning immature womb-born five-sensed aquatic animals: O Gautama! Regarding the question concerning mature womb-born five-sensed aquatic animals: O Gautama! At the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum one thousand *yojanas*. Regarding the question concerning four-footed terrestrial five-sensed animals: O Gautama! At the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*; at the maximum, six *gavyūtas*. Regarding the question concerning immature spontaneously born four-footed terrestrial animals: O Gautama! At the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum also an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*. Regarding the question concerning womb-born four-footed terrestrial animals: O Gautama! At the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*; at the maximum, six *gavyūtas*. Regarding the question concerning immature womb-born four-footed terrestrial animals: O Gautama! At the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum also an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*. Regarding the question concerning mature womb-born four-footed terrestrial animals: O Gautama! At the minimum an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula*, and at the maximum six *gavyūtas*. Question: What is the body size of five-sensed land-crawling reptiles (*bhūaparisappa-thalacara*)? Answer: Gautama! At the minimum, an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); at the maximum, several *gavyūtas*. Question: What is the body size of spontaneously born (*saṃmucchima*) land-crawling reptiles? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum, several *dhanus*. Question: What is the body size of the immature (*apajjattaga*) spontaneously born land-crawling reptiles? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum also an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth. Question: What is the body size of the mature (*pajjattaga*) spontaneously born land-crawling reptiles? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, a *saṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum, several *dhanus*. Question: What is the body size of womb-born (*gabbha*) land-crawling reptiles? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum, several *gavyūtas*. Question: What is the body size of the immature womb-born land-crawling reptiles? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum also an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth. Question: What is the body size of the mature womb-born land-crawling reptiles? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, a *saṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum, several *gavyūtas*. Question: What is the body size of five-sensed air-dwelling creatures (*khahayara*)? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum, several *dhanus*. Regarding spontaneously born air-dwellers, it should be stated exactly as for the spontaneously born land-crawling reptiles in all three categories (immature, mature, and womb-born). Question: What is the body size of womb-born air-dwellers? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum, several *dhanus*. Question: What is the body size of the immature womb-born air-dwellers? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum, an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth. Question: What is the body size of the mature womb-born air-dwellers? Answer: Gautama! Minimum, a *saṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; maximum, several *dhanus*. Herein, there are summary verses (*saṅgahaṇigāhā*), which are as follows: [Summary Verses] Minimum and maximum body sizes for the five-sensed classes of beings— Land-dwellers, water-dwellers, and those moving through the air— Are established here according to their respective types. The minimum is an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; The maximum is several *gavyūtas*, several *dhanus*, or several *yojanas*. For the spontaneously born, it is always an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth. For the womb-born, the minimum is an *asaṃkhyeya* part of a finger-breadth; The maximum is several *gavyūtas*, several *dhanus*, or several *yojanas*. Thus, the body measurements of the five-sensed beings are explained. This concludes the section on the body size of five-sensed beings. [End of Section] The second chapter, concerning the body size of five-sensed beings, is concluded. This concludes the second chapter of the *Prathamānuyoga*. May there be auspiciousness. The height of the spontaneously born (saṃmūrchima) beings is one thousand yojanas and several *gavyūtas*, then several yojanas, and for the two [types], it is several hundred bows (*dhanu*). (Aṇuogaddārā 268)
The height of the snakes is six *gavyūtas* and one thousand *yojanas*; that of the birds is one thousand *yojanas* and several *gavyūtas*, or up to several *dhanus*. (Aṇuogaddārā 269)
—End of Text—

"Venerable Sir, what is the extent of the body's dimensions for humans as it has been taught? Goyama! At the minimum, an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth (aṅgula); at the maximum, three-quarters of a league (gāuya). [Question: What is the extent for spontaneously born (saṃmucchima) humans? [Goyama! At the minimum, an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth; at the maximum also, an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth. [Question: What is the extent for womb-born (gabbhavakkantiya) humans? [Goyama! At the minimum, an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth; at the maximum, three-quarters of a league. [Question: What is the extent for immature (apajjattaga) womb-born humans? [Goyama! At the minimum, an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth; at the maximum also, an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth. [Question: What is the extent for mature (pajjattaga) womb-born humans? [Goyama! At the minimum, a calculable fraction of a finger-breadth; at the maximum, three-quarters of a league."

The types of bodies for the Vāṇamantara gods—the body for maintaining existence and the further transformative body—should be described just as they are for the Asurakumāras; and just as they are for the Vāṇamantaras, so too for the Jyotiṣkas.

"Lord, what is the extent of the body-size (śarīrāvagāhanā) of the gods in the Saudharma Kalpa? Gautama, it is of two kinds: the natural (bhavadhāraṇijjā) and the supernaturally transformed (uttaravēuvviyā). Therein, that which is the natural is at its minimum an incalculable fraction (asaṅkhējjaï-bhāga) of an aṅgula, and at its maximum seven *rayaṇīs*. Therein, that which is the supernaturally transformed is at its minimum a calculable fraction (saṅkhējjaïbhāga) of an aṅgula, and at its maximum one hundred thousand (*sayasahassa*) yojanas. This should be stated for the Īśāna Kalpa as well. Just as the question regarding the gods in the Saudharma Kalpa was asked, so should the questions regarding the gods of the remaining Kalpas be stated, up to the Acyuta Kalpa. In the Sanatkumāra [Kalpa], the natural body-size is at its minimum an incalculable fraction of an aṅgula, and at its maximum six *rayaṇīs*; the supernaturally transformed is as in the Saudharma. The natural body-size should be stated for the Māhendra [Kalpa] just as for the Sanatkumāra. In the Brahma-loka and Lāntaka [Kalpas], the natural body-size is at its minimum an incalculable fraction of an aṅgula, and at its maximum five *rayaṇīs*; the supernaturally transformed is as in the Saudharma. In the Mahāśukra and Sahasrāra [Kalpas], the natural body-size is at its minimum an incalculable fraction of an aṅgula, and at its maximum four *rayaṇīs*; the supernaturally transformed is as in the Saudharma. In all four—Ānata, Prāṇata, Āraṇa, and Acyuta—the natural body-size is at its minimum an incalculable fraction of an aṅgula, and at its maximum three *rayaṇīs*; the supernaturally transformed is as in the Saudharma."

Question regarding the gods of the *Gevijja* (Heavenly) realm: One body for sustaining existence (*bhavadhāraṇijja*) is taught; it is at its minimum an incalculable fraction (*asaṅkhyeya-bhāga*) of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and at its maximum two *ratni*s (cubits). Question regarding the gods who have attained the *Anuttara* (Highest) realm: One body for sustaining existence is taught; it is at its minimum an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth, and at its maximum one *ratni*. [Thus, for all [classes of beings], the two types of bodies for sustaining existence are at their minimum an incalculable fraction of a finger-breadth, and at their maximum they double successively. The *uttaravaikriya* (transformed) bodies are at their minimum a calculable fraction (*saṅkhēya*) of a finger-breadth, and at their maximum they double successively. In this manner, for the Asurakumāras and so forth, up to the inhabitants of the *Anuttara-vimāna*, the dimensions of their respective bodies should be declared.]

Briefly, it is declared to be threefold, namely: the linear finger (sūī-aṅgula), the superficial finger (payara-aṅgula), and the cubic finger (ghana-aṅgula). A line consisting of a single space-unit in length is the linear finger; a line multiplied by a line is the superficial finger; a superficial finger multiplied by a line is the cubic finger. Among these—the linear finger, the superficial finger, and the cubic finger—which is smaller, which is larger, which is equal, or which is superior to the others? The linear finger is the smallest; the superficial finger is an infinite-fold greater than that; the cubic finger is an infinite-fold greater than the superficial finger. This, then, is the height-measure finger (ussēha-aṅgula).

What is that which is the *pramāṇāṅgula* (the standard finger-breadth)? Regarding the *pramāṇāṅgula*: for each individual Universal Monarch (*cāturanta-cakravartin*) possessing the fourfold sovereignty, there is described a golden coin (*kāgaṇi-ratna*) made of eight kinds of gold, having six faces, twelve sides, eight corners, and shaped like a die (*ahigaraṇi*). Each single corner of that coin is one *utsedhāṅgula* in width; that [length] is half an *aṅgula* for the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra. When multiplied by a thousand, that becomes a *pramāṇāṅgula*. By this measure of the *aṅgula*, six *aṅgulas* make a foot (*pāda*); two feet make a span (*vihatthī*); two spans make a *rayaṇī*; two *rayaṇīs* make a *kucchī*; two *kucchīs* make a bow (*dhanu*); two thousand bows make a *gāuya* (four miles); and four *gāuyas* make a *yojana*. What is the purpose of this *pramāṇāṅgula*? By this *pramāṇāṅgula*, the length, width, height, depth, and circumference of the earths, the strata, the netherworlds (*pātāla*), the abodes, the levels of the abodes, the hells, the rows of hells, the levels of the hells, the celestial realms (*kalpa*), the palaces (*vimāna*), the rows of palaces, the levels of the palaces, the peaks (*ṭaṅka*), the summits (*kūḍa*), the mountains (*sela*), the peaks (*siharī*), the plateaus (*pabbhāra*), the regions (*vijaya*), the intermediate ranges (*vakkhāra*), the continents (*vāsa*), the mountain ranges (*vāsahara*), the mountains (*pavvaya*), the shores (*velā*), the walls (*vēiyā*), the gates (*dāra*), the archways (*toraṇa*), the islands (*dīva*), and the oceans (*samudda*) are measured. Briefly, it is threefold: the linear finger-breadth (*seḍhī-aṅgula*), the planar finger-breadth (*payara-aṅgula*), and the cubic finger-breadth (*ghana-aṅgula*). An incalculable number of millions of *koṭis* of *yojanas* is a line (*seḍhī*). A line multiplied by a line is a plane (*payara*). A plane multiplied by a line is a world-system (*loga*). A world-system multiplied by a calculable number is calculable world-systems; multiplied by an incalculable number is incalculable world-systems; multiplied by an infinite number is infinite world-systems. Among these—the linear finger-breadth, the planar finger-breadth, and the cubic finger-breadth—which is less than, more than, equal to, or specifically greater than the others? The linear finger-breadth is the least; the planar finger-breadth is incalculably greater; the cubic finger-breadth is incalculably greater. That is the *pramāṇāṅgula*. That is the derived from division. That is the measurement of space (*khetta-pamāṇa*).
What is the measure of time? The measure of time is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that produced by place (*pradeśa-niṣpanna*) and that produced by division (*vibhāga-niṣpanna*).

What is that which is produced by space (*pradeśaniṣpanna*)? That which is produced by space exists for one moment, two moments, three moments, up to ten moments, a numerable number of moments, or an innumerable number of moments. This is that which is produced by space.
What is that which is produced by division (*vibhāganiṣpanna*)? That which is produced by division—
The units of time are the samaya, āvalikā, muhūrta, day, night, fortnight, month,
year, yuga, palya, sāgara, utsarpiṇī, and parivarta. (Aṇuogaddārāim 274)
—End of Text—

What is that [time]? I shall provide an exposition of time (*samaya*). Suppose there were a weaver’s son who was young, strong, in the prime of life, youthful, free from illness, with steady hands, possessing firmness in his arms, hands, feet, sides, back, chest, and thighs; whose limbs were well-developed; whose arms were like a pair of palms joined together or like iron bars; whose body was compact and well-knit through the constant striking of leather straps, whips, and fists; who was endowed with great physical strength; capable of leaping, running, racing, and exertion; clever, dexterous, experienced, skillful, intelligent, expert, and proficient in his craft. Taking a large piece of cloth, whether made of cotton (*paṭasāḍiya*) or silk (*paṭṭasāḍiya*), he would, in an instant, pull it out by the measure of a hand. In this regard, the challenger (*cōyaē*) said to the expositor (*pannavaya*): "Is that which is the time taken by that weaver’s son to pull out the piece of cotton or silk cloth by the measure of a hand in an instant considered a *samaya*? "No, that is not correct," [the expositor replied]. "Why? Because a single piece of cloth is produced through the collection, assembly, and coming together of a number of threads (*tantū*). While the upper thread is not yet cut, the lower thread cannot be cut. At one moment the upper thread is cut; at another moment the lower thread is cut. Therefore, that [instant] is not a *samaya*. To the expositor speaking thus, the challenger said:

"At the time when the upper thread of that cotton cloth or silk cloth is cut by the weaver’s apprentice, does that constitute a *samaya* (unit of time)? It does not. Why? Because a single thread is produced through the conjunction, collection, and assembly of a finite number of filaments (*pamha*). When the upper filament is not yet cut, the lower filament is not cut; at one time the upper filament is cut, and at another time the lower filament is cut. Therefore, that does not constitute a *samaya*. To the teacher who speaks thus, the questioner says this: 'At the time when the upper filament of that thread is cut by the weaver’s apprentice, does that constitute a *samaya*? It does not. Why? Because a single filament is produced through the conjunction, collection, and assembly of infinite aggregations (*saṅghāya*). When the upper aggregation is not disintegrated, the lower aggregation is not disintegrated; at one time the upper aggregation is disintegrated, and at another time the lower aggregation is disintegrated. Therefore, that does not constitute a *samaya*. Furthermore, O venerable ascetic, a *samaya* is declared to be even more subtle than that. An *āvalikā* is said to be the conjunction, collection, and assembly of an infinite number of *samayas*. A number of *āvalikās* equal to a finite number constitutes an inhalation (*ūsāsa*), and a number of *āvalikās* equal to a finite number constitutes an exhalation (*nīsāsa*')."
For a person who is healthy, free from disease, and unafflicted,
this single inhalation and exhalation is called one breath (pāṇu). — Āvaśyaka Niryukti 276.
Seven *pāṇus* make one *thōva*; seven *thōvas* make one *lava*;
seventy-seven *lavas* are explained as one *muhutta*. (Aṇuogaddārā 277)
Three thousand, seven hundred and seventy-three breaths— this is declared as a *muhūrta* by all those possessed of infinite knowledge. (Aṇuogaddārā 278)

The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Śubhavyūha. He had a son named Candraprabha Kumāra. At that time, the Tathāgata named Sarvalokapriyadarśana appeared in the world. When the prince heard that the Buddha had appeared in the world, he went to the Buddha’s presence with five hundred ministers and five hundred maidens. Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the Buddha and sat to one side. Then the Tathāgata Sarvalokapriyadarśana, knowing the prince’s roots of goodness were mature, preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for him. After hearing this sūtra, the prince attained the stage of non-retrogression. Subsequently, he renounced the world, practiced the bodhisattva path, and after passing through many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, he finally became a Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. The five hundred ministers became his śrāvaka disciples, and the five hundred maidens became pratyekabuddhas. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “Do you think that the prince Candraprabha at that time was someone else? You should not view it in this way; he was none other than me. The five hundred ministers were the five hundred bhikṣus who now follow me. And the five hundred maidens are the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who now follow me. Because I formerly made offerings to that Buddha and heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, I have now attained supreme, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most honored among all dharmas, and it is the foremost of all teachings. If there are those who can hear, accept, hold, read, recite, and explain its meaning to others, they shall quickly attain supreme, perfect enlightenment. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: “Candraprabha, having heard the Dharma, Attained the stage of non-retrogression. After passing through immeasurable kalpas, He became a Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī. His life span was eighty-four thousand years, And his light shone for eighty-four yojanas. The five hundred ministers became his disciples, And the five hundred maidens became pratyekabuddhas. Because I formerly heard this sūtra, I have now become a Buddha. Therefore, you should all diligently seek it; This is the foremost of all teachings. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “If there are good men or good women who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, accept, hold, read, recite, and explain it to others, they shall all attain supreme, perfect enlightenment. Why is this? Because this sūtra is the most honored among all dharmas, and it is the foremost of all teachings. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “Suppose there is a man who, out of compassion for all living beings, takes up Mount Sumeru and carries it on his head for a hundred thousand million billion kalpas. Or suppose another man takes up the entire great trichiliocosm and carries it on his head for a hundred thousand million billion kalpas. Or suppose yet another man takes up all the worlds in the ten directions and carries them on his head for a hundred thousand million billion kalpas. If there is a fourth person who hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and accepts, holds, reads, recites, and explains it to others, the merit of the latter would be far greater than the merit of the former three. Why is this? Because this sūtra is the most honored among all dharmas, and it is the foremost of all teachings. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “Suppose there is a man who, out of compassion for all living beings, fills the great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and gives it as a gift to all the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas. If there is another person who hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and accepts, holds, reads, recites, and explains it to others, the merit of the latter would be far greater than the merit of the former. By this measure of a *muhūrta*, thirty *muhūrtas* constitute a day and night (*ahōratta*); fifteen days and nights constitute a fortnight (*pakkha*); two fortnights constitute a month (*māsa*); two months constitute a season (*uū*); three seasons constitute a solstice (*ayaṇa*); two solstices constitute a year (*saṃvacchara*); five years constitute a *yuga*; twenty *yugas* constitute a century; ten centuries constitute a millennium (*vāsasahassa*); a hundred millennia constitute a hundred-thousand-year period (*vāsasayasahassa*); eighty-four hundred-thousand years constitute one *puvvaṅga*; eighty-four hundred-thousand *puvvaṅgas* constitute one *puvva*; eighty-four hundred-thousand *puvvas* constitute one *tuḍiyaṅga*; eighty-four hundred-thousand *tuḍiyaṅgas* constitute one *tuḍiya*; eighty-four hundred-thousand *tuḍiyas* constitute one *aḍaḍaṅga*; eighty-four hundred-thousand *aḍaḍaṅgas* constitute one *aḍaḍa*. In this same manner: *avavaṅga*, *avava*; *huhuyaṅga*, *huhu*; *uppalaṅga*, *uppala*; *paümaṅga*, *paüma*; *nalinaṅga*, *nalina*; *atthaniuraṅga*, *atthaniura*; *aüyaṅga*, *aüa*; *naüyaṅga*, *naüa*; *paüyaṅga*, *paüa*; *cūliyaṅga*, *cūliyā*; *sīsapahēliyaṅga*: eighty-four hundred-thousand *sīsapahēliyaṅgas* constitute one *sīsapahēliyā*. By this much is the calculation [reckoned], and by this much is the scope of calculation; beyond this, it proceeds by way of analogy (*ōvamiya*).

What is that? It is the *ovamie* (comparative measure). The *ovamie* is of two kinds: the *paliovame* (palyopama) and the *sāgarovame* (sāgaropama). What is the *paliovame*? It is declared to be threefold: the *uddhārapali ovame*, the *addhāpali ovame*, and the *khettapali ovame*. What is the *uddhārapali ovame*? It is declared to be twofold: the subtle (*suhuma*) and the conventional (*vāvahāriya*). Therein, the subtle one is set aside. As for the conventional one: suppose there were a granary (*palla*) one *yojana* in length and breadth, and one *yojana* in height, its circumference being three times that with a slight excess. Suppose this granary were filled to the brim and packed tightly with the tips of hair (*vālagga-koḍī*), each hair-tip grown over seven days—increasing by one, two, or three days up to the maximum of seven days—and such that those hair-tips could not be burned by fire, nor carried away by wind, nor broken, nor destroyed, nor reduced to dust. Then, by removing one hair-tip at each successive moment (*samaya-samaye*), the time required until that granary becomes exhausted, depleted, free of residue, and finished—that is the conventional *uddhārapali ovame*.
If the square of these [numbers] were multiplied ten times over, that would be the measure of one *uddhvasāgarovama* (elevated ocean-measure) of a merchant. (Aṇuogaddārā 281)

What is the purpose of these conventional *uddhāra-palyopamas* and *sāgaropamas*? [Answer: There is no purpose whatsoever for them; they are merely used to provide a conceptual illustration (*pannavaṇā*). This concludes the section on conventional *uddhāra-palyopamas*.

What, then, is the subtle *uddhāra-palyopama*? It is as follows: Suppose there were a granary (*palla*) one *yojana* in length and breadth, and one *yojana* in height, its circumference being three times that with a slight excess. This granary is filled to the brim and packed tightly with the tips of hair (*vālagga-kōḍī*) grown for at most seven nights. Therein, each single hair-tip is divided into an infinite number of fragments. Those hair-tips are an infinite-fold smaller than the range of vision, yet an infinite-fold larger than the body-range of a subtle algae-organism (*paṇaga-jīva*). Those hair-tips would not be burned by fire, nor carried away by wind, nor decompose, nor crumble, nor quickly turn into dust. Then, by removing one hair-tip at each successive moment (*samaya*), the time required until that granary becomes exhausted, void, free of residue, and finished—that is the subtle *uddhāra-palyopama*.
Ten times ten million squared (a koṭākoṭī) of these [units] would be the measure of one subtle *addhāsāgarōvama* (time-measure of an ocean). — Aṇuogaddārāim 283.

What is the purpose of these subtle *uddhāra-palyopamas* and *sāgaropamas*? By means of these *sāgaropamas*, the enumeration of the islands and oceans is apprehended. "Bhante, how many islands and oceans are there according to this enumeration? "Gautama, as many as are the units of time (*samayas*) in two and a half *uddhāra-sāgaropamas*, so many are the islands and oceans. That is the subtle *uddhāra-palyopama*; that is the *uddhāra-palyopama*.

What is that which is called *addhāpalyopama* (the metaphoric measure of time)? It is declared to be of two kinds: the subtle (*suhuma*) and the conventional (*vāvahāriya*). Of these, the subtle one is set aside for now. As for the conventional one: suppose there were a granary (*palla*) one *yojana* in length and breadth, and one *yojana* in height, its circumference being three times that plus a fraction more. Suppose this granary were filled to the brim with the tips of the hair of a single downy hair (*vālaggakōḍī*), increasing by one hair-tip each day until it was full. Suppose those hair-tips could not be burned by fire, nor destroyed, nor reduced to dust. Then, at the passing of every hundred years, if one were to remove a single hair-tip, the time required for that granary to become exhausted, depleted, leveled, and finished—that is the conventional *addhāpalyopama*.
If the bedding of these [beings] were to be multiplied tenfold, it would constitute the measure of one *addhāsāgarovama* (half-aeon) for a worldly person (*vavahāriya*). (Aṇuogaddārā 285)

What is the purpose of these conventional units of time, the *palyopama* and *sāgaropama*? There is no practical purpose whatsoever for these conventional *palyopama* and *sāgaropama* units; they are merely explained for the sake of exposition. Such is the conventional *palyopama*.

What, then, is the subtle *addhāpalyopama* (subtle time-measure based on a pit)? The subtle *addhāpalyopama* is as follows: suppose there were a pit one *yojana* in length and breadth, and one *yojana* high, with a circumference three times that plus a fraction more. Suppose this pit were filled to the brim with the tips of the hair of infants—one, two, and so on—up to a hundred years old. Then, from that [pile], one by one, an infinite number of fragments would be made. Those hair-tips are an infinite-th part of the range of vision, yet they are an infinite-fold greater than the body-range of a minute green mold (*panaka*) living being. Those hair-tips would not be burned by fire, nor would they be destroyed, nor would they quickly become putrid. Then, at the passing of each hundred years, one hair-tip is removed. By such a duration of time, that pit becomes exhausted, depleted, and finished. That is the subtle *addhāpalyopama*.
If the bedding of these [beings] were multiplied ten times over a koṭi-koṭi, that would be the measure of one subtle *addhāsāgarovama*. (Aṇuogadārā 287)

What is the purpose of these subtle time-measures, the *palyopamas* and *sāgaropamas*? By means of these subtle time-measures, the *palyopamas* and *sāgaropamas*, the lifespans of hell-beings, sub-human beings, humans,
and gods are measured.

“Bhante, for how long is the lifespan of hell-beings declared to be? At the minimum, ten thousand years; at the maximum, thirty-three *sāgaropamas*. [This is] as described in the *Pannavaṇā* (Exposition) in the chapter on the lifespan of all beings. [Question: For hell-beings of the *Ratnaprabhā* (Jewel-Lustre) earth? [Answer: At the minimum, ten thousand years; at the maximum, one *sāgaropama*. [Question: For incomplete (*aparyāptaka*) hell-beings of the *Ratnaprabhā* earth? [Answer: At the minimum, an *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, also an *antarmuhūrta*. [Question: For complete (*paryāptaka*) hell-beings of the *Ratnaprabhā* earth? [Answer: O Gautama, at the minimum, ten thousand years minus an *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, one *sāgaropama* minus an *antarmuhūrta*.”

Question regarding the hell-beings of the Sakkarappabhā earth: at the minimum, one *sāgarovama*; at the maximum, three *sāgarovamas*. In this manner, the questions for the remaining earths should be stated: for the hell-beings of the Vāluyappabhā earth, at the minimum three *sāgarovamas*, at the maximum seven *sāgarovamas*; for the hell-beings of the Paṅkappabhā earth, at the minimum seven *sāgarovamas*, at the maximum ten *sāgarovamas*; for the hell-beings of the Dhūmappabhā earth, at the minimum ten *sāgarovamas*, at the maximum seventeen *sāgarovamas*; for the hell-beings of the Tamappabhā earth, at the minimum seventeen *sāgarovamas*, at the maximum twenty-two *sāgarovamas*. "Bhante, for the hell-beings of the Tamatamā earth, how long [is the duration]? "Goyama, at the minimum twenty-two *sāgarovamas*, at the maximum thirty-three *sāgarovamas*."

"Venerable Sir, regarding the question of the Asura-kumāras: at the minimum ten thousand years, at the maximum slightly more than one *sāgaropama*. Regarding the question of the Asura-kumāra goddesses: at the minimum ten thousand years, at the maximum four and a half *palyopamas*. Venerable Sir, regarding the Nāga-kumāras: at the minimum ten thousand years, at the maximum slightly less than two *palyopamas*. Venerable Sir, regarding the Nāga-kumāra goddesses: at the minimum ten thousand years, at the maximum slightly less than one *palyopama*. Just as it has been stated for the Nāga-kumāra gods and goddesses, so it should be recited for all [the other classes] up to the Stanita-kumāra gods and goddesses."

[Question on] earth-bodied beings: [The answer is] at least one *antarmuhūrta*, at most twenty-two thousand years. [Question on] subtle earth-bodied beings—both those that are non-evolved (*aparyāpta*) and those that are evolved (*paryāpta*]: Gautama! For all three, at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most one *antarmuhūrta*. [Question on] gross earth-bodied beings: Gautama! At least one *antarmuhūrta*, at most twenty-two thousand years. [Question on] non-evolved gross earth-bodied beings: Gautama! At least and at most one *antarmuhūrta*. [Question on] evolved gross earth-bodied beings: Gautama! At least one *antarmuhūrta*, at most twenty-two thousand years minus one *antarmuhūrta*. In this same manner, the question and statement regarding the remaining types of beings should be recited.

For water-bodied beings (*āukāiya*), the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is seven thousand years. For subtle water-bodied beings (*suhuma-āukāiya*), whether they are non-evolved (*apajjattaga*) or evolved (*pajjattaga*), the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is also one *antōmuhutta*. For gross water-bodied beings (*bādara-āukāiya*), it is as for the general [category]; for non-evolved gross water-bodied beings, the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is also one *antōmuhutta*. For evolved gross water-bodied beings, the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is seven thousand years less one *antōmuhutta*.

For fire-bodied beings (*teukkāiya*), the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is three days and nights. For subtle fire-bodied beings (*suhuma-teukkāiya*), whether they are non-evolved (*apajjattaga*) or evolved (*pajjattaga*), the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is also one *antōmuhutta*. For gross fire-bodied beings (*bādara-teukkāiya*), the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is three days and nights. For non-evolved gross fire-bodied beings, the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is also one *antōmuhutta*. For evolved gross fire-bodied beings, the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is three days and nights less one *antōmuhutta*.

For wind-bodied beings (*vāukāiya*), the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is three thousand years. For subtle wind-bodied beings (*suhuma-vāukāiya*), whether general, incomplete (*apajjattaga*), or complete (*pajjattaga*), for all three the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is also one *antōmuhutta*. For gross wind-bodied beings (*bādara-vāukāiya*), the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is three thousand years. For incomplete gross wind-bodied beings, the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is also one *antōmuhutta*. For complete gross wind-bodied beings, the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is three thousand years less one *antōmuhutta*. For plant-bodied beings (*vaṇassaïkāiya*), the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is ten thousand years. For subtle plant-bodied beings (*suhuma-vaṇassaïkāiya*), whether general, incomplete, or complete, for all three the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is also one *antōmuhutta*. For gross plant-bodied beings (*bādara-vaṇassaïkāiya*), the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is ten thousand years. For incomplete gross plant-bodied beings, both the minimum and the maximum are one *antōmuhutta*. For complete gross plant-bodied beings, the minimum is one *antōmuhutta* and the maximum is ten thousand years less one *antōmuhutta*.

Question regarding two-sensed beings: at the minimum, one muhūrta; at the maximum, twelve years. Question regarding immature (aparyāptaka) two-sensed beings: O Gautama! at the minimum, one muhūrta; at the maximum, also one muhūrta. Question regarding mature (paryāptaka) two-sensed beings: O Gautama! at the minimum, one muhūrta; at the maximum, twelve years less one muhūrta.

Question regarding three-sensed beings: [The duration] is at minimum one *antarmuhūrta* and at maximum forty-nine days and nights. Question regarding immature (*aparyāptaka*) three-sensed beings: O Gautama! At minimum one *antarmuhūrta* and at maximum also one *antarmuhūrta*. Question regarding mature (*paryāptaka*) three-sensed beings: O Gautama! At minimum one *antarmuhūrta* and at maximum forty-nine days and nights less one *antarmuhūrta*.

"Venerable Sir, what is the duration of life declared for four-sensed beings? Goyama! At the minimum, one muhūrta; at the maximum, six months. Regarding the question concerning immature four-sensed beings: Goyama! At the minimum, one muhūrta; at the maximum, also one muhūrta. Regarding the question concerning mature four-sensed beings: Goyama! At the minimum, one muhūrta; at the maximum, six months less one muhūrta."

Question: [What is the lifespan] of five-sensed animals of the animal realm? Answer: Gautama! At the minimum, one *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, three *palyopamas*. Question: [What is the lifespan] of five-sensed aquatic animals of the animal realm? Answer: Gautama! At the minimum, one *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, one *pūrvakoṭī*. Question: [What is the lifespan] of spontaneously born (*saṃmūrchima*) five-sensed aquatic animals of the animal realm? Answer: Gautama! At the minimum, one *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, one *pūrvakoṭī*. Question: [What is the lifespan] of immature (*aparyāptaka*) spontaneously born five-sensed aquatic animals? Answer: Gautama! At the minimum, one *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, also one *antarmuhūrta*. Question: [What is the lifespan] of mature (*paryāptaka*) spontaneously born five-sensed aquatic animals? Answer: Gautama! At the minimum, one *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, one *pūrvakoṭī* less one *antarmuhūrta*. Question: [What is the lifespan] of womb-born (*garbhavyutkrāntika*) five-sensed aquatic animals? Answer: Gautama! At the minimum, one *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, one *pūrvakoṭī*. Question: [What is the lifespan] of immature womb-born five-sensed aquatic animals? Answer: Gautama! At the minimum, one *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, also one *antarmuhūrta*. Question: [What is the lifespan] of mature womb-born five-sensed aquatic animals? Answer: Gautama! At the minimum, one *antarmuhūrta*; at the maximum, one *pūrvakoṭī* less one *antarmuhūrta*.

Regarding the question on the maximum lifespan of five-sensed, four-footed terrestrial beings: it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most three *palyopamas*. Regarding the question on spontaneously born (*saṃmucchima*) five-sensed, four-footed terrestrial beings: O Gautama! it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most eighty-four thousand years. Regarding the question on immature (*apajjattaya*) spontaneously born five-sensed, four-footed terrestrial beings: O Gautama! it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most also one *antarmuhūrta*. Regarding the question on mature (*pajjattaya*) spontaneously born five-sensed, four-footed terrestrial beings: O Gautama! it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most eighty-four thousand years minus one *antarmuhūrta*.

Regarding womb-born (gabbhavakkantiya) four-footed terrestrial five-sensed beings, O Gautama, [the maximum life span] is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most three *palyopamas*. Regarding incomplete (apajjattaga) womb-born four-footed terrestrial five-sensed beings, O Gautama, it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most also one *antarmuhūrta*. Regarding complete (pajjattaga) womb-born four-footed terrestrial five-sensed beings, O Gautama, it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most three *palyopamas* less one *antarmuhūrta*. Regarding chest-crawling (uraparisappa) terrestrial five-sensed beings, O Gautama, it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most a *pūrvakoṭī*. Regarding spontaneously born (saṃmucchima) chest-crawling terrestrial five-sensed beings, O Gautama, it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most fifty-three thousand years. Regarding incomplete spontaneously born chest-crawling terrestrial five-sensed beings, O Gautama, it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most also one *antarmuhūrta*. Regarding complete spontaneously born chest-crawling terrestrial five-sensed beings, O Gautama, it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most fifty-three thousand years less one *antarmuhūrta*.

Regarding the five-sensed womb-born chest-crawling land-dwellers, O Gautama, [the maximum life span] is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most one *pūrvakoṭi*. Regarding the five-sensed womb-born chest-crawling land-dwellers while they are in the state of being undeveloped (*aparyāptaka*), O Gautama, it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most also one *antarmuhūrta*. Regarding the five-sensed womb-born chest-crawling land-dwellers while they are in the state of being developed (*paryāptaka*), O Gautama, it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most one *pūrvakoṭi* less one *antarmuhūrta*.

O Gautama, for the terrestrial five-sensed crawling animals (bhujaparisarpa), the minimum is one *antarmuhūrta* and the maximum is one *pūrvakoṭī*. O Gautama, for the spontaneously born (saṃmūrchima) terrestrial five-sensed crawling animals, the minimum is one *antarmuhūrta* and the maximum is forty-two thousand years. O Gautama, for the immature (aparyāptaka) spontaneously born terrestrial five-sensed crawling animals, the minimum is one *antarmuhūrta* and the maximum is also one *antarmuhūrta*. O Gautama, for the mature (paryāptaka) spontaneously born terrestrial five-sensed crawling animals, the minimum is one *antarmuhūrta* and the maximum is forty-two thousand years less one *antarmuhūrta*.

O Gautama, for the five-sensed terrestrial reptiles born from a womb, the minimum [duration] is one internal muhūrta and the maximum is one *pūrvakoṭi*. O Gautama, for the five-sensed terrestrial reptiles born from a womb who are *aparyāptaka* (undeveloped), the minimum is one internal muhūrta and the maximum is also one internal muhūrta. O Gautama, for the five-sensed terrestrial reptiles born from a womb who are *paryāptaka* (developed), the minimum is one internal muhūrta and the maximum is one *pūrvakoṭi* less one internal muhūrta.

[Regarding] the five-sensed aerial beings (*khahayara-pañcindiya*), up to: "O Gautama! [their life span is] at minimum one *antarmuhūrta*, at maximum an incalculable fraction (*asaṅkhijja-bhāga*) of a *palyopama*. Regarding the spontaneously born (*saṃmucchima*) five-sensed aerial beings, up to: O Gautama! at minimum one *antarmuhūrta*, at maximum seventy-two thousand years. Regarding the immature (*apajjattaya*) spontaneously born five-sensed aerial beings, up to: O Gautama! at minimum one *antarmuhūrta* and at maximum also one *antarmuhūrta*. Regarding the mature (*pajjattaga*) spontaneously born five-sensed aerial beings, up to: O Gautama! at minimum one *antarmuhūrta*, at maximum seventy-two thousand years less one *antarmuhūrta*."

"O Gautama! For womb-born, sky-dwelling five-sensed beings, [the lifespan] is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most an *asaṃkhyeya*th part of a *palyopama*. O Gautama! For undeveloped (aparyāpta) womb-born, sky-dwelling five-sensed beings, it is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most also one *antarmuhūrta*. O Venerable One! What is the duration of life declared for developed (paryāpta) womb-born, sky-dwelling five-sensed sub-human beings? O Gautama! It is at least one *antarmuhūrta* and at most an *asaṃkhyeya*th part of a *palyopama* less one *antarmuhūrta*. Herein, there are these summary verses (*saṅgrahaṇī-gāthās*), as follows:"
For those born by spontaneous generation (saṃmūrchima), the maximum duration is eighty-four thousand previous koṭis of years, fifty-three [thousand],
forty-two [hundred], and seventy-two fortnights. (Aṇuogaddārā 290)
In the womb, the maximum lifespan is three *palyopamas* and a *pūrvakoṭi*;
for snakes and reptiles, it is a *pūrvakoṭi* and an incalculable fraction (*asaṅkhyabhāga*) of a *palyopama*. (Āvaśyaka-niryukti 291)

The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a lotus flower that has not yet opened its petals; the person who is like a lotus flower that has opened its petals; the person who is like a blue lotus; and the person who is like a white lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower that has not yet opened its petals? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of lust, accompanied by lust, burning with lust, inflamed by lust. He does not understand as it really is: 'This is suffering,' nor does he understand as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering,' nor does he understand as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' nor does he understand as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower that has not yet opened its petals. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower that has opened its petals? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of lust, accompanied by lust, burning with lust, inflamed by lust. But he understands as it really is: 'This is suffering,' he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering,' he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' and he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower that has opened its petals. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of lust, accompanied by lust, burning with lust, inflamed by lust. And he does not understand as it really is: 'This is suffering,' nor does he understand as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering,' nor does he understand as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' nor does he understand as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. However, he is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from lust, devoid of lust, cooled, calmed, and tranquil. He understands as it really is: 'This is suffering,' he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering,' he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' and he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, he is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. This, monks, is called a person like a white lotus. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and departed. Then those monks, having understood the meaning of what the Blessed One had said, were delighted and rejoiced in it. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this was stated by the Blessed One: 'There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. "It is so, Ānanda, it is so! There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. And how, Ānanda, is one a person like a lotus flower that has not yet opened its petals... [as above] ... These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then the Venerable Ānanda, thinking: "The Teacher has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling," rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and with his hands joined in reverent salutation toward the Blessed One, uttered this inspired utterance three times: "O how wonderful! O how marvelous! How well this was stated by the Blessed One: 'There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Then the Blessed One, emerging from seclusion in the evening, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, why did you stand before me with your hands joined in reverent salutation and utter this inspired utterance three times? "Venerable sir, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling after saying: 'There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world,' I thought: 'The Teacher has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling,' and so I stood before the Blessed One with my hands joined in reverent salutation and uttered this inspired utterance three times. "It is so, Ānanda, it is so! There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. And how, Ānanda, is one a person like a lotus flower that has not yet opened its petals... [as above] ... These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. ---------------------------------------------------------------------

"Venerable Sir, for how long is the lifespan of humans declared to be? Gautama, at the minimum it is one *muhūrta*, and at the maximum it is three *palyopamas*. For spontaneously born (*saṃmucchima*) humans, Gautama, it is at the minimum one *muhūrta* and at the maximum also one *muhūrta*. For womb-born (*gabbhavakkantia*) humans, Gautama, it is at the minimum one *muhūrta* and at the maximum three *palyopamas*. For undeveloped (*apajjattaya*) womb-born humans, Gautama, it is at the minimum one *muhūrta* and at the maximum also one *muhūrta*. For developed (*pajjattaya*) womb-born humans, Gautama, it is at the minimum one *muhūrta* and at the maximum three *palyopamas* less one *muhūrta*."

“Venerable sir, what is the lifespan of the Vāṇamantara gods? “Gautama, at the minimum ten thousand years; at the maximum one *palyopama*. What is the lifespan of the Vāṇamantara goddesses? “Gautama, at the minimum ten thousand years; at the maximum half a *palyopama*. Venerable sir, what is the lifespan of the Jyotiṣka gods? “Gautama, at the minimum slightly more than an eighth part of a *palyopama*; at the maximum one *palyopama* plus one hundred thousand years. Venerable sir, what is the lifespan of the Jyotiṣka goddesses? “Gautama, at the minimum an eighth part of a *palyopama*; at the maximum half a *palyopama* plus fifty thousand years.”

“Venerable sir, regarding the question of the gods of the Moon palaces: Gautama, at the minimum it is a quarter of a *palyopama*, and at the maximum it is one *palyopama* plus one hundred thousand years. Venerable sir, regarding the question of the goddesses of the Moon palaces: Gautama, at the minimum it is a quarter of a *palyopama*, and at the maximum it is half a *palyopama* plus fifty thousand years.”

“Bhante, what is the lifespan of the gods in the Sun celestial mansions? “Gautama, at the minimum it is one-quarter of a *palyopama*, and at the maximum it is one *palyopama* plus one thousand years. Bhante, what is the lifespan of the goddesses in the Sun celestial mansions? “Gautama, at the minimum it is one-quarter of a *palyopama*, and at the maximum it is half a *palyopama* plus five hundred years.”

“Bhante, what is the lifespan of the gods of the planetary mansions? Goyama, it is at least one-quarter of a *palyopama* and at most one *palyopama*. Bhante, what is the lifespan of the goddesses of the planetary mansions? Goyama, it is at least one-quarter of a *palyopama* and at most half a *palyopama*. Bhante, what is the lifespan of the gods of the lunar mansion mansions? Goyama, it is at least one-quarter of a *palyopama* and at most half a *palyopama*. [Regarding] the question concerning the goddesses of the lunar mansion mansions: Goyama, it is at least one-quarter of a *palyopama* and at most slightly more than one-quarter of a *palyopama*.”

"Venerable sir, what is the lifespan of the gods in the star palaces? Gautama, it is at least slightly more than one-eighth of a *palyopama*, and at most one-quarter of a *palyopama*. Venerable sir, what is the lifespan of the goddesses in the star palaces? Gautama, it is at least one-eighth of a *palyopama*, and at most slightly more than one-eighth of a *palyopama*."

"Of the Vaimānika gods, O Lord? "Gautama, at the minimum one *palyopama*, at the maximum thirty-three *sāgaropamas*. Of the Vaimānika goddesses, O Lord? "Gautama, at the minimum one *palyopama*, at the maximum fifty-five *palyopamas*."

“Bhante, what is the lifespan of the gods in the Saṃhama kalpa? “Gautama, at the minimum one *palyopama*, and at the maximum two *sāgaropamas*. Bhante, what is the lifespan of the possessed goddesses (*parigṛhītā-devī*) in the Saṃhama kalpa? “Gautama, at the minimum one *palyopama*, and at the maximum seven *palyopamas*. Bhante, what is the lifespan of the unpossessed goddesses (*aparigṛhītā-devī*) in the Saṃhama kalpa? “Gautama, at the minimum one *palyopama*, and at the maximum fifty *palyopamas*.”

“Bhante, what is the lifespan of the gods in the Īśāna kalpa? “Gautama, it is at least slightly more than one *palyopama*, and at most slightly more than two *sāgaropamas*. Bhante, what is the lifespan of the possessed goddesses (*parigṛhītā-devī*) in the Īśāna kalpa? “Gautama, it is at least slightly more than one *palyopama*, and at most nine *palyopamas*. Bhante, what is the lifespan of the unpossessed goddesses (*aparigṛhītā-devī*) in the Īśāna kalpa? “Gautama, it is at least slightly more than one *palyopama*, and at most fifty-five *palyopamas*.”

What is that which is like a field-measure (*khettapaliōvama*)? The field-measure is explained as being of two kinds: the subtle (*suhuma*) and the conventional (*vāvahāriya*). Of these, the subtle one is set aside. As for the conventional one, it is as follows: suppose there were a granary (*palla*) one *yojana* in length and breadth, and one *yojana* in height, its circumference being three times that plus a fraction more. Suppose this granary were filled to the brim with the tips of the ends of hairs (*vālaggakōḍī*), increasing by one each day, until it was full. These hair-tips would not be burned by fire, nor would they be reduced to dust. Then, from those points of space (*āgāsapaēsa*) in that granary which have been touched by those hair-tips, if one were to remove a single point of space at every moment (*samaē-samaē*), the time required for that granary to become exhausted—[empty, free of residue, and finished]—that is the conventional field-measure.
If the square of these [units] were multiplied ten times over, that would be the measure of one *vāvahāriya* (practical) *kṣetrasāgaropama* (ocean-measure of space). — Aṇuogaddārā 294.

What is the purpose of these conventional *kṣetrapalyopamas* and *sāgaropamas*? There is no practical purpose for these conventional *kṣetrapalyopamas* and *sāgaropamas*; they are merely explained for the sake of exposition. This concludes the conventional *kṣetrapalyopama*. What is the subtle *kṣetrapalyopama*? As for the subtle *kṣetrapalyopama*: suppose there were a pit (*palla*) one *yojana* in length and breadth, and one *yojana* in height, its circumference being three times that with a slight excess. Suppose this pit were filled to the brim and completely packed with the tips of the finest hairs (*vālaggakōḍī*), growing for at most seven nights, increasing by one, two, or three [hair-tips] each day. In that pit, each single hair-tip is divided into innumerable (*asaṅkhējja*) fragments. Those hair-tips are innumerable parts of the range of vision (*diṭṭhīōgāhaṇā*), yet they are innumerable times larger than the range of the body of a subtle green mold-organism (*paṇagajīva*). Those hair-tips would not be burned by fire, nor destroyed, nor would they quickly become putrid. From among the space-points (*ākāsapaēsa*) of that pit, whether touched or untouched by those hair-tips, if one space-point is removed at each successive moment until the pit is exhausted and finished—that duration of time is the subtle *kṣetrapalyopama*. In this regard, an objector said this to the expositor:

Are there any points of space in that *palla* (a specific measure of volume) that have not been touched by those hair-tips? Yes, there are. What is the illustration for this? It is as follows: suppose there were a granary filled with *kōhaṇḍa* gourds; if *māuliṅga* fruits were thrown into it, they too would be contained; if *billā* fruits were thrown in, they too would be contained; if *āmalaga* fruits were thrown in, they too would be contained; if *bayara* fruits were thrown in, they too would be contained; if *caṇaga* beans were thrown in, they too would be contained; if *mugga* beans were thrown in, they too would be contained; if *sarisava* seeds were thrown in, they too would be contained; and if *gaṅgāvāluya* (Ganges sands) were thrown in, even they would be contained. Just so, by this illustration, there are indeed points of space in that *palla* that have not been touched by those hair-tips. [This is the subtle *kṣetrasāgaropama* (unit of time)].
If the square of these [atoms] were multiplied tenfold to become a koṭākoṭī, that would be the measure of one subtle *kṣetrasāgaropama*. (Aṇuogaddārā 296)
What is the purpose of these subtle *kṣetrapalyopamas* and *sāgaropamas*? By means of these subtle *kṣetrapalyopamas* and *sāgaropamas*, substances (*dravyas*) are measured in the *Dṛṣṭivāda*.

“Bhante, how many kinds of substances (*davva*) are taught? “Gautama, two kinds of substances are taught: namely, living substances (*jīvadavva*) and non-living substances (*ajīvadavva*). “Bhante, how many kinds of non-living substances are taught? “Gautama, non-living substances are taught as being of two kinds: namely, formless non-living substances (*arūviajīvadavva*) and material non-living substances (*rūviajīvadavva*). “Bhante, how many kinds of formless non-living substances are taught? “Gautama, ten kinds are taught: namely, the medium of motion (*dhammatthikāya*), the space-points of the medium of motion (*dhammatthikāyassa dēsa*), the individual points of the medium of motion (*dhammatthikāyassa paēsa*); the medium of rest (*adhammatthikāya*), the space-points of the medium of rest (*adhammatthikāyassa dēsa*), the individual points of the medium of rest (*adhammatthikāyassa paēsa*); the medium of space (*āgāsatthikāya*), the space-points of the medium of space (*āgāsatthikāyassa dēsa*), the individual points of the medium of space (*āgāsatthikāyassa paēsa*), and time (*addhāsamaē*). “Bhante, how many kinds of material non-living substances are taught? “Gautama, material non-living substances are taught as being of four kinds: namely, aggregates (*khandha*), parts of aggregates (*khandhadēsa*), individual points of aggregates (*khandhappaēsa*), and subatomic particles (*paramāṇupōggala*). “Bhante, are they numerable (*saṅkhējja*), innumerable (*asaṅkhējja*), or infinite (*ananta*)? “Gautama, they are neither numerable nor innumerable; they are infinite. “For what reason, Bhante, is it said that they are neither numerable nor innumerable, but infinite? “Gautama, there are infinite subatomic particles (*paramāṇupōggala*); there are infinite aggregates consisting of two space-points (*dupaēsiya khandha*), up to infinite aggregates consisting of infinite space-points (*anantapaēsiya khandha*). For that reason, Gautama, it is said that they are neither numerable nor innumerable, but infinite.”

“Venerable sir, are living substances (*jīvadavva*) numerable, innumerable, or infinite? “Gautama, they are neither numerable nor innumerable; they are infinite. “For what reason, venerable sir, is it said thus? “Gautama, there are innumerable hell-beings (*nairayika*); innumerable asura-kumāras; likewise up to innumerable stanita-kumāras; innumerable earth-bodied beings (*pṛthivīkāyika*) up to innumerable air-bodied beings (*vāyukāyika*); infinite plant-bodied beings (*vanaspatikāyika*); innumerable two-sensed beings; innumerable four-sensed beings; innumerable five-sensed animals (*tiryagyoni*); innumerable humans; innumerable *vānavyantara* gods; innumerable *jyotiṣka* gods; innumerable *vaimānika* gods; and infinite perfected souls (*siddha*). For that reason, Gautama, it is said that living substances are neither numerable nor innumerable, but infinite.”
—End of Text—

"Venerable Sir, how many bodies are taught? Gautama, five bodies are taught, namely: the physical (audārika), the transformational (vaikriya), the assimilative (āhāraka), the fiery (taijasa), and the karmic (kārmaṇa). Venerable Sir, how many bodies are taught for hell-beings? Gautama, three bodies are taught, namely: the transformational, the fiery, and the karmic. For the Asura-kumāras, how many bodies are taught? Gautama, three bodies... the transformational, the fiery, and the karmic. In this very same way, three bodies each are to be declared for all [beings] up to the Stanita-kumāras."

"O Lord, how many bodies are taught for the earth-bodied beings? O Gautama, three bodies are taught, namely: the physical (audārika), the fiery (taijasa), and the karmic (kārmaṇa). In the same way, these same three bodies are to be stated for the water-bodied, fire-bodied, and plant-bodied beings. For the air-bodied beings, four bodies are taught, namely: the physical, the transformational (vaikriya), the fiery, and the karmic. For the two-sensed, three-sensed, and four-sensed beings, it is as for the earth-bodied beings. For the five-sensed animals (tiryag-yoni), it is as for the air-bodied beings. For humans, O Gautama, up to five bodies are taught, namely: the physical, the transformational, the assimilative (āhāraka), the fiery, and the karmic. For the Vāṇavyantara, Jyotiṣka, and Vaimānika gods, it is as for the hell-beings."

"Lord, how many *audārika* (physical) bodies are taught? Gautama! They are of two kinds: those currently bound (*baddhellaya*) and those already liberated (*mukellaya*). Among them, those that are currently bound are innumerable; in terms of time, they are exhausted over innumerable *utsarpiṇīs* and *avasarpiṇīs*; in terms of space, they occupy innumerable worlds (*lokas*). Among them, those that are already liberated are infinite; in terms of time, they are exhausted over infinite *utsarpiṇīs* and *avasarpiṇīs*; in terms of space, they occupy infinite worlds; in terms of substance, they are infinitely greater than the number of those destined never to attain liberation (*abhavyasiddhas*), and they constitute an infinite fraction of the perfected ones (*siddhas*). "Lord, how many *vaikriya* (transformative) bodies are taught? Gautama! They are taught as being of two kinds: those currently bound and those already liberated. Among them, those that are currently bound are innumerable; in terms of time, they are exhausted over innumerable *utsarpiṇīs* and *avasarpiṇīs*; in terms of space, they occupy innumerable linear arrays (*śreṇīs*) and an innumerable fraction of a spatial plane (*prataras*). Among them, those that are already liberated are infinite; in terms of time, they are exhausted over infinite *utsarpiṇīs* and *avasarpiṇīs*. The rest regarding these should be stated just as for the already liberated *audārika* bodies. "Question: Lord, how many *āhāraka* (assimilatory) bodies are taught? Gautama! They are taught as being of two kinds: those currently bound and those already liberated. Among them, those that are currently bound may exist or may not exist. If they exist, at the minimum there is one, two, or three, and at the maximum a thousand or more. Those that are already liberated should be stated just as for the *audārika* bodies."

Regarding the question on the *teyaga* (taijasa) body: O Gautama, they are declared to be of two kinds, namely, those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are liberated (*mukkelaya*). Among them, those that are bound are infinite; in terms of time, they are exhausted over infinite *ussappiṇīs* and *osappiṇīs*; in terms of space, they occupy infinite worlds; in terms of substance, they are infinitely greater than the Siddhas and less than an infinite fraction of all living beings (*sarvajīva*). Among them, those that are liberated are infinite; in terms of time, they are exhausted over infinite *ussappiṇīs* and *osappiṇīs*; in terms of space, they occupy infinite worlds; in terms of substance, they are infinitely greater than all living beings and constitute an infinite fraction of the total aggregate of all living beings (*sarvajīvavarga*).

Question regarding the karmic body (kammagasarīra): O Goyama! It is declared to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound (baddhellaya) and those that are liberated (mukkellaya). Just as it was stated regarding the fiery body (tēyagasarīra), so too should it be explained for the karmic body.

"O Lord, how many types of *audārika* (physical) bodies are taught for hell-beings? O Gautama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are liberated (*mukkelaya*). Among these, those that are bound do not exist. As for those that are liberated, they should be described in the same manner as the general *audārika* bodies. O Lord, how many types of *vaikriya* (transformative) bodies are taught for hell-beings? O Gautama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound and those that are liberated. Among these, those that are bound are innumerable-in-numerous; in terms of time, they are exhausted over innumerable *utsarpiṇīs* and *avasarpiṇīs*; in terms of space, they occupy an innumerable fraction of a *prādeśika-pratara* (a spatial unit of a flat layer), and the width of those *śreṇīs* (linear arrays) is equal to the square root of the first power of an *aṅgula* multiplied by the second power of the *aṅgula*, or alternatively, it is equal to the cubic measure of the square root of the second power of an *aṅgula*. As for those that are liberated, they should be described in the same manner as the general *audārika* bodies. O Lord, how many types of *āhāraka* (assimilative) bodies are taught for hell-beings? O Gautama, they are of two kinds: those that are bound and those that are liberated. Among these, those that are bound do not exist. As for those that are liberated, they should be described in the same manner as the general *audārika* bodies. The *taijasa* (fiery) and *kārmaṇa* (karmic) bodies should be described in the same manner as their *vaikriya* bodies."

"Venerable Sir, how many types of *audārika* (physical) bodies are taught for the Asura-kumāras? "Gautama, they are to be described just like the *audārika* bodies of the hell-beings (*nairayika*). "Venerable Sir, how many types of *vaikriya* (transformative) bodies are taught for the Asura-kumāras? "Gautama, two types are taught: namely, those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are released (*mukellaya*). Among them, those that are bound are innumerable; in terms of time, they are exhausted over innumerable *utsarpiṇīs*; in terms of space, they occupy innumerable *śreṇīs* (linear arrays), an innumerable fraction of a *pratar* (plane), and the width-thickness (*vikhaṃbhasūī*) of those *śreṇīs* is an innumerable fraction of the square root of the first [innumerable] unit of an *aṅgula*. Those that are released are to be described just like the general *audārika* bodies. "Venerable Sir, how many types of *āhāraka* (assimilative) bodies are taught for the Asura-kumāras? "Gautama, they are taught as two types: namely, those that are bound and those that are released. They are to be described just like the *audārika* bodies of these very same beings. Their *taijasa* (fiery) and *kārmaṇa* (karmic) bodies are to be described just like their *vaikriya* bodies. Just as it is for the Asura-kumāras, so it should be described up to the Stanita-kumāras."

“Blessed One, how many types of physical bodies (*audārika-śarīra*) are taught for earth-bodied beings (*pṛthvikāyika*)? Goyama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are released (*mukcellaya*). Thus, they should be described in the same manner as the general physical bodies. Blessed One, how many types of transformation bodies (*vaikriya-śarīra*) are taught for earth-bodied beings? Goyama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound and those that are released. Among these, those that are bound do not exist; those that are released should be described in the same manner as the general physical bodies. The assimilative bodies (*āhāraka-śarīra*) should also be described in exactly the same way. The fiery (*taijasa*) and karmic (*kārmaṇa*) bodies should be described in the same manner as their own physical bodies. Just as it is for earth-bodied beings, so too should all the bodies of water-bodied (*apkāyika*) and fire-bodied (*teukāyika*) beings be described.”

“Bhante, how many types of organic bodies (*orāliya-sarīra*) are taught for wind-bodied beings (*vāukāiya*)? Goyama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are liberated (*mukkellaya*). They should be described in the same way as the organic bodies of earth-bodied beings. Bhante, how many types of transformational bodies (*veuvviya-sarīra*) are taught for wind-bodied beings? Goyama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound and those that are liberated. Among these, those that are bound—if removed one by one at every moment—would be exhausted in a period of time equal to an infinitesimal fraction of a *kṣetrapalyopama*, yet they could never actually be exhausted. The liberated transformational bodies and the assimilative bodies (*āhāraga-sarīra*) should be described in the same way as those of earth-bodied beings. The fiery (*teyaga*) and karmic (*kammaga*) bodies should be described in the same way as those of earth-bodied beings.”

The *audārika*, *vaikriya*, and *āhāraka* bodies of the vegetable-bodied beings (*vanaspatikāyika*) should be described in the same manner as those of the earth-bodied beings (*pṛthivīkāyika*). [Question: "Venerable Sir, how many *taijasa* and *kārmaṇa* bodies of the vegetable-bodied beings are taught? [Answer: "Gautama, they are taught to be of two kinds. Just as the general *taijasa* and *kārmaṇa* bodies [are described], so too should the *taijasa* and *kārmaṇa* bodies of the vegetable-bodied beings be described."

“Bhante, how many material bodies (*orāliya-sarīra*) of two-sensed beings are taught? Goyama, they are taught to be of two kinds: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are liberated (*mukkelaya*). Among them, those that are bound are exhausted in time through incalculable upon incalculable *ussappiṇīs* and *osappiṇīs*; in space, they occupy incalculable *seḍhīs*, an incalculable fraction of a *prādeśika-pratara*. The width of those *seḍhīs* is incalculable crores of crores of *yojanas*, or incalculable square roots of *seḍhīs*. A *pratara* is exhausted by the bound material bodies of two-sensed beings in time through incalculable *ussappiṇīs* and *osappiṇīs*, and in space through an incalculable fraction of an *āvalikā* of an *aṅgula-pratara*. Those that are liberated should be described just like the general material bodies. There are no bound *vaikriyika* or *āhāraka* bodies; those that are liberated should be described just like the general material bodies. The *taijasa* and *kārmaṇa* bodies should be described just like their own material bodies.”

As it is for two-sensed beings, so it should be stated for three-sensed and four-sensed beings; for five-sensed animals (*pañcendriya-tiryag-yoni*) as well, the *audārika* bodies are to be described in exactly the same way. "Venerable Sir, how many *vaikriya* bodies are taught for five-sensed animals? "Gautama, they are taught to be of two kinds: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are liberated (*mukellaya*). Among these, those that are bound are innumerable (*asaṅkhyeya*); in terms of time, they are exhausted over innumerable *utsarpiṇīs* and *avasarpiṇīs*; in terms of space, they occupy an innumerable part of a *prataras* (plane) of innumerable *śreṇīs* (linear arrays). The width of those *śreṇīs* is an innumerable part of the first square root of an *aṅgula*. Those that are liberated are to be described just like the general *audārika* bodies. The *āhāraka* bodies are as for two-sensed beings; the *taijasa* and *kārmaṇa* bodies are as for the *audārika*."

"Venerable Sir, how many types of physical bodies (orāliya-sarīra) of human beings are taught? "O Gautama, they are taught to be of two kinds: those that are bound (baddhellaya) and those that are liberated (mukkelaya). Among these, as for those that are bound, they may be numerable (saṅkhejja) or innumerable (asaṅkhejja). At the minimum level, they are numerable—specifically, more than twenty-nine places (sthāna) above the third power-level (trijamalapada) and below the fourth power-level (caüjamalapada); or else, the sixth power (varga) multiplied by the fifth power; or else, ninety-six times the mass of the cutting-off (chēyaṇaga) heap. At the maximum level, they are innumerable. In terms of time, they are exhausted over innumerable aeons of increase and decrease (ussappiṇī-ōsappiṇī). In terms of space, at the maximum level, if humans were to be placed one after another, a single line (śreṇī) would be exhausted; in terms of time, this takes innumerable aeons of increase and decrease; in terms of space, it is the square root of the first power of an angula multiplied by the square root of the third power. As for those that are liberated, they should be described in the same manner as the general physical bodies."

"Venerable Sir, how many types of transformation bodies (*vaikriyika-śarīra*) are taught for human beings? Gautama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are liberated (*mukellaya*). Among these, as for those that are bound, even if one were to remove them one by one at every moment, they would be removed in a finite amount of time; yet they could never be completely exhausted. Those that are liberated are to be described in the same manner as the ordinary (*audhika*) liberated gross bodies (*audārika*)."

“Venerable Sir, how many types of assimilative bodies (*āhāraga-sarīra*) are taught for human beings? Goyama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are liberated (*mukkelaya*). Among these, as for those that are bound, they may exist or they may not exist; if they exist, at a minimum one, two, or three, and at a maximum a thousand or more. Those that are liberated are as described for the ordinary (*ōhiya*) organic bodies (*ōrāliya*). The fiery (*tēyaga*) and karmic (*kammaga*) bodies are to be explained in the same manner as the organic bodies of these very same [beings].”

The gross physical bodies (*audārika-śarīra*) of the Vāṇamantara gods are like those of the hell-beings. "Bhante, how many transformational bodies (*vaikriya-śarīra*) are taught for the Vāṇamantara gods? "Gautama, they are taught to be of two kinds: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are liberated (*mukellaya*). Among these, those that are bound are exhausted in terms of time over innumerable-innumerable *utsarpiṇīs* and *avasarpiṇīs*; in terms of space, they occupy innumerable *seḍhis* (linear arrays), which is an innumerable fraction of a *pratar* (surface layer); and the width of those *seḍhis* is an innumerable hundred-yojana square-rooted fraction of a *pratar*. Those that are liberated are to be understood as they were explained for the general gross physical bodies. The assimilative bodies (*āhāraka-śarīra*) are of two kinds, and both are to be understood as they were for the Asurakumāras. "Bhante, how many fiery (*taijasa*) and karmic (*kārmaṇa*) bodies are taught for the Vāṇamantara gods? "Gautama, just as their transformational bodies are described, so too should their fiery and karmic bodies be stated."

The physical bodies (*audārika-śarīra*) of the celestial beings (*jyotiṣka*) are as [described] for the hell-beings. "Bhante, how many transformation-bodies (*vaikriya-śarīra*) are taught for the celestial beings? "Gautama, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are liberated (*mukellaya*). Therein, as for those that are bound, [the description continues] up to: the width-line (*vikhaṃbhasūī*) of those rows is a sixty-fifth part of a square of one hundred finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) of the plane (*pratarassa*). Those that are liberated are to be described just like the general physical bodies. The assimilative bodies (*āhāraka-śarīra*) are to be described just as for the hell-beings. The fiery (*taijasa*) and karmic (*kārmaṇa*) bodies are to be described just as their own transformation-bodies."

“Lord, how many *audārika* (physical) bodies are taught for the Vaimānika [gods]? “Gautama, as for the hell-beings, so it is for the Vaimānikas. “Lord, how many *vaikriya* (transformative) bodies are taught for the Vaimānikas? “Gautama, they are of two kinds: those that are bound (*baddhellaya*) and those that are released (*mukellaya*).
