Among them, those that are bound are innumerable; in terms of time, they are traversed by innumerable *utsarpiṇīs*; in terms of space, they are innumerable rows (*śreṇīs*) of the innumerable part of a *pratar* (flat surface). The width-measure of those rows is the square root of the second root of an *aṅgula*, multiplied by the third root; or else, they are rows measuring the cube of the third root of an *aṅgula*. Those that are released should be described just like the general *audārika* bodies. The *āhāraka* (assimilative) bodies are as for the hell-beings. The *taijasa* (fiery) and *kārmaṇa* (karmic) bodies should be described just like their own *vaikriya* bodies. “That is the subtle *kṣetrapalyopama*. That is the *kṣetrapalyopama*. That is the *palyopama*. That is the *vibhāganippanna* (produced by division). That is the measure of time (*kālapramāṇa*).”

What then is the measure of states (*bhāvappamāṇa*)? The measure of states is declared to be threefold, namely: the measure of qualities (*guṇappamāṇa*), the measure of viewpoints (*nayappamāṇa*), and the measure of numbers (*saṅkhappamāṇa*).

What is that which is the measurement of qualities (*guṇappamāṇa*)? The measurement of qualities is declared to be twofold, namely: the measurement of qualities of living beings (*jīva*) and the measurement of qualities of non-living beings (*ajīva*). What is that which is the measurement of qualities of non-living beings? The measurement of qualities of non-living beings is declared to be fivefold, namely: the measurement of qualities of color (*vaṇṇa*), the measurement of qualities of smell (*gandha*), the measurement of qualities of taste (*rasa*), the measurement of qualities of touch (*phāsa*), and the measurement of qualities of shape (*saṇṭhāṇa*).

What is that which is the measurement of the qualities of color (*vaṇṇaguṇappamāṇa*)? It is fivefold, as follows: the measurement of the quality of black color, up to the measurement of the quality of white color. That is the measurement of the qualities of color. What is that which is the measurement of the qualities of odor (*gandhaguṇappamāṇa*)? It is twofold: the measurement of the quality of pleasant odor and the measurement of the quality of unpleasant odor. That is the measurement of the qualities of odor. What is that which is the measurement of the qualities of taste (*rasaguṇappamāṇa*)? It is fivefold, as follows: the measurement of the quality of bitter taste, up to the measurement of the quality of sweet taste. That is the measurement of the qualities of taste. What is that which is the measurement of the qualities of touch (*phāsaguṇappamāṇa*)? It is eightfold, as follows: the measurement of the quality of hard touch, up to the measurement of the quality of rough touch. That is the measurement of the qualities of touch. What is that which is the measurement of the qualities of shape (*saṇṭhāṇaguṇappamāṇa*)? It is fivefold, as follows: the measurement of the quality of circular shape, up to the measurement of the quality of elongated shape. That is the measurement of the qualities of shape. That is the measurement of the qualities of non-living matter (*ajīvaguṇappamāṇa*).

What is that which concerns the measurement of the qualities of the soul (*jīvaguṇappamāṇa*)? The measurement of the qualities of the soul is declared to be threefold, namely: the measurement of the quality of knowledge (*nāṇaguṇappamāṇa*), the measurement of the quality of vision (*daṃsaṇaguṇappamāṇa*), and the measurement of the quality of conduct (*carittaguṇappamāṇa*). What is that which concerns the measurement of the quality of knowledge? It is declared to be fourfold, namely: direct perception (*paccakkha*), inference (*anumāna*), analogy (*ovamma*), and scripture (*āgama*). What is that which concerns direct perception? It is twofold, namely: sensory direct perception (*indiyapaccakkha*) and non-sensory direct perception (*noindiyapaccakkha*). What is that which concerns sensory direct perception? It is fivefold, namely: sensory direct perception through the sense of smell (*sōindiya-paccakkha*) up to sensory direct perception through the sense of touch (*phāsindiyapaccakkha*); this is sensory direct perception. What is that which concerns non-sensory direct perception? It is threefold: direct perception through clairvoyance (*ōhināṇapaccakkha*), direct perception through telepathy (*maṇapajjavanāṇapaccakkha*), and direct perception through omniscience (*kēvalanāṇapaccakkha*); this is non-sensory direct perception. This is direct perception.

What is that inference (*anumāna*)? It is threefold, namely: based on prior experience (*pūrvavat*), based on the remainder (*śeṣavat*), and based on observed similarity (*dṛṣṭasādharmyavat*). What is that based on prior experience?
Just as a mother [recognizes] her son who had been lost and has now returned in his youth...
How could one recognize [him] by any former sign? (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 302)

It is as follows: by a caste, or by a clan, or by a mark, or by a mole, or by a sesame seed. That is "by prior occurrence" (*pūrvavat*). What is "by remainder" (*śeṣavat*)? It is fivefold, namely: by effect, by cause, by quality, by part, and by expectation. What is "by effect"? It is as follows: one identifies a conch by its sound, a drum by its beating, a bull by its bellowing, a peacock by its cry, a horse by its neighing, an elephant by its trumpeting, and a chariot by its rattling. That is "by effect. What is "by cause"? It is as follows: threads are the cause of a cloth, but the cloth is not the cause of the threads; *vīraṇa* grass is the cause of a mat, but the mat is not the cause of the *vīraṇa* grass; a lump of clay is the cause of a jar, but the jar is not the cause of the lump of clay. That is "by cause."

What is identification by quality (*guṇa*)? It is as follows: gold by its streak, a flower by its fragrance, salt by its taste, wine by its flavor, and clothing by its texture. This is identification by quality. What is identification by a limb (*avayava*)? Identification by a limb is: a buffalo by its horn; a cock by its crest; an elephant by its tusk; a boar by its tusk; a peacock by its plumage; a horse by its hoof; a tiger by its claw; a yak by the tip of its tail-hair; a monkey by its tail; humans by their two legs; cattle and so forth by their four legs; cows and so forth by their many legs; a lion by its mane; a bull by its hump; and a woman by her arm adorned with bracelets.
One may recognize a warrior by his belt, a woman by her garment,
a *dōṇapāga* broth by its rice, and a poet by a single verse. (Aṇuogaddārā 304)

This is by means of a part. What is that which is by means of expectation (*āsā*)? By means of expectation: one infers fire from smoke, water from cranes, rain from changes in the clouds, and a man of noble family from his conduct and behavior. This is [inference] by means of expectation; this is inference by remainder (*śeṣavat*).

What is that which consists of observed similarity (*diṭṭhasāhammavaṃ*)? It is declared to be twofold: namely, general observation (*sāmannadiṭṭhaṃ*) and specific observation (*visēsadiṭṭhaṃ*). What is general observation? It is as follows: as is one man, so are many men; as are many men, so is one man; as is one *karisāvaṇa* (a measure of land), so are many *karisāvaṇas*; as are many *karisāvaṇas*, so is one *karisāvaṇa*. This is general observation.

What is that which is seen through specific characteristics (*visesadiṭṭha*)? It is as follows: Suppose, for example, a certain man were to recognize among many men a person previously seen, thinking, "This is that man"; or suppose he were to recognize among many measures of grain a measure of grain previously seen, thinking, "This is that measure of grain. His apprehension (*gahaṇa*) is, in brief, threefold: apprehension of the past time, apprehension of the present time, and apprehension of the future time. What is apprehension of the past time? Apprehension of the past time is when, having seen withered forests, the earth with ripened crops, or ponds, lakes, rivers, pools, and reservoirs full of water, one concludes: "There was good rain. That is apprehension of the past time. What is apprehension of the present time? Apprehension of the present time is when, having seen a monk who has gone out on his alms-round with abundant food and drink distributed [to him], one concludes: "There is a time of plenty (*subhikkha*). That is apprehension of the present time. What is apprehension of the future time?
The cloudless clarity of the sky, the dark clouds together with lightning, the thunder, the wind, the radiance, the twilight, and the clear [moonlight]— AṇuŪg. 306.
—End of Text—

Having seen an auspicious omen, such as one pertaining to Varuṇa or Mahinda, or any other praised portent, it is declared by that [omen]: "There will be good rain. That is apprehension regarding the future time. Furthermore, the opposite of these constitutes a threefold apprehension, namely: apprehension regarding the past time, up to apprehension regarding the future time. What is apprehension regarding the past time? Having seen forests stripped of leaves, crops that have not yet ripened, parched ground, or dried-up wells, lakes, rivers, ponds, and tanks, it is declared by that [evidence]: "There was bad rain. That is apprehension regarding the past time. What is apprehension regarding the present time? Having seen a virtuous monk who has gone out on his alms-round and is not obtaining alms, it is declared by that [observation]: "Famine is prevailing. That is apprehension regarding the present time. What is apprehension regarding the future time?
The quarters of the sky are smoking as they behold the earth; the winds, unattached, indeed bring about such a terrible rainstorm. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 308)

Having seen an omen in the east, or in the north-west, or any other unfavorable portent, it is explained to them that there will be a bad rain; this is the apprehension of the future time, this is the specific observation, this is the similarity of what has been seen, and this is inference (*anumāna*).

What is that which is based on similarity (*ovamma*)? It is twofold, as follows: that which is brought forward through commonality (*sāhammōvaṇīya*) and that which is brought forward through difference (*vēhammōvaṇīya*). What is that which is brought forward through commonality? It is threefold, as follows: partial commonality (*kiñcisāhamma*), near-commonality (*pāyasāhamma*), and total commonality (*savvasāhamma*). What is partial commonality? For example: as is Mount Mandara, so is a mustard seed; as is a mustard seed, so is Mount Mandara. As is the ocean, so is a puddle; as is a puddle, so is the ocean. As is the sun, so is a firefly; as is a firefly, so is the sun. As is the moon, so is the water-lily (*kumuda*); as is the water-lily, so is the moon. This is partial commonality. What is near-commonality? For example: as is a cow, so is a calf; as is a calf, so is a cow. This is near-commonality. What is total commonality? There is no [actual] similarity, yet a comparison is made with that very thing: just as an Arhat has been made like an Arhat, a Wheel-turning King (*cakkavaṭṭi*) like a Wheel-turning King, a Baladeva like a Baladeva, a Vāsudeva like a Vāsudeva, and a Sage (*sāhu*) like a Sage. This is total commonality. This is that which is brought forward through commonality.

What is that which is brought forward by way of dissimilarity (*vehammōvaṇīya*)? It is declared to be threefold, namely: partial dissimilarity (*kiñcivēhamma*), near dissimilarity (*pāyavēhamma*), and total dissimilarity (*savvavēhamma*). What is partial dissimilarity? For example, as is a *sāmalēru* tree, so is not a *bāhulēru* tree; as is a *bāhulēru* tree, so is not a *sāmalēru* tree. This is partial dissimilarity. What is near dissimilarity? For example, as is a crow (*vāyasa*), so is not a pigeon (*pāyasa*); as is a pigeon, so is not a crow. This is near dissimilarity. What is total dissimilarity? There is no [true] analogy, yet an analogy is made for it by means of that very thing—just as a low person has done what is like a low person, a slave has done what is like a slave, a crow has done what is like a crow, a dog has done what is like a dog, and a pauper has done what is like a pauper. This is total dissimilarity. This is that which is brought forward by way of dissimilarity; this is that which is brought forward by way of analogy (*ōvamma*).

What is that which is scripture (*āgama*)? It is declared to be twofold: namely, worldly (*laukika*) and supramundane (*lokottara*). What is that which is worldly scripture? That which has been conceived according to the whims of their own intellect and mind by those who are ignorant and hold false views—namely, the *Bhārata*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and so forth, up to the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (*sāṅgopāṅga*). This is worldly scripture. What is that which is supramundane scripture? Supramundane scripture is that which was composed by the Arhats, the Blessed Ones, who possess arisen knowledge and vision, who know the past, present, and future, who are omniscient and all-seeing, and who are honored, revered, and worshipped throughout the three worlds—the twelvefold collection of the *Gaṇipiṭaka*, namely: the *Ācāra* [Sūtra] up to the *Dṛṣṭivāda*. This is supramundane scripture.

Alternatively, scripture (*āgama*) is declared to be threefold: namely, scriptural scripture (*suttāgama*), scriptural meaning (*atthāgama*), and both together (*tadubhayāgama*). Alternatively, scripture is declared to be threefold: namely, self-scripture (*attāgama*), immediate scripture (*anantarāgama*), and traditional scripture (*paramparāgama*). For the Tīrthaṅkaras, there is self-scripture regarding the meaning; for the Gaṇadharas, there is self-scripture regarding the words and immediate scripture regarding the meaning; for the disciples of the Gaṇadharas, there is immediate scripture regarding the words and traditional scripture regarding the meaning. Beyond that, for both the words and the meaning, there is neither self-scripture nor immediate scripture, but only traditional scripture. That is the transcendent scripture; that is scripture. That is the authority based on the quality of knowledge.

What is that which constitutes the standard of the quality of vision (*daṃsaṇa-guṇappamāṇa*)? The standard of the quality of vision is declared to be fourfold, namely: the standard of the quality of visual vision (*cakkhu-daṃsaṇa*), the standard of the quality of non-visual vision (*acakkhu-daṃsaṇa*), the standard of the quality of limited vision (*ōhi-daṃsaṇa*), and the standard of the quality of absolute vision (*kevala-daṃsaṇa*). Visual vision belongs to one possessing visual vision with respect to substances such as pots, cloths, mats, and chariots. Non-visual vision belongs to one possessing non-visual vision with respect to their own internal nature (*āyabhāva*). Limited vision belongs to one possessing limited vision with respect to all material forms (*rūvi-davva*), but not with respect to all modifications (*pajjava*). Absolute vision belongs to one possessing absolute vision with respect to all substances and all modifications. This is the standard of the quality of vision.

What is that? It is the measure of the qualities of conduct (*caritta-guṇappamāṇa*). The measure of the qualities of conduct is declared to be fivefold, namely: the measure of the qualities of conduct of equanimity (*sāmāiya*), the measure of the qualities of conduct of re-institution after interruption (*chedovaṭṭhāvaṇiya*), the measure of the qualities of conduct of purification through penance (*parihāravisuddhiya*), the measure of the qualities of conduct of subtle passion (*suhumasamparāya*), and the measure of the qualities of conduct of the natural state (*ahakkhāya*). The measure of the qualities of conduct of equanimity is declared to be twofold, namely: temporary (*ittariya*) and lifelong (*āvakahia*). The measure of the qualities of conduct of re-institution after interruption is declared to be twofold, namely: with transgressions (*sāiyāra*) and without transgressions (*niraïyāra*). The measure of the qualities of conduct of purification through penance is declared to be twofold, namely: the one undergoing penance (*nivvisamāṇaya*) and the one who has completed the penance (*nivviṭṭhakāiya*). The measure of the qualities of conduct of subtle passion is declared to be twofold, namely: the one becoming defiled (*saṅkilissamāṇaya*) and the one becoming purified (*visujjhamāṇaya*). The measure of the qualities of conduct of the natural state is declared to be twofold, namely: subject to regression (*paḍivāī*) and not subject to regression (*apaḍivāī*); or alternatively, the one with limited vision (*chaümatthi*) and the omniscient one (*kēvali*). That is the measure of the qualities of conduct. That is the measure of the qualities of the soul (*jīvaguṇappamāṇa*). That is the measure of the qualities (*guṇappamāṇa*).
— End of Text —

What is the authority of the viewpoints (*nayapramāṇa*)? The authority of the viewpoints is declared to be threefold: namely, by way of the example of the vessel (*patthaga*), by way of the example of the dwelling (*vasahi*), and by way of the example of the space-point (*paesa*). What is the example of the vessel? Suppose a certain man, taking an axe, were to go deep into the forest. Seeing him, someone might ask: "Where are you going, sir? The impure *negama-naya* would say: "I am going for a vessel. Then, seeing him cutting [wood], someone might ask: "What are you cutting, sir? The more purified *negama-naya* would say: "I am cutting a vessel. Then, seeing him carving it, someone might ask: "What are you carving, sir? The even more purified *negama-naya* would say: "I am carving a vessel. Then, seeing him engraving it, someone might ask: "What are you engraving, sir? The still more purified *negama-naya* would say: "I am engraving a vessel. Thus, for the increasingly purified *negama-naya*, the vessel is that which has its name applied to it. The same applies to the *vyavahāra-naya*. For the *saṅgraha-naya*, the vessel is that which is piled up, measured, and mounted upon a measuring-standard. For the *ṛjusūtra-naya*, the vessel is the vessel itself, and the measuring-standard is also the vessel. For the three verbal *nayas* (*śabdanaya*), the vessel is the knower of the object of the vessel, or that by whose influence the vessel is produced. This is the example of the vessel.

What is that? It is by way of the illustration of dwelling (*vasahi-diṭṭhanta*). Regarding the illustration of dwelling: suppose a certain man were to ask another man, "Where do you live? The impure *naigama* (the first mode of cognition) says, "I live in the world. The world is declared to be threefold: namely, the upper world (*uḍḍhalōga*), the lower world (*ahēlōga*), and the middle world (*tiriyalōga*). "Do you live in all of those? The pure *naigama* says, "I live in the middle world. In the middle world, there are declared to be innumerable continents and oceans, beginning with Jambudvīpa and ending with Sayambhuramaṇa. "Do you live in all of those? The purer *naigama* says, "I live in Jambudvīpa. In Jambudvīpa, ten regions (*khetta*) are declared: namely, Bharata, Airāvata, Haimavata, Hairaṇyavata, Harivarṣa, Ramyakavarṣa, Devakuru, Uttarakuru, Pūrvavideha, and Aparavideha. "Do you live in all of those? The purer *naigama* says, "I live in the region of Bharata. The region of Bharata is declared to be twofold: namely, Southern Bharata and Northern Bharata. "Do you live in both of those? The purer *naigama* says, "I live in Southern Bharata. In Southern Bharata, there are many villages, towns, cities, market towns, hamlets, fortified towns, seaports, royal capitals, crossroads, and settlements. "Do you live in all of those? The purer *naigama* says, "I live in Pāṭaliputra. In Pāṭaliputra, there are many houses. "Do you live in all of those? The purer *naigama* says, "I live in the house of Devadatta. In the house of Devadatta, there are many storerooms. "Do you live in all of those? The purer *naigama* says, "I live in the inner chamber. Thus, for the increasingly pure *naigama*, one lives where one actually dwells. The same applies to the *vyavahāra* (practical) mode. For the *saṅgraha* (synthetic) mode, one lives upon the bed or seat. For the *ṛjusūtra* (straight-line) mode, one lives in whichever space-points of the ether (*ākāśa*) one occupies. For the three verbal modes (*śabdanaya*), one lives in one's own self (*āyabhāva*). That is the illustration by way of dwelling.

What is the illustration by way of parts (*paēsa-diṭṭhanta*)? Regarding the illustration by way of parts, the Naigama says: "There are six parts, namely: the part of matter (*dhamma-paēsa*), the part of non-matter (*adhamma-paēsa*), the part of space (*āgāsa-paēsa*), the part of a soul (*jīva-paēsa*), the part of a composite whole (*khaṇḍha-paēsa*), and the part of a portion (*dēsa-paēsa*). To the Naigama speaking thus, the Saṅgraha says: "What you say—that there are six parts—is not so. Why? Because that which is a part of a portion (*dēsa-paēsa*) belongs to that very same substance (*davva*). What is the illustration? [It is like saying: 'I have bought a donkey from my slave; the slave is mine and the donkey is also mine. Do not say 'six parts'; say 'five parts,' namely: the part of matter, the part of non-matter, the part of space, the part of a soul, and the part of a composite whole. To the Saṅgraha speaking thus, the Vyavahāra says: "What he says—that there are five parts—is not so. Why? If, as in the case of five herdsmen who possess some common property, such as silver, gold, wealth, or grain, then it is appropriate to say 'the parts of five. Do not say 'five parts'; say 'fivefold parts,' namely: the part of matter, the part of non-matter, the part of space, the part of a soul, and the part of a composite whole. To the Vyavahāra speaking thus, the Rjusūtra says: "What you say—that there are fivefold parts—is not so. Why? If those fivefold parts were such that each single part were itself fivefold, then for you there would be twenty-five kinds of parts. Do not say 'fivefold parts'; say 'the part is to be considered' (*bhaiyavva paēsa*), such that it may be a part of matter, it may be a part of non-matter, it may be a part of space, it may be a part of a soul, or it may be a part of a composite whole. To the Rjusūtra speaking thus, the Śabda-naya says: "What you say—that the part is to be considered—is not so. Why? If for you the part is to be considered, then even a part of matter (*dhamma-paēsa*) might be a part of matter, or a part of non-matter, or a part of space, or a part of a soul, or a part of a composite whole. Likewise, a part of non-matter might be a part of matter, or a part of non-matter, or a part of space, or a part of a soul, or a part of a composite whole. Likewise, a part of space might be a part of matter, or a part of non-matter, and so on up to a part of a composite whole. Likewise, a part of a soul might be a part of matter, and so on up to a part of a composite whole. Likewise, a part of a composite whole might be a part of matter, and so on up to a part of a composite whole. In this way, there would be an infinite regress (*aṇavatthā*). Do not say 'the part is to be considered.'"

"Speak! Regarding 'the region of Dharma is that region, Dharma'; 'the region of Adharma is that region, Adharma'; 'the region of space is that region, space'; 'the region of a soul is that region, non-soul'; 'the region of a composite is that region, non-composite'—to him who speaks thus, the Samabhirūḍha says: 'What you say—that the region of Dharma is that region, Dharma, and so on up to "the region of a soul is that region, non-soul," and "the region of a composite is that region, non-composite"—that is not so. Why? Because here there are indeed two types of compounds (*samāsa*): namely, the *tatpuruṣa* and the *karmadhāraya*. It is not known by which compound you speak? Is it by the *tatpuruṣa*, or is it by the *karmadhāraya*? If you speak by the *tatpuruṣa*, then do not speak thus. But if you speak by the *karmadhāraya*, then speak specifically: "Dharma and its region, that region is Dharma"; "Adharma and its region, that region is Adharma"; "Space and its region, that region is space"; "Soul and its region, that region is non-soul"; "Composite and its region, that region is non-composite. To him who speaks thus, the Sampaī (Evambhūta) says: "Whatever you say, all of it is total, complete, without remainder, and grasped by a single apprehension. Even in a part (*dēsa*) it is non-substantial for me; even in a region (*paēsa*) it is non-substantial for me. That is according to the illustration of the region; that is according to the measure of the perspective (*naya*')."

What is reckoning (*saṅkhappamāṇa*)? Reckoning is explained as being of eight kinds, namely: reckoning by name (*nāma-saṅkhā*), reckoning by representation (*ṭhavaṇa-saṅkhā*), reckoning by substance (*davva-saṅkhā*), reckoning by analogy (*ōvamma-saṅkhā*), reckoning by measure (*parimāṇa-saṅkhā*), reckoning by knowledge (*jāṇaṇā-saṅkhā*), reckoning by enumeration (*gaṇaṇā-saṅkhā*), and reckoning by state (*bhāva-saṅkhā*).

What is this enumeration by name (*nāmasaṅkhā*)? Enumeration by name is that for which the designation "enumeration" is applied to a single soul or non-soul, to many souls or non-souls, or to both together; that is enumeration by name.

What is this enumeration by representation (*ṭhavaṇasaṅkhā*)? Enumeration by representation is that which exists in woodwork, painting, bookwork, and so forth; that is enumeration by representation. What is the distinction between name and representation? Name is lifelong, whereas representation may be temporary or lifelong.

What is that which is the enumeration of substance (*davvasaṅkhā*)? The enumeration of substance is declared to be twofold: namely, from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) and from the perspective of non-scripture (*nōāgama*). [This continues] up to: what is that which is the enumeration of substance distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future being (*jāṇagasarīra-bhaviyasarīra-vatirittā davvasaṅkhā*)? The enumeration of substance distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future being is declared to be threefold: namely, the one-lifetime-bound (*ēgabhaviē*), the bound-to-rebirth (*baddhāuē*), and the one whose name and lineage are imminent (*abhimuhanāmagōttē*).

"O Blessed One, how long does one who has only one more birth (ēgabhavika) remain as such in terms of time? At minimum for an antarmuhūrta, at maximum for a pūrvakoṭi. O Blessed One, how long does one whose lifespan is fixed (baddhāyuṣka) remain as such in terms of time? At minimum for an antarmuhūrta, at maximum for one-third of a pūrvakoṭi. O Blessed One, how long does one whose name and lineage are imminent (abhimukhanāmagotra) remain as such in terms of time? At minimum for one moment (samaya), at maximum for an antarmuhūrta."

Now, which *naya* accepts what kind of enumeration (*saṅkha*)? In this regard, the *negama*, *saṅgraha*, and *vyavahāra* accept three kinds of enumeration: namely, that which pertains to a single birth (*ēgabhaviya*), that for which the life-span is bound (*baddhāuya*), and that whose name and lineage are imminent (*abhimuhanāmagōtta*). The *ujjusua* accepts two kinds of enumeration: namely, that for which the life-span is bound and that whose name and lineage are imminent. The three *śabda-nayas* accept as enumeration only that whose name and lineage are imminent. This is the substantial enumeration (*davvasaṅkhā*) distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the one destined to become [an omniscient being]. This is the substantial enumeration from the perspective of non-scriptural authority (*nōāgamaō*). This is the substantial enumeration.

What is that which is called comparison (*ōvammasaṅkhā*)? Comparison is declared to be fourfold, namely: there is that which exists compared with what exists; there is that which exists compared with what does not exist; there is that which does not exist compared with what exists; and there is that which does not exist compared with what does not exist. Among these, that which exists is compared with what exists, as follows: the Arhats, who exist, are compared with existing excellent cities, with existing door-panels, and with existing calves. That is to say: [The text continues with specific examples of such comparisons.]
All twenty-four Jinas have the excellent city-gates as their chest, arms like iron bars, voices deep as the sound of kettledrums, and chests marked with the śrīvatsa. (Aṇuogaddārāim 312)

The existent is compared with the non-existent, just as the existents— the lifespans of hell-beings, animals, humans, and gods— are compared with the non-existent *palyopamas* and *sāgaropamas*; likewise, the non-existent is compared with the existent.
With his limbs completely withered, his joints moving, his skin falling away, having reached his end,
fallen into calamity,
and arrived at the time of death, he recites this verse. (Aṇuogaddārāim 314)
"As you are, so are we; and you too shall become as we are," thus the falling yellow leaf admonishes the young shoots.
(Āvaśyaka Niryukti 315)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a conversation regarding the young and pale leaves;
this is indeed a metaphor employed for the purpose of awakening those destined for liberation.
(Aṇuogaddārā 316)

This non-existent is compared to another non-existent; just as the horn of a donkey, so too is the horn of a rabbit. That is the enumeration by analogy (*ovamma-saṅkhā*). What is the enumeration by measure (*parimāṇa-saṅkhā*)? The enumeration by measure is declared to be twofold: the enumeration by measure of the scriptures of the Kālika period (*kāliya-suya*) and the enumeration by measure of the scriptures of the Diṭṭhivāda. What is the enumeration by measure of the Kālika scriptures? It is declared to be of many kinds, namely: the enumeration of modes (*pajjava*), the enumeration of syllables (*akkhara*), the enumeration of compounds (*saṅghāya*), the enumeration of phrases (*pada*), the enumeration of quarters (*pāya*), the enumeration of stanzas (*gāhā*), the enumeration of verses (*silōga*), the enumeration of Vedhas, the enumeration of Nijjuttis, the enumeration of Anuyogadvāras, the enumeration of sections (*uddesaga*), the enumeration of chapters (*ajjhayaṇa*), the enumeration of scriptural divisions (*suyakhaṃdha*), and the enumeration of Angas. That is the enumeration by measure of the Kālika scriptures.

What is that? It is the enumeration of the extent of the *Diṭṭhivāya* scripture. It is declared to be of many kinds, namely: the enumeration of modes (*pajjava*), up to the enumeration of the sub-sections (*anuōgada*), the enumeration of chapters (*pāhuḍa*), the enumeration of sub-chapters (*pāhuḍapāhuḍa*), the enumeration of sections (*pāhuḍiyā*), the enumeration of sub-sections (*pāhuḍapāhuḍiyā*), and the enumeration of topics (*vatthu*). This is the enumeration of the extent of the *Diṭṭhivāya* scripture; this is the enumeration of extent.

What is that which is called knowledge-enumeration (*jāṇaṇā-saṅkhā*)? Knowledge-enumeration is when one knows what is to be known, as follows: the sound-knower [knows] sound, the astrologer [knows] astrology, the soothsayer [knows] omens, the chronologist [knows] time, and the physician [knows] medicine. This is knowledge-enumeration. What is that which is called calculation-enumeration (*gaṇaṇā-saṅkhā*)? In calculation-enumeration, the number one does not constitute a calculation; enumeration begins from two. It is as follows: the countable (*saṅkhējja*), the uncountable (*asaṅkhējja*), and the infinite (*ananta*).

What is that which is numerable (*saṅkhējja*)? The numerable is declared to be threefold, namely: the lowest (*jahanna*), the highest (*ukkōsa*), and that which is neither lowest nor highest (*ajahannamanukkōsa*). What is that which is innumerable (*asaṅkhējja*)? The innumerable is declared to be threefold, namely: the limited innumerable (*parittāsaṅkhējja*), the combined innumerable (*juttāsaṅkhējja*), and the innumerable-innumerable (*asaṅkhējjāsaṅkhējja*). What is that which is the limited innumerable? The limited innumerable is declared to be threefold, namely: the lowest, the highest, and that which is neither lowest nor highest. What is that which is the combined innumerable? The combined innumerable is declared to be threefold, namely: the lowest, the highest, and that which is neither lowest nor highest. What is that which is the innumerable-innumerable? The innumerable-innumerable is declared to be threefold, namely: the lowest, the highest, and that which is neither lowest nor highest.

What is that which is infinite (*ananta*)? The infinite is declared to be threefold, namely: limited-infinite (*parittānanta*), combined-infinite (*juttānanta*), and infinite-of-the-infinite (*anantānanta*). What is that which is limited-infinite? Limited-infinite is declared to be threefold, namely: lowest (*jahanna*), highest (*ukkōsa*), and neither-lowest-nor-highest (*ajahanna-maṇukkōsa*). What is that which is combined-infinite? Combined-infinite is declared to be threefold, namely: lowest, highest, and neither-lowest-nor-highest. What is that which is infinite-of-the-infinite? Infinite-of-the-infinite is declared to be twofold, namely: lowest and neither-lowest-nor-highest. How much is the lowest numberable (*saṅkhējja*)? It consists of two forms; beyond that, there are places that are neither-lowest-nor-highest until one reaches the highest numberable. How much is the highest numberable? I shall provide the exposition of the highest numberable.

Suppose there were a granary (*palla*) one hundred thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, and three hundred sixteen thousand two hundred twenty-seven *yojanas*, three *krośas*, two hundred and twenty-eight *dhanus*, thirteen *aṅgulas*, and half an *aṅgula*, plus a small fraction more in circumference. Suppose this granary were filled with mustard seeds (*siddhattha*). From those mustard seeds, an extraction (*uddhāra*) of islands and oceans would be performed—one island, one ocean, one island, one ocean—and as they are thus being added, however many islands and oceans are covered by those mustard seeds, that much space is designated as a "granary. When that granary is filled with mustard seeds, and from those mustard seeds an extraction of islands and oceans is performed—one island, one ocean—and as they are thus being added, however many islands and oceans are covered by those mustard seeds, that much space constitutes the first stroke (*salāgā*). Even if worlds as numerous as these strokes were filled, even then the highest countable number (*saṅkhējjaya*) would not be reached. What is the illustration for this?

Suppose, for example, there were a chest filled with *āmalaka* fruits. If one *āmalaka* is placed therein, it would not fit; another is placed, and that too does not fit; yet another is placed, and that too does not fit. As they continue to be placed in this manner, there will come a point where the chest becomes full. There will be one *āmalaka* which, when placed, causes the chest to be full; there will be another *āmalaka* which cannot fit there. In the same way, when the highest countable (*ukkosae saṅkhejjae*) unit is added to the lowest limited-countable (*jahannayaṃ parittāsaṅkhejjayaṃ*), it becomes the lowest limited-innumerable (*parittāsaṅkhejjaya*). Beyond that, there are intermediate positions until the highest limited-innumerable is reached. What is the magnitude of the highest limited-innumerable? The highest limited-innumerable is the product of as many groups as there are units in the lowest limited-innumerable, minus one. Alternatively, the highest limited-innumerable is the lowest appropriate-innumerable (*juttāsaṅkhejjaya*) minus one. What is the magnitude of the lowest appropriate-innumerable? The lowest appropriate-innumerable is the product of as many groups as there are units in the lowest limited-innumerable, made complete. Alternatively, when one unit is added to the highest limited-innumerable, it becomes the lowest appropriate-innumerable. An *āvalikā* (a specific measure of time) is also of this same magnitude. Beyond that, there are intermediate positions until the highest appropriate-innumerable is reached. What is the magnitude of the highest appropriate-innumerable? The highest appropriate-innumerable is the product of the lowest appropriate-innumerable multiplied by an *āvalikā*, minus one. Alternatively, the highest appropriate-innumerable is the lowest innumerable-innumerable (*asaṅkhejjāsaṅkhejjaya*) minus one. What is the magnitude of the lowest innumerable-innumerable? The lowest innumerable-innumerable is the product of the lowest appropriate-innumerable multiplied by an *āvalikā*, made complete. Alternatively, when one unit is added to the highest appropriate-innumerable, it becomes the lowest innumerable-innumerable. Beyond that, there are intermediate positions until the highest innumerable-innumerable is reached. What is the magnitude of the highest innumerable-innumerable? The highest innumerable-innumerable is the product of as many groups as there are units in the lowest innumerable-innumerable, minus one. Alternatively, the highest innumerable-innumerable is the lowest limited-unbounded (*parittāṇantaya*) minus one.

What is the measure of the lowest *parittānantaya* (limited-infinite)? The complete mutual multiplication of as many groups as there are in the lowest *asaṅkhējjāsaṅkhējja* (infinite-infinite) is the lowest *parittānantaya*. Alternatively, when one unit is added to the highest *asaṅkhējjāsaṅkhējja*, it becomes the lowest *parittānantaya*. Beyond that, there are intermediate positions, neither the lowest nor the highest, until the highest *parittānantaya* is reached. What is the measure of the highest *parittānantaya*? The complete mutual multiplication of as many groups as there are in the lowest *parittānantaya*, minus one, is the highest *parittānantaya*. Alternatively, the lowest *juttānantaya* (countable-infinite), minus one, is the highest *parittānantaya*. What is the measure of the lowest *juttānantaya*? The complete mutual multiplication of as many groups as there are in the lowest *parittānantaya* is the lowest *juttānantaya*. Alternatively, when one unit is added to the highest *parittānantaya*, it becomes the lowest *juttānantaya*. Even the *abhavasiddhiyas* (those incapable of attaining liberation) are exactly that many. Beyond that, there are intermediate positions, neither the lowest nor the highest, until the highest *juttānantaya* is reached. What is the measure of the highest *juttānantaya*? The mutual multiplication of the *abhavasiddhiyas* by the lowest *juttānantaya*, minus one, is the highest *juttānantaya*. Alternatively, the lowest *anantānantaya* (infinite-infinite), minus one, is the highest *juttānantaya*. What is the measure of the lowest *anantānantaya*? The complete mutual multiplication of the *abhavasiddhiyas* by the lowest *juttānantaya* is the lowest *anantānantaya*. Alternatively, when one unit is added to the highest *juttānantaya*, it becomes the lowest *anantānantaya*. Beyond that, there are only intermediate positions, neither the lowest nor the highest. This is the enumeration (*gaṇaṇāsaṅkhā*).

What is the enumeration of states (*bhāvasaṅkhā*)? The enumeration of states refers to those living beings who experience the karmas of the names and lineages of the *saṅkha* (conch) class; that is the enumeration of states. That is the measure of enumeration, that is the measure of states, that is the measure.

What is the discourse (*vattavvayā*)? Discourse is declared to be threefold, namely: discourse concerning one's own doctrine (*sasamayavattavvayā*), discourse concerning another's doctrine (*parasamayavattavvayā*), and discourse concerning both one's own and another's doctrine (*sasamaya-parasamayavattavvayā*).

What is the discourse on one's own doctrine (*sasamayavattavvayā*)? That wherein one's own doctrine is proclaimed, explained, demonstrated, shown, illustrated, and pointed out—that is the discourse on one's own doctrine. What is the discourse on another's doctrine (*parasamayavattavvayā*)? The discourse on another's doctrine is that wherein another's doctrine is proclaimed, and so forth, up to being pointed out—that is the discourse on another's doctrine. What is the discourse on both one's own and another's doctrine (*sasamaya-parasamayavattavvayā*)? That wherein both one's own doctrine and another's doctrine are proclaimed, and so forth, up to being pointed out—that is the discourse on both one's own and another's doctrine. Now, which *naya* accepts which discourse? In this regard, the *negama*, *saṅgraha*, and *vavahāra* accept three kinds of discourse.

That is as follows: the *Ṛjusūtra* accepts two kinds of discourse (*vaktavyatā*), namely: discourse concerning one's own doctrine (*sasamayavaktavyatā*) and discourse concerning another’s doctrine (*parasamayavaktavyatā*). In this regard, that which is discourse concerning one's own doctrine is included within one's own doctrine; that which is discourse concerning another’s doctrine is included within another’s doctrine. Therefore, there are two kinds of discourse, not three. The three *Śabda-nayas* accept only one kind of discourse—discourse concerning one's own doctrine—and maintain that there is no discourse concerning another’s doctrine. Why? Because they consider that in another’s doctrine there is no purpose, no reason, non-existence, inactivity, a false path, lack of instruction, and wrong view. Therefore, all [discourse] is discourse concerning one's own doctrine; there is no discourse concerning another’s doctrine, nor is there discourse concerning both one's own and another’s doctrine. Such is discourse.
What then is the subject matter? It is the subject matter of each respective chapter— that is, the subject matter of whichever chapter it may be.

Abstinence from blameworthy activity, praising [the vows], practicing the virtues, repentance for what has been transgressed, treating the wound [of the transgression], and maintaining the virtues. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 320)
Thus ends the section on the subject matter.

What is that which is called *samōyāra* (combination)? *Samōyāra* is declared to be of six kinds, namely: *nāma-samōyāra*, *ṭhavaṇa-samōyāra*, *davva-samōyāra*, *khētta-samōyāra*, *kāla-samōyāra*, and *bhāva-samōyāra*. The [definitions of] name and representation have already been explained; this concludes the *bhaviyasarīra-davva-samōyāra*. What is that which is *jāṇagasarīra-bhaviyasarīra-vatiritta-davva-samōyāra* (substantial combination distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future being)? *Jāṇagasarīra-bhaviyasarīra-vatiritta-davva-samōyāra* is declared to be of three kinds, namely: *āya-samōyāra* (self-combination), *para-samōyāra* (other-combination), and *tadubhaya-samōyāra* (both-combination). All substances indeed combine with their own nature through *āya-samōyāra*; through *para-samōyāra*, as for example, jujube fruits in a bowl; through *tadubhaya-samōyāra*, as for example, a pillar in a house [combining] with its own nature, or a neck in a jar [combining] with its own nature. Alternatively, *jāṇagasarīra-bhaviyasarīra-vatiritta-davva-samōyāra* is declared to be of two kinds, namely: *āya-samōyāra* and *tadubhaya-samōyāra*. A sixty-four-fold [measure] combines with its own nature through *āya-samōyāra*, and it combines with a thirty-two-fold [measure] through *tadubhaya-samōyāra* with its own nature; a thirty-two-fold [measure] combines with its own nature through *āya-samōyāra*, and it combines with a sixteen-fold [measure] through *tadubhaya-samōyāra* with its own nature; a sixteen-fold [measure] combines with its own nature through *āya-samōyāra*, and it combines with an eight-fold [measure] through *tadubhaya-samōyāra* with its own nature; an eight-fold [measure] combines with its own nature through *āya-samōyāra*, and it combines with a four-fold [measure] through *tadubhaya-samōyāra* with its own nature; a four-fold [measure] combines with its own nature through *āya-samōyāra*, and it combines with a half-measure (*addhāmāṇī*) through *tadubhaya-samōyāra* with its own nature; a half-measure combines with its own nature through *āya-samōyāra*, and it combines with a full measure (*māṇī*) through *tadubhaya-samōyāra* with its own nature. This is *jāṇagasarīra-bhaviyasarīra-vatiritta-davva-samōyāra*. This is *no-āgamao davva-samōyāra*. This is *davva-samōyāra*.

What is that which pertains to the spatial inclusion (*khetta-samoyāra*)? It is declared to be twofold: namely, inclusion by way of self (*āya-samoyāra*) and inclusion by way of both (*tadubhaya-samoyāra*). In the region of Bharata, by way of inclusion by self, it is included within its own nature; by way of inclusion by both, it is included within Jambūdvīpa as its own nature. In Jambūdvīpa, by way of inclusion by self, it is included within its own nature; by way of inclusion by both, it is included within the transverse world (*tiriyalōga*) as its own nature. In the transverse world, by way of inclusion by self, it is included within its own nature; by way of inclusion by both, it is included within the world (*lōga*) as its own nature. In the world, by way of inclusion by self, it is included within its own nature; by way of inclusion by both, it is included within the non-world (*alōga*) as its own nature. This is the spatial inclusion.

What is that which is the integration of time (*kāla-samōyārē*)? The integration of time is declared to be twofold: namely, integration by one's own nature (*āya-samōyārē*) and integration by both [one's own nature and another]. By integration by one's own nature, it integrates into its own being (*āyabhāvē*) in a single moment (*samaē*). By integration by both, it integrates into its own being within a *āvaliyā*. In this same manner, it integrates into its own being within a breath (*āṇāpāṇū*), a *thōvē*, a *lavē*, a *muhuttē*, a day and night (*ahōrattē*), a fortnight (*pakkhē*), a month (*māsē*), a season (*ūū*), a solstice (*ayanē*), a year (*saṁvaccharē*), a *jugē*, a hundred years (*vāsasaē*), a thousand years (*vāsasahassē*), a hundred thousand years (*vāsasayasahassē*), a *puvvaṅgē*, a *puvvē*, a *tuḍiaṅgē*, a *tuḍiē*, an *aḍaḍaṅgē*, an *aḍaḍē*, an *avavaṅgē*, an *avavē*, a *hūhūaṅgē*, a *hūhūē*, an *uppalaṅgē*, an *uppalē*, a *paüaṅgē*, a *paümaṅgē*, a *paümē*, a *nalinaṅgē*, a *nalinē*, an *acchiniuraṅgē*, an *acchiniurē*, an *aüaṅgē*, an *aüē*, a *naüaṅgē*, a *naüē*, a *paüaṅgē*, a *paüē*, a *cūliaṅgē*, a *cūliē*, a *sīsapahēliaṅgē*, a *sīsapahēliē*, a *paliōvamē*, and a *sāgarōvamē*. By integration by one's own nature, it integrates into its own being in a single moment; by integration by both, it integrates into its own being within an *ōsappiṇī* and *ussappiṇī*. By integration by one's own nature, the *ōsappiṇī* and *ussappiṇī* integrate into their own being in a single moment; by integration by both, they integrate into their own being within a *pōggalapariyaṭṭē*. By integration by one's own nature, the *pōggalapariyaṭṭē* integrates into its own being in a single moment; by integration by both, it integrates into its own being within the past time (*tītaddhā*) and the future time (*anāgataddhā*). By integration by one's own nature, the past and future times integrate into their own being in a single moment; by integration by both, they integrate into their own being within all time (*savvaddhā*). This is the integration of time.

What is that which is the assimilation of states (*bhāvasamōyāra*)? The assimilation of states is declared to be twofold, namely: assimilation by self (*āyasamōyāra*) and assimilation by both (*tadubhayasamōyāra*). Through assimilation by self, anger (*kōha*) assimilates into its own state (*āyabhāva*); through assimilation by both, pride (*māṇa*) assimilates into its own state. In the same way, pride, deceit (*māyā*), greed (*lōbha*), passion (*rāga*), and the deluding karma (*mōhaṇijja*)—through assimilation by self, these eight types of karmic matter (*aṭṭhakammapagaḍī*) assimilate into their own state; through assimilation by both, they assimilate into the sixfold state (*chavvihē bhāvē*) and into their own state. In the same way, the sixfold state assimilates into the soul (*jīva*), and the soul-substance (*jīvatthikāya*)—through assimilation by self, assimilates into its own state; through assimilation by both, it assimilates into all substances (*savvadavvēsu*) and into its own state. Here is the summary verse (*saṅgahaṇī gāhā*):
Karma-nature (prakṛti),

state (bhāva), the soul (jīva), the category of soul-substance (jīvāstikāya), and all substances (sarvadravya) [are associated with] anger, pride, deceit, greed, attachment, and deluding karma (mohanīya). — Āvaśyaka Niryukti 323.
That is the convergence of dispositions; that is convergence. That is the application of means.

What is that which is called "deposit" (nikkhēva)? Deposit is declared to be threefold, namely: produced from a root (ōhanipphanna), produced from a name (nāmanipphanna), and produced from a scriptural passage (suttālāvaganipphanna).

What is that which is accomplished through etymological derivation (*ōhanipphanna*)? That which is accomplished through etymological derivation is declared to be fourfold, namely: study (*ajjhayaṇa*), non-depletion (*ajjhīṇa*), approach (*āya*), and effacement (*jhavaṇā*). What is that which is study (*ajjhayaṇa*)? Study is declared to be fourfold, namely: nominal study (*nāmajjhayaṇa*), conventional study (*ṭhavaṇajjhayaṇa*), substantial study (*davvajjhayaṇa*), and modal study (*bhāvajjhayaṇa*). The categories of name and convention have already been explained. What is that which is substantial study (*davvajjhayaṇa*)? Substantial study is declared to be twofold: from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) and from the perspective of non-scripture (*noāgama*). What is substantial study from the perspective of scripture? Substantial study from the perspective of scripture refers to one for whom the word "study" has been learned, mastered, conquered, measured, and fully internalized—up to the point where, as many as there are [instances] not currently being employed, that many are the substantial studies from the perspective of scripture according to the *Nayic* school of the Nigaṃtha. It is the same for the *Vyavahāra* school. According to the *Saṅgraha* school, it is one or many, up to that point. This is substantial study from the perspective of scripture.

What is non-scriptural (nōāgamaō) substance-study (davvajjhayaṇē)? Non-scriptural substance-study is declared to be threefold, namely: substance-study as the body of the knower (jāṇagasarīradavvajjhayaṇē), substance-study as the body of the potential being (bhaviyasarīradavvajjhayaṇē), and substance-study distinct from the bodies of both the knower and the potential being (jāṇagasarīrabhaviyasarīravatirittē davvajjhayaṇē). What is substance-study as the body of the knower? Substance-study as the body of the knower refers to the body of one who knows the meaning and subject matter of the term "study" (ajjhayaṇē), which is a body that has departed, passed away, fallen, been cast off, and abandoned by the soul—[a body] through which, by means of the state seen by the Jina, the word "study" has been proclaimed, explained, demonstrated, shown, pointed out, and illustrated. What is the illustration? "This was a pot of honey; this was a pot of ghee. This is substance-study as the body of the knower. What is substance-study as the body of the potential being? Substance-study as the body of the potential being refers to a living being who has emerged from the womb and birth, and who, by means of this very physical aggregate seen by the Jina, will in the future learn the word "study" through the state [of realization], though he does not yet learn it. What is the illustration? "This will become a pot of honey; this will become a pot of ghee. This is substance-study as the body of the potential being. What is substance-study distinct from the bodies of the knower and the potential being? Substance-study distinct from the bodies of the knower and the potential being is that which is written on palm leaves or in books. This is substance-study distinct from the bodies of the knower and the potential being. This is non-scriptural substance-study. This is substance-study.

What is that which is the study of the internal state (*bhāva-adhyayana*)? The study of the internal state is declared to be of two kinds, namely: from the perspective of the scriptural authority (*āgama*) and from the perspective of what is not the scriptural authority (*no-āgama*). What is that which is the study of the internal state from the perspective of the scriptural authority? The study of the internal state from the perspective of the scriptural authority is one who knows [the subject] and is engaged [in it]. That is the study of the internal state from the perspective of the scriptural authority. What is that which is the study of the internal state from the perspective of what is not the scriptural authority? The study of the internal state from the perspective of what is not the scriptural authority is as follows:
The leading toward the inner self (*adhyātma*), the destruction of accumulated karmas, and the attainment of the highest state.
And because of the recitation of new [scriptures], for that reason they desire the *adhyayana*.
(Aṇuogaddārāim 326) That is the *bhāvādhyayana* from the perspective of non-scriptural authority (*noāgama*). That is the *bhāvādhyayana*. That is the *adhyayana*.

What is that which is "unexhausted" (*ajjhīṇa*)? Unexhausted is explained as being fourfold, namely: nominal unexhausted (*nāma-ajjhīṇa*), notional unexhausted (*ṭhavaṇa-ajjhīṇa*), substantial unexhausted (*davva-ajjhīṇa*), and modal unexhausted (*bhāva-ajjhīṇa*). The categories of name and notion have already been explained. What is that which is substantial unexhausted? Substantial unexhausted is explained as being twofold, namely: from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) and from the perspective of non-scripture (*noāgama*). What is that which is substantial unexhausted from the perspective of scripture? Substantial unexhausted from the perspective of scripture refers to one by whom the word "unexhausted" has been studied [but who has not yet realized its meaning]; this is substantial unexhausted from the perspective of scripture. What is that which is substantial unexhausted from the perspective of non-scripture? Substantial unexhausted from the perspective of non-scripture is explained as being threefold, namely: substantial unexhausted as the body of the knower (*jñāyaka-śarīra-davva-ajjhīṇa*), substantial unexhausted as the body of the potential being (*bhavya-śarīra-davva-ajjhīṇa*), and substantial unexhausted distinct from both the body of the knower and the body of the potential being.

What is that which is the substance-destruction of the body of the knower (*jñāyaka-śarīra-dravyājīrṇa*)? The substance-destruction of the body of the knower is "destruction" because it refers to the subject matter of the knower; that body which has departed, fallen away, been cast off, and abandoned, being devoid of the soul, should be described just as in the chapter on substances (*dravyādhyayana*), up to: "that is the substance-destruction of the body of the knower. What is that which is the substance-destruction of the body of the potential being (*bhavya-śarīra-dravyājīrṇa*)? The substance-destruction of the body of the potential being refers to those souls who have emerged from the womb and birth, as described in the chapter on substances, up to: "that is the substance-destruction of the body of the potential being. What is that which is the substance-destruction distinct from both the body of the knower and the body of the potential being (*jñāyaka-śarīra-bhavya-śarīra-vyatirikta-dravyājīrṇa*)? The substance-destruction distinct from both the body of the knower and the body of the potential being is the entire linear series of space (*sarvākāśa-śreṇi*). That is the substance-destruction distinct from both the body of the knower and the body of the potential being. That is substance-destruction by way of non-scriptural authority (*no-āgama*). That is substance-destruction.

What is that which is the destruction of dispositions (*bhāvajjhīṇē*)? The destruction of dispositions is declared to be of two kinds: namely, from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) and from the perspective of non-scripture (*nōāgama*). What is the destruction of dispositions from the perspective of scripture? The destruction of dispositions from the perspective of scripture is one who knows [the subject] and is engaged [in it]. That is the destruction of dispositions from the perspective of scripture. What is the destruction of dispositions from the perspective of non-scripture? The destruction of dispositions from the perspective of non-scripture is as follows:
Just as a lamp may illuminate a hundred lamps, yet that lamp itself remains shining.
The teachers are like lamps; they shine themselves and cause others to shine.
(Aṇuogaddārā 328) That, then, is the destruction of states by way of non-scriptural knowledge (*noāgamato bhāvajjhīṇe*); that is the destruction of states. That is destruction.

What is that [which is called] *āya* (income/acquisition)? *Āya* is declared to be fourfold, namely: by name (*nāmāya*), by representation (*ṭhavaṇāya*), by substance (*davvāya*), and by state (*bhāvāya*). Name and representation have been explained. What is that which is by substance? Substance is declared to be twofold, namely: from the perspective of scripture (*āgama*) and from the perspective of non-scripture (*noāgama*). What is that which is by substance from the perspective of scripture? Substance from the perspective of scripture is one for whom the word "āya" has been studied and mastered [but who does not currently employ it]. Why? Because, according to the principle that "substance is that which is not currently in operation," for the Nigaṃtha school, as many [instances of the word] as are not currently in operation are as many substances; such is substance from the perspective of scripture.

What is substance from the perspective of non-scriptural authority (*nō-āgama*)? Substance from the perspective of non-scriptural authority is declared to be threefold, namely: substance as the body of the knower (*jñāyaka-śarīra-dravya*), substance as the body of the potential being (*bhavya-śarīra-dravya*), and substance distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the potential being. What is substance as the body of the knower? Substance as the body of the knower refers to the physical body of one who knows the subject matter of the discourse, which is a body that has departed, passed away, fallen off, and been relinquished—just as described in the *Dravyādhyayana*—up to [the end of that section]. This is substance as the body of the knower. What is substance as the body of the potential being? Substance as the body of the potential being refers to those living beings who have emerged from the womb and birth—just as described in the *Dravyādhyayana*—up to [the end of that section]. This is substance as the body of the potential being. What is substance distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the potential being? Substance distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the potential being is declared to be threefold, namely: worldly (*laukika*), pertaining to false doctrines (*kupravacanika*), and supramundane (*lokottara*).

What is that which pertains to the world (*lōiē*)? That which pertains to the world is declared to be threefold, namely: animate (*sacittē*), inanimate (*acittē*), and mixed (*mīsaē*). What is that which is animate? The animate is declared to be threefold, namely: bipeds, quadrupeds, and those without feet. Bipeds are male and female slaves; quadrupeds are horses and elephants; those without feet are mangoes, hog-plums, and jackfruits. This is the animate. What is that which is inanimate? It is the acquisition of gold, silver, gems, pearls, conch-shells, crystals, coral, and red jewels—of all that is existing, essential, and valuable. This is the inanimate. What is that which is mixed? The mixed is the acquisition of male and female slaves, horses, and elephants, who are fully adorned with ornaments and finery. This is the mixed. This is that which pertains to the world.

What is that which pertains to false doctrine (*kuppāvayaṇiya*)? False doctrine is declared to be threefold, namely: with consciousness (*sacitta*), without consciousness (*acitta*), and mixed (*mīsa*). All three are as explained in the worldly context, up to the point of "that is the mixed"; such is that which pertains to false doctrine.

What is that which is supramundane (*lōguttariya*)? The supramundane is declared to be threefold, namely: with consciousness (*sacitta*), without consciousness (*acitta*), and mixed (*mīsa*). What is that which is with consciousness? That which is with consciousness is the acquisition of disciples (*sīsa*) and female disciples (*sissiṇī*); that is what is with consciousness. What is that which is without consciousness? That which is without consciousness is the acquisition of alms-bowls (*paḍiggaha*), robes (*vattha*), blankets (*kambala*), and brooms (*pāyapuñchaṇa*); that is what is without consciousness. What is that which is mixed? That which is mixed is the acquisition of disciples and female disciples together with their belongings, vessels, and requisites (*sabhaṇḍamattōvagaraṇa*); that is what is mixed. That is the supramundane. That is the substance-acquisition (*davvāē*) distinct from the body of the knower and the body of the future being. That is substance-acquisition by way of non-scriptural knowledge (*nōāgamaō*). That is substance-acquisition.

What is that which is by way of disposition (*bhāvāē*)? Disposition is declared to be of two kinds: that which is by way of scripture (*āgamaō*) and that which is not by way of scripture (*nōāgamaō*). What is that which is by way of scripture? Disposition by way of scripture is one who knows [the teaching] and is currently engaged in it; that is disposition by way of scripture. What is that which is not by way of scripture? Disposition not by way of scripture is declared to be of two kinds: the commendable (*pasatthē*) and the non-commendable (*apasatthē*). What is the commendable? The commendable is declared to be threefold: knowledge (*nāṇāē*), vision (*daṁsaṇāē*), and conduct (*carittāē*); that is the commendable. What is the non-commendable? The non-commendable is declared to be fourfold: anger (*kōhāē*), pride (*māṇāē*), deceit (*māyāē*), and greed (*lōbhāē*); that is the non-commendable. That is disposition not by way of scripture; that is disposition. That is acquisition (*āē*).

What is that which is called effacement (*jhavaṇā*)? Effacement is declared to be fourfold, namely: name-effacement (*nāmajjhavaṇā*), representation-effacement (*ṭhavaṇajjhavaṇā*), substance-effacement (*davvajjhavaṇā*), and state-effacement (*bhāvajjhavaṇā*). Name and representation have already been explained. What is that which is called substance-effacement? Substance-effacement is declared to be twofold, namely: from the perspective of scripture (*āgamao*) and from the perspective of non-scripture (*noāgamao*). What is that which is called substance-effacement from the perspective of scripture? Substance-effacement from the perspective of scripture is one for whom the word "effacement" has been studied [but not yet realized], up to that point it is substance-effacement from the perspective of scripture. What is that which is called substance-effacement from the perspective of non-scripture? Substance-effacement from the perspective of non-scripture is the physical body of one who possesses right view, or the physical body of one who is a monk practicing effacement; this is substance-effacement from the perspective of non-scripture. What is that which is called state-effacement? State-effacement is the destruction of the defilements (*kaṣāya*) through the practice of the twelve types of asceticism (*pariṣaha*). This is state-effacement. What is that which is called the fruit of effacement? The fruit of effacement is the destruction of all karma. This is the fruit of effacement. This is the fifth lesson on the fruits of the vows. End of the fifth lesson. End of the second chapter on the fruits of the vows. End of the *Daśavaikālika-sūtra*. What is non-scriptural (nō-āgama) destruction of matter (*davvajjhavaṇā*)? Non-scriptural destruction of matter is declared to be threefold, namely: destruction of matter pertaining to the body of the knower (*jāṇagasarīra-davvajjhavaṇā*), destruction of matter pertaining to the body of the potential being (*bhaviya-sarīra-davvajjhavaṇā*), and destruction of matter distinct from the bodies of both the knower and the potential being (*jāṇagasarīra-bhaviya-sarīra-vatirittā davvajjhavaṇā*). What is the destruction of matter pertaining to the body of the knower? The destruction of matter pertaining to the body of the knower is the body of one who knows the subject matter of the term "destruction" (*jhavaṇā*); it is that which is devoid of death, fallen away, and cast off, just as in the case of the destruction of matter (*davvajjhayaṇā*). [This continues] until: that is the [destruction of matter pertaining to the body of the knower]. What is the destruction of matter pertaining to the body of the potential being? It is as follows: those souls who have emerged from the womb and birth; the rest is just as in the case of the destruction of matter (*davvajjhayaṇā*), until: that is the [destruction of matter pertaining to the body of the potential being].

What is that which is the substantial reduction (davvajjhavaṇā) distinct from the bodies of the knower and the future body? Just as the substantial [reduction] was described as being distinct from the bodies of the knower and the future body, so it should be stated up until: "That is the mixed; that is the supramundane. That is the substantial reduction distinct from the bodies of the knower and the future body. That is the substantial reduction from the non-scriptural perspective (nōōgamaō). That is the substantial reduction.

What is that which is the reduction of states (bhāvajjhavaṇā)? The reduction of states is declared to be twofold: namely, the reduction of states from the scriptural perspective (āgamaō) and the reduction of states from the non-scriptural perspective (nōāgamaō).

What is that which is the subsidence of passions through scripture (*āgamato bhāvajjhavaṇā*)? It is when one who possesses knowledge is engaged [in it]; that is the subsidence of passions through scripture. What is that which is the subsidence of passions not through scripture (*nōāgamato bhāvajjhavaṇā*)? The subsidence of passions not through scripture is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the commendable (*pasatthā*) and the non-commendable (*apasatthā*).

What is the commendable? The commendable is declared to be of four kinds, namely: the subsidence of anger (*kōhajjhavaṇā*), the subsidence of pride (*māṇajjhavaṇā*), the subsidence of deceit (*māyajjhavaṇā*), and the subsidence of greed (*lōbhajjhavaṇā*); that is the commendable.

What is that which is censurable? Censurable [states] are declared to be threefold, namely: the descent into knowledge (*nāṇajjhavaṇā*), the descent into vision (*daṁsaṇajjhavaṇā*), and the descent into conduct (*carittajjhavaṇā*). This is that which is censurable; this is that which is the descent into states not derived from scripture (*nōāgamaō bhāvajjhavaṇā*); this is that which is the descent into states (*bhāvajjhavaṇā*); this is that which is the descent (*jhavaṇā*); this is that which is produced by the *ōha* (compendium).

What is that which is produced by name (*nāmanippanna*)? That which is produced by name—right conduct (*sāmāiya*)—is taught to be fourfold in brief, namely: right conduct by name (*nāmasāmāiya*), right conduct by representation (*ṭhavaṇasāmāiya*), right conduct as substance (*davvasāmāiya*), and right conduct as state (*bhāvasāmāiya*). Name and representation have been explained; right conduct as substance is likewise, up to: "that is right conduct as substance pertaining to the body of one destined for liberation (*bhaviyasarīradavvasāmāiya*)."

What is that? It is the substantial equanimity (dravyasāmāyika) distinct from the body of the knower and the body of one who will become [an omniscient being]. What is the substantial equanimity distinct from the body of the knower and the body of one who will become [an omniscient being]? It is that which is written on palm leaves or in books. That is the substantial equanimity distinct from the body of the knower and the body of one who will become [an omniscient being]. That is substantial equanimity from the perspective of non-scriptural authority (noāgama). That is substantial equanimity.

What is that which is called equanimity of disposition (*bhāvasāmāiya*)? Equanimity of disposition is declared to be of two kinds, namely: through scripture (*āgama*) and not through scripture (*no-āgama*). What is equanimity of disposition through scripture? Equanimity of disposition through scripture is one who knows [the teaching] and is engaged [in it]. That is equanimity of disposition through scripture. What is equanimity of disposition not through scripture? Equanimity of disposition not through scripture—
He whose self is equanimous in self-restraint, observance, and austerity—for him there is equanimity (sāmāyika); thus it was spoken by the Kevalin. (Āvaśyakaniryukti 330)
He who is equal toward all beings, both those that move and those that are stationary, possesses equanimity (*sāmāyika*); thus it has been spoken by the Kevalins.
(Āvaśyaka Niryukti 331)

Just as suffering is not dear to me, knowing that it is exactly the same for all living beings, he neither kills nor causes others to kill; because he conducts himself with equanimity, he is a *śramaṇa*. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 332)
He has no partiality toward anyone, nor any greater affection for any; he is equal toward all living beings.
By this, he becomes a śramaṇa; this is another aspect [of his nature]. (Aṇuogaddārā 333)
He who is like a serpent, a mountain, fire, the ocean, the surface of the sky, and a multitude of trees;
and who is like a bee, a deer, the earth, a lotus, the sun, and the wind—he is a śramaṇa.
(Āvaśyaka Niryukti 334)
That ascetic is truly a śramaṇa if he is well-minded and does not become evil-minded in his disposition;
if he is equal toward kinsmen and strangers alike, and equal in both honor and dishonor. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 335)
That is non-scriptural substance-equanimity. That is substance-equanimity. That is equanimity. That is what is produced by name.

What, then, is that which is accomplished through the arrangement of sutras and phrases (*suttālāvaganipphanna*)? Regarding the accomplishment through the arrangement of sutras and phrases, one now desires the exposition (*nikkheva*). Why is it not expounded here, even though it possesses the characteristics [of being explained]? For the sake of brevity (*lāghavattha*); for this reason, since there is the third section on the "Comprehension" (*anugama*) in the *Anuyogadvāra*, when it is expounded there, it becomes expounded here; or when it is expounded here, it becomes expounded there. Therefore, it is not expounded here; it will be expounded in that very place. This is the exposition (*nikkheva*).

What is that which is the method of following (anugama)? The method of following is declared to be twofold, namely: the method of following the Sūtra (suttānugama) and the method of following the Nijjutti (nijjuttianugama). What is that which is the method of following the Nijjutti? The method of following the Nijjutti is declared to be threefold, namely: the method of following the Nijjutti of the headings (nikkheva), the method of following the Nijjutti of the introduction (uvagghāya), and the method of following the Nijjutti that touches upon the Sūtra (suttaphāsiya).

What is that which follows the exposition and etymological analysis (*nikkheva-nijjuttianugama*)? When the exposition and etymological analysis have been followed, that is the exposition and etymological analysis.

What is that which follows the introductory etymological analysis (*uvagghāya-nijjuttianugama*)? The introductory etymological analysis is to be understood by means of these two summary verses (*dāragāhā*), as follows:
[The two summary verses follow.]
In the enumeration, the detailed exposition, the derivation, the field, the time, the person,
the cause, the condition, the characteristic, the method, the application, and the inference. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 338)
What [is it], of how many kinds, for whom, where, in which [substances], how, for how long a time does it exist?
What is the interval, what is the uninterrupted [state], what is the extraction from existence (*bhava-ākarṣa*), what is contact (*sparśana*), and what is the etymological definition (*nirukti*)?
(Aṇuogaddārā 339)
Thus ends the introduction to the *Niryukti-anugama*.

What then is the sequential commentary on the Niryukti of the Sūtra-phāṣiya? First, the Sūtra must be recited—unerring, unconfused, not jumbled, complete, with a full resonance of voice, released from the throat and lips, and received through the oral instruction of the Guru. Then, therein one will recognize whether it is a term of one's own doctrine (sasamaya), a term of another's doctrine (parasamaya), a term concerning bondage (bandha), a term concerning liberation (mokṣa), a term of equanimity (sāmāiya), or a term of non-equanimity (nosāmāiya). Once that has been recited, for some Blessed Ones certain subject matters are already mastered, while for others certain [matters] are not yet mastered. Therefore, for the sake of mastering those subjects that have not yet been mastered, I shall explain word by word.

Know that the sixfold characteristic consists of: the *saṃhitā*, the word (*pada*), the meaning of the word (*padattha*), the analysis of the word (*padaviggaha*), the examination (*cālaṇā*), and the established conclusion (*pasiddhī*). (Aṇuogaddārā 341)
This is the sequential exposition of the Nijjutti-commentary on the Sutta-text; this is the Nijjutti-anugama; this is the Anugama.

What is that? [It is] the "new" (naya). Seven root standpoints (*mūlanaya*) are taught, namely: Naigama, Saṅgraha, Vyavahāra, Rjusūtra, Śabda, Samabhirūḍha, and Evambhūta. Therein— He measures by means of many measures; this is the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of Naigama.

Now listen as I shall explain the characteristic of the remaining viewpoints (nayās) as well. (Anuyogadvāra 344) They say that the "comprehensive statement" (saṅgrahavayana) expresses the summarized and condensed meaning in brief.
Legal procedure proceeds by determining the meaning with respect to all substances.
(Āvaśyaka-niryukti 345) The method of the *ṛjusūtra* perspective should be understood as grasping only the present.

The *naya* called Śabda desires [the object] to be even more specifically determined as it exists in the present. In the *naya* called Samabhirūḍha, there is a transition from a substance (*vatthu*) to a non-substance (*avatthu*). Aṇuogaddārāim 346.

The *evambhūta* [naya] distinguishes between the word, the meaning, and both together. (Aṇuogaddārā 347) — Regarding the object that is to be grasped and that which is not to be grasped... (Aṇuogaddārā 348)
"The teaching that 'one must indeed strive'— that is called the *naya*. (Aṇuogaddārāim 348) Having heard the manifold discourse of all the *nayās*, [one should understand them].
That which is pure through all perspectives (nayas) is the ascetic who is established in conduct and virtue. (Aṇuogaddārā 349)
This concludes the section on Naya.
